paragraphs: Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil brought an army chroniclers put in the tens of thousands, with roughly a hundred siege engines, against a garrison of a few thousand defenders when he reached Acre in April 1291. Qalawun, his father, had begun assembling the force the year before and died before he could lead it himself.

The walls, breached in several places after weeks of bombardment, gave way on 18 May. Most of the remaining Templars died defending their fortress by the harbour days later, and the fall of Acre, after a century as the kingdom's capital, ended organised Crusader rule on the Levantine mainland.

American and British forces began bombing Taliban and al-Qaeda targets across Afghanistan on 7 October 2001, less than a month after the September 11 attacks. The Taliban government had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, whom it was sheltering, and Kabul fell to opposition Northern Alliance forces backed by American air power within weeks.

The campaign scattered al-Qaeda's leadership into the mountains along the Pakistani border but did not capture bin Laden, who evaded American forces at Tora Bora that December. The war outlasted every other American conflict of the era, continuing for nearly two decades until the last troops withdrew in August 2021.

Gnaeus Julius Agricola governed Roman Britain from 78 CE and spent several campaigning seasons pushing north through territory no Roman army had held before, building forts as far as the Moray Firth. The one named battle, Mons Graupius in 83, is recorded only because Agricola's son in law, the historian Tacitus, wrote his biography; no other source survives, and its location has never been identified.

Tacitus put Calgacus's dead at 10,000 against 360 Roman losses, a lopsided figure treated with suspicion since Tacitus wrote to praise his father in law. He also gave Calgacus a speech condemning Roman conquest as robbery dressed up as peace, almost certainly his own invention. Rome never occupied the far north permanently, and Agricola was recalled soon after the battle.

Airlangga survived the destruction of the Medang court around 1006, when a rival ruler's raid killed his father in law, King Dharmawangsa, and scattered the royal family. He escaped into the forest with a single loyal follower and lived for years as an ascetic before local lords began rallying to him as the surviving legitimate heir.

By 1019 he had gathered enough support to be installed as king, and over the following decades he rebuilt a functioning state around Kahuripan in eastern Java, restoring irrigation works and river trade along the Brantas. Near the end of his reign he divided the kingdom between his sons, an act later Javanese chronicles remember as the origin of the rival states of Janggala and Kediri.

Aksum, centred in the highlands of what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, controlled the Red Sea port of Adulis and grew rich taxing goods moving between Africa, Arabia and the Mediterranean. Nubia, further up the Nile around Meroe, sat on a different set of trade routes into the African interior, and the two states pressed against each other along the middle Nile.

A Ge'ez inscription attributed to the Aksumite king Ezana records a campaign against the Noba and Kasu peoples of the Nile valley, describing burned towns and captured cattle and grain. The inscription is one of the few written accounts from either side, and it lines up with the archaeological collapse of Meroitic power in the fourth century.

Alauddin Khalji took the Delhi throne in 1296 after murdering his uncle and predecessor, Jalaluddin, then spent much of his reign fighting Mongol raiders pressing in from the northwest. His generals repelled several separate invasions in the early 1300s, at one point defeating a Mongol force outside Delhi itself.

Southward, Alauddin sent his general Malik Kafur on campaigns that reached as far as the Pandya kingdom in the far south, extracting tribute from Hindu kingdoms including Devagiri and Warangal rather than annexing most of them outright. He also imposed strict price controls and market regulation across his territory, a rare instance of a medieval Indian ruler managing an economy at that scale.

Pope Innocent III had tried preaching and diplomacy against Cathar belief in Languedoc for years before the murder of his legate, Pierre de Castelnau, in January 1208 gave him cause for war instead. He called for a crusade against the region's own Christian nobility, offering the usual crusader indulgences and, more pointedly, a claim on Cathar-tolerating lords' lands to any northern noble willing to fight.

Simon de Montfort emerged as the crusade's leading commander, and the campaign became known for massacres such as Béziers in 1209, where the killing reportedly spared neither Cathars nor Catholics sheltering with them. The fighting dragged on for two decades, ending with the south's great lordships absorbed into the French crown's territory rather than left independent.

At Gaugamela in 331 BCE, Darius III chose a flat plain near modern Erbil and even had it levelled for his chariots and elephants, expecting his far larger army to overwhelm Alexander in open ground. Alexander answered by pulling his flanks back at an angle and punching a wedge of cavalry through the gap it opened in the Persian line.

Darius fled the field before the battle was fully decided, and his own governors turned on him within two years. Alexander took the Persian capitals of Babylon, Susa and Persepolis with little further resistance, ending the Achaemenid Empire that had ruled from Egypt to the Indus for two centuries.

Alfred, king of Wessex, took London from Viking control in 886, more than a decade after the city had fallen under Danish rule during the wars that followed the great heathen army's invasion of England. Rather than simply garrison the existing town, Alfred had it refortified and partly rebuilt within the old Roman walls, moving settlement away from the exposed riverside.

He then handed the city to his son in law, Aethelred of Mercia, tying the two remaining English kingdoms together against further Danish attack. The move is treated as a marker of Alfred's wider claim to speak for the English people rather than for Wessex alone, a claim later charters and chroniclers built on when they began calling him king of the Anglo Saxons.

The Front de Liberation Nationale coordinated a wave of over thirty bombings and attacks on police, military and infrastructure targets across Algeria on 1 November 1954, an operation later called Toussaint Rouge after the All Saints holiday it fell on. French authorities initially dismissed it as banditry rather than the start of an organised independence movement.

The war that followed drew in French conscripts, colonial settlers and Algerian civilians alike, and became infamous for the widespread use of torture by French forces and terror bombings by the FLN. France granted Algeria independence in 1962 after eight years of fighting that killed several hundred thousand people, and roughly a million French settlers left the country within months.

At 4:30am on 12 April 1861, Confederate batteries under General Pierre Beauregard opened fire on Fort Sumter, a Union garrison on an island in Charleston harbour commanded by Major Robert Anderson. The fort held out for roughly 34 hours of bombardment before Anderson surrendered it. No one on either side was killed in the exchange itself.

Lincoln had refused to abandon the fort and answered the attack by calling for 75,000 volunteers, which pushed four more slave states into the Confederacy rather than the Union. The war that followed lasted four years, and the number of soldiers who died in it, estimated at over 600,000, remains the deadliest in American history.

British troops marched out of Boston before dawn on 19 April 1775 to seize colonial arms stored at Concord. At Lexington, they found a small militia company already assembled on the green; a shot was fired from an unknown side, and volleys followed that killed eight militiamen. Nobody at the time could say who fired first.

At Concord's North Bridge, colonial militia returned fire and forced the British column back toward Boston, harried the entire way by musket fire from behind walls and trees. British casualties for the day ran close to 300, more than three times the colonial losses, and the fighting persuaded thousands of New England militia to besiege Boston within days.

An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent who had risen high in Tang favour, declared himself emperor of a rival state at Luoyang in December 755 and marched on the Tang capitals. The court fled Chang'an, the emperor's favourite concubine Yang Guifei was killed by his own escort at Mawei, and the rebellion dragged on for eight years even after An Lushan's own son had him murdered in 757.

A census taken in 754 counted about 53 million people in Tang territory; one taken a decade later found under 17 million. Scholars now doubt the gap measures deaths directly, since the war also shattered the census system itself, but even cautious estimates put the toll in the tens of millions. Tang China never fully recovered its central authority over its provinces afterward.

Roman administration had withdrawn from Britain by 410, and the historian Bede, writing three centuries later, describes Angles, Saxons and Jutes crossing from what is now northern Germany and Denmark, first as hired soldiers and then as settlers. Archaeology shows the movement was gradual, spread over generations rather than a single crossing in 449.

The newcomers established small kingdoms across eastern and southern England, Kent, Wessex, Mercia and others, while Latin and British Celtic speech retreated westward into Wales and Cornwall. Old English, the language that grew from their dialects, is the direct ancestor of modern English, and place names ending in -ham or -ton still mark where these early settlements stood.

Portugal granted Angola independence on 11 November 1975, and the three movements that had fought Portuguese rule immediately turned on each other: the MPLA in Luanda, UNITA in the south and centre, and the FNLA in the north. Cuba sent troops to back the MPLA within weeks of independence, and South Africa moved forces in to support UNITA.

The war outlasted the Cold War that had fed it. Soviet arms and Cuban soldiers kept the MPLA government in power through the 1980s while the United States and South Africa funded Jonas Savimbi's UNITA, and fighting continued after both foreign patrons withdrew, ending only with Savimbi's death in combat in 2002, twenty seven years after independence.

Crusader forces reached Antioch in October 1097 and found a city too large to fully encircle, ringed by walls that ran for miles over hills and along the Orontes river. The siege dragged into 1098, with the besiegers themselves running short of food, until an Armenian guard named Firuz, holding a tower, agreed to let a party climb in by night.

Antioch fell in June 1098, but a relieving army under Kerbogha arrived within days and trapped the crusaders inside the same walls they had just taken. A sortie led by Bohemond of Taranto broke the siege, and Bohemond kept the city for himself rather than handing it to Byzantium as earlier crusader oaths had promised, founding the Principality of Antioch.

Voting ran from 26 to 29 April 1994, and queues of South Africans of every race stretched for hours outside polling stations, some voting for the first time in their lives. Nelson Mandela, released from prison in 1990 after 27 years, led the African National Congress to victory and was inaugurated president on 10 May.

The election closed a system of racial law that had assigned people to residential areas, jobs and schools by classification since 1948. F.W. de Klerk, the last apartheid president, became Mandela's deputy in a government of national unity, a deliberate arrangement meant to hold the transition together rather than settle old scores at once.

Amr ibn al-As led an Arab army into Egypt in 639 with a force small enough that the Byzantine governor at first dismissed it as a raid rather than an invasion. After sieges of Babylon fortress and Alexandria, Egypt's Byzantine garrison surrendered by treaty in 641, ending direct Greco-Roman administration of the Nile valley that had run continuously since Alexander's conquest nearly a thousand years before.

Amr founded a new garrison town, Fustat, on the site that would grow into Cairo, and Egypt's Coptic Christian population, many of whom had chafed under Byzantine religious policy, initially found Arab rule less intrusive. Conversion to Islam and the spread of Arabic as an administrative language followed over the next several centuries rather than at once.

The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, fled from battle to battle for years after his armies collapsed at Qadisiyyah and Nahavand before Arab Muslim forces. In 651 he was murdered near Merv, reportedly by a miller who wanted his belongings and did not know who he was, ending a dynasty that had ruled Persia for over four centuries.

The conquest brought Persia into the caliphate but did not erase it. Persian administrators, coinage practices and court customs were absorbed into Muslim rule almost wholesale, and Persian soon became one of the great languages of Islamic scholarship and government. Zoroastrian communities survived, some fleeing to India, where their descendants remain known as Parsis.

A Tunisian street vendor named Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire on 17 December 2010 after officials confiscated his goods, and his death weeks later helped trigger protests that drove President Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali from power that January. Demonstrations spread rapidly to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Syria and Bahrain within weeks.

Egypt's Hosni Mubarak resigned in February 2011 after eighteen days of protest in Tahrir Square, but the wave's outcomes diverged sharply elsewhere. Libya and Syria fell into prolonged civil war, Yemen's transition unravelled into conflict, and only Tunisia sustained a working democratic transition through the following decade.

Governor Martin Garcia Onez de Loyola travelled south with only about fifty soldiers and camped for the night at Curalaba without setting proper watch. Mapuche fighters under the toqui Pelantaru, aware of the party's presence, staged a night ambush with several hundred warriors and killed the governor along with almost his entire escort.

News of a dead Spanish governor triggered a coordinated uprising across the region south of the Bio Bio river, planned in advance by the leader Paillamachu. Spanish towns and forts there were destroyed within a few years, and Chilean historians generally mark this defeat as the end of the original conquest period south of the river.

Franz Ferdinand's car took a wrong turn onto Franz Josef Street on the morning of 28 June 1914, straight past Gavrilo Princip, who had given up after an earlier bomb attempt that morning missed the archduke's car. Princip fired twice from close range, hitting the archduke in the neck and his wife Sophie in the abdomen. Both died within the hour.

Princip was nineteen, a member of the Bosnian Serb group Young Bosnia, and too young under Austro-Hungarian law to face execution. He was sentenced to twenty years and died of tuberculosis in an Austrian prison fortress in 1918, months before the war his shot had begun finally ended.

On the night of 24 April 1915, Ottoman authorities arrested several hundred Armenian intellectuals, clergy and community leaders in Constantinople and had most of them killed. That arrest, still marked as the genocide's anniversary, opened a campaign of deportation and massacre carried out under cover of the First World War against Armenians across Anatolia.

Men were typically separated and shot outright. Women, children and the elderly were marched south toward the Syrian desert with little food or water, and death squads and Kurdish militias attacked the convoys along the way. Talat Pasha's interior ministry directed the deportation orders. Survivors scattered into exile communities across the Middle East, Europe and the Americas.

Akwamu had grown rich taxing the coastal trade routes between the Gold Coast's forts and the interior, but its ruling class was split by succession disputes when Asante forces moved against it in 1717. The Asante campaign broke Akwamu's hold on those routes within a matter of months.

The victory gave Asante direct access to European trading posts at the coast and to the gold and captives that funded further expansion under successive Asantehene rulers. Displaced Akwamu groups resettled further east, some founding new states, while Asante went on to dominate the Gold Coast's interior trade for the rest of the century.

Osei Tutu built the Asante state around 1701 by uniting several Akan groups under a shared Golden Stool, and its army grew around a core of musketeers supplied through coastal trade with Europeans in exchange for gold and captives. Unlike many neighbouring forces, Asante fielded standing regiments rather than gathering levies only for a campaign.

That standing army let Asante defeat the rival Denkyira state within a few years of its founding and then extend authority over much of the Gold Coast's interior trade routes. Firearms bought with gold bought more gold, a cycle that made Asante the dominant regional power for the next century.

On 13 May 1981, as Pope John Paul II rode through a crowded St Peter's Square in an open jeep, Mehmet Ali Agca fired several shots from a semi-automatic pistol, hitting the Pope in the abdomen, hand and arm. Surgeons operated for more than five hours and removed part of his intestine; he lost nearly three quarters of his blood before reaching the operating table.

Agca, a Turkish far right militant, had escaped from prison after an earlier murder and crossed several countries before Rome. Theories linking the shooting to Bulgarian or Soviet intelligence, aired at a lengthy 1980s trial, never produced a conviction. In 1983, John Paul visited Agca in his Italian prison cell and told reporters he had forgiven him.

On 30 March 1981, John Hinckley Jr. fired six shots at President Reagan as he left a speaking engagement at the Washington Hilton, hoping the act would impress the actress Jodie Foster, whom he had never met. One bullet ricocheted off the presidential limousine and struck Reagan under his left arm, collapsing a lung close to his heart.

Press secretary James Brady was shot in the head and left permanently disabled, and a Secret Service agent and a police officer were also wounded. Reagan underwent emergency surgery and was back at the White House within two weeks. Hinckley was found not guilty by reason of insanity, a verdict that prompted several US states to tighten their insanity defence laws.

Alexander II had survived at least five earlier attempts on his life, including a mine under a train and a dining-room bomb, by the time the radical group Narodnaya Volya struck again on 1 March 1881 in St Petersburg. A first bomb thrown at his carriage wounded a Cossack guard and a bystander; the Tsar, unhurt, stepped out to check on the wounded.

A second attacker, Ignacy Hryniewiecki, threw a bomb at his own feet as Alexander approached, killing himself and fatally wounding the Tsar, who died within the hour. He had freed Russia's serfs in 1861 and was weighing further constitutional reforms; his son Alexander III responded instead with repression, reversing much of the liberalising course his father had begun.

Charles Guiteau had campaigned for James Garfield with a single, badly received speech and then bombarded the White House and State Department with letters demanding a consulship as repayment. Turned away repeatedly, he bought a revolver, practised firing it, and shot Garfield in the back at a Washington railway station on 2 July 1881 while the president waited for a train.

Garfield did not die immediately; he lingered for eleven weeks while doctors probed the wound with unsterilised fingers and instruments, likely worsening the infection that eventually killed him that September. Guiteau was hanged in 1882 insisting his act was divinely ordered. The killing of a president by a spurned office-seeker gave Congress the push it needed to pass the Pendleton Civil Service Act in 1883.

On the morning of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was walking through the garden of her New Delhi residence toward an interview with the actor Peter Ustinov when two of her own Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, opened fire on her at close range. She was hit more than thirty times and died at the hospital that afternoon.

The killing came four months after Gandhi had ordered Indian troops into the Golden Temple in Amritsar to remove armed Sikh separatists sheltering inside the shrine, an operation that killed hundreds and outraged Sikhs worldwide. Her assassination set off anti-Sikh riots across northern India in which mobs killed thousands of Sikhs over the following days, an outbreak of violence that later inquiries found police in Delhi did little to stop.

William McKinley was greeting the public in a receiving line at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo on 6 September 1901 when Leon Czolgosz, an unemployed factory worker drawn to anarchist ideas, approached with a revolver wrapped in a handkerchief to hide it and fired twice at close range.

McKinley lingered for eight days before dying of gangrene from a wound doctors never fully located, since the exposition's new x-ray machine, on display nearby, was not used to search for the bullet. Czolgosz was executed within six weeks. Vice President Theodore Roosevelt, at 42 the youngest man to hold the office, was sworn in the same day McKinley died.

The bomb, nicknamed Fat Man, was not aimed at Nagasaki by design. The primary target that morning, 9 August 1945, was Kokura, but cloud and smoke over the city forced the crew of the B-29 Bockscar to divert to the secondary target. Nagasaki itself was obscured by cloud until a brief gap opened over the Urakami valley, an industrial district some distance from the city centre, where the bomb detonated.

The plutonium core produced a blast roughly a third larger than Hiroshima's, but Nagasaki's hills contained much of the damage to that valley. Estimates of the dead by the end of 1945 range from about 40,000 to 75,000, with many more dying later of burns and radiation sickness. Japan's Supreme War Council agreed to surrender terms six days later.

By 451 Attila had already extracted decades of tribute from Constantinople and ruled a confederation stretching from the Rhine to the steppe beyond the Black Sea. He turned west that year with a coalition of Huns and subject peoples, sacking cities across Gaul including Metz before moving on Orleans.

The Roman general Aetius answered by assembling an unlikely alliance of Visigoths, Franks and other former enemies of Rome. The armies met near Chalons at the Catalaunian Plains, where Attila's advance stopped for the first time. He survived the battle and invaded Italy the following year instead, but Gaul itself was not overrun.

Attila led the Huns across the Rhine into Gaul in early 451, burning towns including Metz and pressing as far as Orleans before an unusual alliance turned against him. The Roman general Aetius joined forces with the Visigothic king Theodoric, his own longstanding enemy, because a Hunnic victory threatened both of them equally.

The armies met at the Catalaunian Plains, probably near modern Chalons, in a battle so large that ancient accounts describe streams running with blood, a detail impossible to verify but repeated by several chroniclers. Theodoric was killed, yet the coalition held and Attila withdrew from Gaul. He invaded Italy the following year instead, but never again threatened the west on the same scale.

Aurangzeb moved his court to the Deccan in 1681 and stayed there for the rest of his reign, determined to absorb the last independent sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda and to break the rising Maratha power under descendants of Shivaji. Mughal armies took Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687, ending both kingdoms outright.

The Marathas refused to fight the kind of set battles the Mughals wanted, instead raiding supply lines and melting into hill country the imperial cavalry struggled to hold. The campaign consumed Mughal treasury and manpower for twenty five years without ever pacifying the region, and Aurangzeb was still fighting it when he died in 1707.

Aurelian became emperor in 270 with Rome split into three pieces: a Gallic Empire in the west, a Palmyrene Empire under Zenobia in the east, and a shrunken centre barely holding Italy and the Balkans. He spent four years marching against both breakaway states rather than negotiating with either.

At Immae and Emesa in 272 he broke Zenobia's forces and took Palmyra, and in 274 he defeated the Gallic emperor Tetricus at Chalons. Coins afterward called him restitutor orbis, restorer of the world. He was murdered by his own officers in 275, less than a year after the reunification he had spent his reign forcing through.

Prussia's chancellor Otto von Bismarck manoeuvred Austria into war in June 1866 over control of Schleswig and Holstein, territory the two powers had jointly seized from Denmark only two years before. Most other German states sided with Austria, expecting a long, evenly matched fight between the two great German powers.

Prussia's army, reorganised around railways, telegraphs and the breech loading Dreyse rifle, won the decisive battle at Koniggratz on 3 July after barely seven weeks of campaigning. Austria was forced out of German affairs entirely, and Bismarck used the quick, cheap victory to fold the northern German states into a Prussian led confederation within a year.

Ayutthaya had been Siam's capital since 1351 and, by the 1760s, one of the largest cities in Southeast Asia, its canals lined with temples and foreign trading houses from Portugal, Japan and the Dutch Republic. A Burmese army under King Hsinbyushin besieged it for over a year before breaching the walls on 7 April 1767.

The city was burned, its libraries, temple archives and royal chronicles destroyed, and much of the population marched off to Burma as captives. A former provincial governor, Taksin, gathered surviving forces and founded a new Siamese capital at Thonburi within the year, later moved across the river to become modern Bangkok.

Saladin had gone to Egypt as a lieutenant to his uncle Shirkuh, serving the last Fatimid caliph as vizier almost by circumstance after Shirkuh's sudden death in 1169. When the caliph al-Adid died in September 1171, Saladin simply stopped naming him in Friday prayers, ending the two-century-old Shia Fatimid caliphate without a battle and restoring Sunni allegiance to the Abbasids in Baghdad.

He still nominally served the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din in Syria, but after Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 Saladin moved to bring Damascus and eventually most of Syria under his own family's rule, founding the Ayyubid dynasty. That combined base in Egypt and Syria gave him the resources, over the following decade, to face the crusader kingdoms directly rather than fight them piecemeal.

Montezuma I, known also as Moctezuma Ilhuicamina, ruled Tenochtitlan from 1440 and pushed the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan well beyond the Valley of Mexico. Campaigns reached toward the Gulf coast and south into the Mixtec and Oaxaca regions, bringing tribute in cotton, cacao and feathers back to the capital.

Conquered towns generally kept their own rulers and religion, paying tribute rather than being absorbed outright, which let the Alliance expand quickly without governing every new subject directly. This tribute economy, built largely under Montezuma I, financed the temples and causeways that later astonished the Spanish when they reached Tenochtitlan in 1519.

Nebuchadnezzar's army had already deported Jerusalem's elite once, in 597 BC, after an earlier revolt. When Judah's king Zedekiah rebelled again, the Babylonians returned, besieged the city for months, and in 586 BC breached its walls, burned the Temple built under Solomon, and tore down its treasures.

The deportations that followed sent priests, officials and craftsmen to live in Babylon itself, where a captive community kept its own laws and records. That exile lasted until the Persian king Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC and allowed the exiles to return, an episode that later shaped how Jewish identity was written and remembered outside the land it started in.

A suicide bomber walked into Paddy's Pub on Kuta's tourist strip on 12 October 2002 and detonated a vest bomb, driving survivors into the street outside Sari Club, where a much larger car bomb went off seconds later. Most of the dead were foreign tourists, many of them young Australians on holiday. The bombers belonged to Jemaah Islamiyah, a regional network with links to al-Qaeda.

Police traced the attack through a chassis number recovered from the wrecked van and arrested Amrozi bin Nurhasyim within weeks. He, his brother Ali Imron, and field commander Imam Samudra were convicted; Samudra and two others were executed by firing squad in 2008. Spiritual leader Abu Bakar Bashir was given a shorter sentence on lesser charges. Bali's tourism economy took years to recover.

The war began on 26 March 1971, when Pakistan's army launched a crackdown on Bengali nationalists in Dhaka after the Awami League won elections the Pakistani military government refused to honour. Bengali fighters, the Mukti Bahini, waged a guerrilla resistance for months while millions of refugees crossed into India.

India entered directly on 3 December 1971 after Pakistan struck Indian airbases, and its forces advanced alongside the Mukti Bahini for less than two weeks before the Pakistani garrison in Dhaka surrendered on 16 December. Bangladesh emerged as an independent state from what had been East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by more than a thousand miles of Indian territory.

Simon bar Kokhba led Judean rebels against Rome starting in 132, retaking Jerusalem and minting his own coins as a sign of restored independence. The revolt lasted three years before Hadrian sent additional legions who besieged and starved the rebel strongholds one by one, ending at the fortress of Betar in 135, where bar Kokhba was killed.

The Roman senator Cassius Dio, writing decades later, put the dead at 580,000 with fifty fortresses and nearly a thousand villages razed, and said those lost to famine and disease could not be counted at all. Whatever the true figure, Hadrian renamed the province Syria Palaestina and barred Jews from Jerusalem, ending organised Jewish self rule there for centuries.

American merchant ships in the Mediterranean had paid tribute to the Barbary states of Tripoli, Algiers, Tunis and Morocco since the 1790s to avoid seizure and the enslavement of their crews. In 1801, Tripoli's ruler Yusuf Karamanli raised his demands and declared war after Thomas Jefferson, newly president, refused to pay more.

Jefferson sent a naval squadron to blockade Tripoli, and the war dragged on for four years, including the loss of the frigate Philadelphia and a famous overland march by a small mercenary force to capture the town of Derna in 1805. A treaty that June ended the tribute demands from Tripoli, though Algiers kept exacting payments until a second, shorter war in 1815.

After Kleidion broke Bulgarian resistance, Basil II spent the following years mopping up remaining strongholds rather than pursuing one decisive final battle. By 1018 the last claimants to Samuel's throne had submitted, and Bulgaria, independent for over three centuries, was absorbed directly into Byzantine administration as a province rather than left as a client state.

Basil allowed Bulgarian nobles to keep local privileges and did not impose the harshest terms he might have, a pragmatism that helped the new territory settle quickly under Byzantine rule. The epithet Bulgaroktonos, Bulgar Slayer, attached to him only after his death, and his reign left Byzantium at its largest territorial extent since the seventh century.

Byzantine troops trapped the Bulgarian army in a mountain pass near Kleidion on 29 July 1014 after finding a way around the earthworks Tsar Samuel had built to block it. Samuel escaped, but thousands of his soldiers were captured, and the chronicler John Skylitzes, writing decades later, says Basil II had them blinded, leaving one man in every hundred a single eye so he could lead the rest home.

Skylitzes himself hedged the number at fifteen thousand with the phrase 'as they say', and modern historians treat the figure as likely inflated by later retelling rather than a battlefield count. Samuel is said to have collapsed and died within two days of seeing his blinded men return, and Bulgarian resistance to Basil's advance broke apart within four years.

Fulgencio Batista had already ruled Cuba once, from 1933 to 1944, before retiring to Florida with a fortune. He returned to run for president in 1952, and when polling showed him losing badly, he moved first. On 10 March 1952 army units loyal to him seized barracks, radio stations and the presidential palace before dawn, and President Carlos Prio Socarras fled into exile without a fight.

Batista cancelled the election he was about to lose and ruled instead by decree, courting American business and organised gambling money into Havana. The takeover left no constitutional path back to power for his opponents, which is why a young lawyer named Fidel Castro concluded within weeks that Batista could only be removed by force, and began planning the attack on the Moncada barracks the following year.

Octavian's admiral Agrippa cut off Antony and Cleopatra's fleet's supply lines in the Gulf of Ambracia for months before the fleets finally engaged off Actium on 2 September 31 BCE. Antony's ships were larger but slower, and many were reportedly undermanned after disease and desertion thinned his crews over the blockade.

Cleopatra's squadron withdrew partway through the battle, and Antony followed her rather than staying with his main fleet, which then surrendered. Both fled to Egypt and took their own lives within a year as Octavian's forces closed in, leaving Octavian, later Augustus, the sole ruler of Rome's territories.

Emperor Valens marched out from Adrianople on 9 August 378 without waiting for the reinforcements his nephew Gratian was bringing from the west, confident he could crush the Gothic force alone. Roman cavalry was routed early, and the infantry, packed too tightly to manoeuvre in the summer heat, was surrounded and cut down through the afternoon.

Ancient writers put Roman losses at two thirds of the army, a figure modern historians treat with caution but do not dismiss. Valens died in the fighting, and his body was never recovered; one later account claims he was burned alive in a farmhouse where he had taken shelter. It was the worst defeat suffered by a Roman army since Cannae, and the empire never again fielded an army of that size in the east.

On 25 October 1415, Henry V's army, worn down by dysentery and a march from Harfleur, met a much larger French force on a narrow field near Agincourt. Rain had turned the ploughed ground to mud, and the French men at arms, packed shoulder to shoulder in heavy armour, struggled forward into volleys from English archers stationed on both flanks behind sharpened stakes.

French chroniclers later put their own dead at several thousand, including three dukes and dozens of counts, against a fraction that on the English side. Henry ordered many prisoners killed when he feared a second French attack was forming, a decision that troubled even writers sympathetic to him. Shakespeare's play, written nearly two centuries later, fixed the battle in English memory far beyond its immediate military weight.

Union and Confederate troops fought along Antietam Creek near Sharpsburg, Maryland on 17 September 1862 after a Union soldier found a copy of Lee's marching orders wrapped around some cigars, dropped by a careless courier. Fighting swept through a cornfield, a sunken farm lane later called Bloody Lane, and a stone bridge over the creek.

Roughly 23,000 men were killed, wounded or went missing in a single day, more American casualties than any other day of the Civil War. Lee's outnumbered army held its ground but withdrew into Virginia afterward, and the narrow Union claim to victory gave Lincoln the opening he had been waiting for to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

Napoleon deliberately abandoned high ground near Austerlitz in December 1805 and let his army appear weaker than it was, drawing the combined Austrian and Russian force, led nominally by Tsar Alexander I, into attacking his right flank on ground he had chosen. Fog covered the French centre until the moment it advanced.

French troops split the allied army by taking the Pratzen Heights, then drove retreating Russian units onto frozen lakes where, according to French accounts, artillery fire broke the ice under them. The battle, fought on the first anniversary of Napoleon's coronation, forced Austria out of the war within days and dissolved the coalition that Britain, Austria and Russia had built against France that year.

On 13 August 1704, the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy attacked a Franco-Bavarian army camped along the Danube near the village of Blindheim, from which the English took the name Blenheim. Marshal Tallard had expected the allies to retreat, not to march across open ground and force a fight on his own position.

The French and Bavarian force lost tens of thousands killed, wounded or captured, including Tallard himself, against far lighter allied losses by most accounts. The defeat, the first major one France had suffered in decades, broke the siege on Vienna and ended Louis XIV's hopes of dictating peace. Queen Anne rewarded Marlborough with land at Woodstock, where Blenheim Palace still stands.

Near Leipzig on 17 September 1631, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden brought his army against an Imperial force under Count Tilly that still fought in the massive, slow moving tercio blocks that had dominated European battlefields for a century. Gustavus had reorganised his infantry into smaller, more mobile units and paired them with lighter, faster firing field guns that could be moved during the fighting itself.

Swedish cavalry, trained to charge and fire pistols rather than trot up and wheel away, helped seize Tilly's artillery early in the battle, and the Imperial tercios were ground down once they lost their guns' support. Tilly's army broke apart, and the defeat established Sweden as a major military power in Germany and gave Protestant forces their first significant field victory of the war.

Hitler needed air superiority before any invasion of England could be attempted, so from July 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked shipping, airfields and radar stations, then shifted to London and other cities that September. Fighter Command, guided by radar and a chain of observers, scrambled Hurricanes and Spitfires against formations often several times their number.

By late October the Luftwaffe had lost more aircraft than the RAF and Hitler postponed the invasion, codenamed Operation Sea Lion, indefinitely. Churchill's tribute to the fighter pilots, that never had so much been owed by so many to so few, was delivered in Parliament in August 1940, while the battle was still being fought overhead.

Hitler committed nearly all remaining German reserves to a surprise offensive through the Ardennes on 16 December 1944, aiming to split American and British forces and seize the port of Antwerp before winter cover and low cloud, which grounded Allied aircraft, lifted. Thin American units along the front were overrun in the first days, and the line bulged westward on maps that gave the battle its name.

The Belgian town of Bastogne held out under siege while surrounded, its commander famously replying with a single word, nuts, to a German demand to surrender. Clearing skies around Christmas let Allied aircraft resume attacking German columns, and by late January the offensive had been reversed at a cost of roughly 19,000 American dead, the deadliest single battle the US Army fought in the war.

Colonial militia fortified Breed's Hill, not Bunker Hill itself, overlooking Boston on the night of 16 June 1775, and British commanders chose to dislodge them with a frontal assault rather than cut off their retreat. It took three attempts and heavy losses before the redcoats finally took the position on 17 June, after the defenders ran out of powder.

British casualties, over a thousand killed and wounded, were roughly double the American losses despite the American retreat. Colonel William Prescott is remembered for ordering the defenders not to fire until the whites of the enemy's eyes were visible, though its exact wording and even whether he said it is disputed. The cost convinced British officers that this rebellion would not be put down cheaply.

At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal let his weaker centre bow backward under Roman pressure while his African infantry on the flanks held firm, then closed in on both sides as his cavalry finished encircling the Roman rear. A numerically superior Roman army found itself boxed in on every side at once.

Polybius put Roman dead at around 70,000, Livy nearer 50,000, both writing well after the battle from partisan or secondhand testimony; modern estimates run lower but still count it among the costliest single days in ancient warfare. Rome refused to negotiate afterward and rebuilt its armies rather than seeking terms.

Crassus led roughly 40,000 Roman troops into Mesopotamia in 53 BC seeking the kind of military glory Caesar and Pompey already had, and marched them across open desert rather than following the Euphrates. The Parthian commander Surena met him there with about 10,000 men, most of them horse archers who could outrun and outshoot any formation the legions could form.

Roman shields and formations that worked against infantry gave no protection against arrows fired from every direction, and the legions were worn down over hours rather than broken in one charge. Crassus was killed during a failed attempt to negotiate, and only a fraction of his army made it back to Roman Syria.

Edward III's army, retreating toward Flanders after raiding through Normandy, turned to face a much larger French force near Crecy on 26 August 1346. English longbowmen, positioned on rising ground alongside dismounted knights, loosed volleys fast enough to break repeated charges by French and allied Genoese crossbowmen and cavalry.

Genoese crossbowmen, sent forward first, were cut down by the faster English rate of fire, and successive waves of French cavalry rode over their retreating infantry into the same volleys. French chroniclers put their own dead among the nobility alone at over a thousand, including the king of Bohemia, who fought blind, led into the fray tied to his knights. The longbow's edge over armoured cavalry was a lesson other armies studied for decades.

French commanders chose Dien Bien Phu, a valley near the Laotian border, hoping to lure the Viet Minh into a fight their artillery could win. Viet Minh forces under Vo Nguyen Giap instead hauled heavy guns up surrounding mountains by hand, over trails built for the purpose, and ringed the French garrison before the siege opened on 13 March 1954.

The garrison held out for 56 days before surrendering on 7 May 1954, with roughly 11,000 French and colonial troops taken prisoner. News of the defeat reached the Geneva Conference the next day, where talks on Indochina were already underway, and within weeks France agreed to withdraw, splitting Vietnam at the 17th parallel and ending nearly a century of French colonial rule there.

General Bernard Montgomery took command of Britain's Eighth Army in August 1942 and spent weeks building up tanks, artillery and troops before attacking Erwin Rommel's Panzerarmee Afrika at El Alamein on 23 October. A twelve-day battle of attrition ground down German and Italian forces that had already outrun their fuel supplies.

Rommel, weakened by illness and low on petrol, was ordered by Hitler to hold to the last man but withdrew his surviving forces westward regardless, retreating over 1,500 miles into Tunisia over the following months. Churchill later said that before Alamein the British had not won a battle and after it they had not lost one, a line that overstates the case but captures how the campaign was received at home.

Lee's second invasion of the North collided with the Union Army of the Potomac almost by accident at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania on 1 July 1863, as troops sent to seize supplies ran into Union cavalry. Three days of fighting followed across ridges and farmland south of the town, culminating on 3 July when roughly 12,500 Confederate soldiers crossed open ground in Pickett's Charge into Union artillery and rifle fire.

The charge was repulsed with heavy losses, and Lee withdrew toward Virginia the next day, never again invading the North. Combined casualties over the three days reached about 50,000, the highest of any battle fought on American soil, and the town's residents spent weeks afterward burying the dead and treating the wounded left behind.

The Confederate ironclad CSS Virginia, built on the hull of the scuttled steam frigate Merrimack, sank two wooden Union warships off Hampton Roads, Virginia on 8 March 1862, and cannon fire simply bounced off her sloped iron plating. The Union's own ironclad, USS Monitor, arrived overnight and met her the next morning.

Neither ship could seriously damage the other over about four hours of close-range fighting, and both eventually withdrew, leaving the battle a draw. It was still the first engagement between ironclad ships anywhere, and news of it pushed navies across Europe to speed up their own conversion from wooden fleets to armoured ones.

Vice Admiral Reinhard Scheer took the German High Seas Fleet into the North Sea on 31 May 1916 hoping to isolate and destroy part of Britain's Grand Fleet. Instead he ran into the whole of it under Admiral John Jellicoe. Over roughly twelve hours off the coast of Jutland, Denmark, some 250 ships fired on each other, the only clash between British and German dreadnought battleships of the war.

Germany sank fourteen British ships against eleven of its own and inflicted around 6,800 British casualties to its own 3,058, a result Berlin announced as a victory. Jellicoe's fleet, though bloodied, remained intact and put back to sea within days, while the High Seas Fleet returned to port and largely stayed there. Britain kept its blockade of Germany running for the rest of the war.

Ramesses II led one Egyptian army division into an ambush near Kadesh on the Orontes river in 1274 BCE, after Hittite scouts fed him false information about where Muwatalli II's army actually was. Thousands of Hittite chariots struck the exposed division before the rest of Egypt's forces arrived, and Ramesses's own camp came close to being overrun.

Both sides later claimed victory. Egypt's temple reliefs show Ramesses fighting alone against the odds, while a Hittite account describes Kadesh as a rout of the Egyptians. The stalemate held: roughly fifteen years later the two empires signed one of the earliest surviving peace treaties, its text carved in both Egyptian hieroglyphs and Hittite cuneiform.

On 10 Muharram, 680, a small party travelling with Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, was surrounded on the plain of Karbala by a much larger Umayyad force under Yazid I's governor. Husayn had refused to pledge allegiance to Yazid's rule and was denied access to the Euphrates for days before the fighting began.

Husayn and most of the men with him, reportedly numbering only a few dozen, were killed, and his surviving family were taken captive to Damascus. The day is marked every year as Ashura, and Karbala itself became the site of his shrine and a destination for pilgrimage that has continued for over thirteen centuries.

North Vietnamese artillery began shelling the American Marine combat base at Khe Sanh, near the border with Laos, on 21 January 1968, opening a siege that would last 77 days. Roughly 6,000 Marines and South Vietnamese troops held the base against a force American commanders estimated at two full divisions.

The Pentagon flew in supplies and dropped enormous tonnages of bombs on the surrounding hills under Operation Niagara, and American television crews covered the siege closely alongside the Tet Offensive unfolding elsewhere that same week. The base held until North Vietnamese forces withdrew in April, though American commanders abandoned and dismantled it only months later, a decision that fed public doubt about what the siege had achieved.

Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow met the forces of Mamai, a khan of the Golden Horde, at the Kulikovo field on the Don on 8 September 1380. Dmitry had gathered troops from several rival Russian princes, an unusual union against a common enemy that Russian chronicles later treated as a first step toward a single Russian state.

After hours of close fighting, a flanking charge by a reserve under Vladimir of Serpukhov broke Mamai's line, and Dmitry took the name Donskoy, after the river. The victory did not end Mongol overlordship: two years later a rival khan, Tokhtamysh, sacked Moscow while Dmitry's weakened army could offer little resistance, and tribute continued for another century.

Hitler delayed his 1943 summer offensive against the Kursk salient for weeks, waiting for new Panther and Tiger tanks to reach the front in greater numbers, which let Soviet intelligence learn the attack's location and build deep, layered defences around it. German forces attacked on 5 July into minefields, anti-tank guns and prepared armour that had been waiting for them.

The clash around Prokhorovka on 12 July was long described as the largest tank engagement of the war, though postwar research has revised down the vehicle counts once claimed for it on both sides. Kursk was Germany's last major strategic offensive on the Eastern Front; afterward its forces fought defensively as the Red Army advanced west.

Magyar horsemen besieged Augsburg in August 955, and its bishop Ulrich organised the city's defence while Otto I gathered troops from across the German duchies. Otto reached the Lech river near Augsburg on 10 August and struck the Magyar force while much of it was still scattered raiding the countryside.

Contemporary writers put the Magyar force in the tens of thousands, though such figures are unverifiable this far back. Most of the raiders were killed or captured in the retreat, and several of their leaders were later executed. The defeat ended a half century of Magyar raiding into Germany and Italy, and within decades their descendants had settled permanently in the Carpathian basin as a Christian kingdom.

Around half a million men fought at Leipzig between 16 and 19 October 1813, more than had met on any European battlefield before. Napoleon commanded roughly 185,000 French and allied troops against a coalition of Austrians, Prussians, Russians and Swedes numbering over 300,000, drawn in from three directions around the city.

The four days cost close to 90,000 casualties combined, and a bridge over the Elster was blown prematurely as French troops were still crossing it, drowning many and cutting off a rearguard. Napoleon retreated toward the Rhine with a fraction of the army he had brought into Germany, and Saxony, his last German ally, changed sides within days.

A fleet of the Holy League, ships supplied by Spain, Venice and the Papacy under the command of Don John of Austria, met the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Patras on 7 October 1571. Over two hundred galleys faced a similarly sized Ottoman fleet, and the League's six large galleasses, armed with heavier guns than the galleys around them, broke up the Ottoman formation before the two lines closed for boarding.

Christian accounts from the time claim roughly thirty thousand Ottoman dead or captured against far fewer League losses, and most of the Ottoman fleet was sunk, burned or taken. It was the last major battle fought mainly between oar powered galleys rather than sailing warships, and the Ottomans rebuilt their navy within a year, though it never again threatened the western Mediterranean on the same scale.

Sparta's army had not lost a major land battle in living memory when it met the Thebans on the plain of Leuctra in 371 BC. The Theban commander Epaminondas broke with convention by massing his best troops, the Sacred Band among them, in a deep column on his left, opposite the Spartan king Cleombrotus, instead of spreading his line evenly as custom demanded.

The concentrated Theban wing crushed the Spartan right before the rest of the battle line had properly engaged, and Cleombrotus was killed along with a substantial part of Sparta's citizen soldiers, a class too small to easily replace. Thebes followed the victory by invading the Peloponnese itself and helping Sparta's subject region of Messenia break free, work that undid generations of Spartan dominance in the Greek mainland.

On 25 June 1876, Lieutenant Colonel George Custer split his 7th Cavalry into three columns along the Little Bighorn river in Montana, sending Marcus Reno to attack a Lakota and Cheyenne village he badly underestimated in size. Reno's charge collapsed under return fire, and Custer's own detachment of roughly 210 men, riding on alone, was surrounded on a ridge above the river.

None of the men with Custer survived. Frederick Benteen's column, held back with the pack train, reached only Reno's survivors and dug in on a nearby hill for two more days before the warriors withdrew. Total army losses across the battle came to 268 dead, a defeat that shocked a country then celebrating its centennial.

Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes marched deep into eastern Anatolia in 1071 to confront the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan near the fortress of Manzikert. Part of his army, under a rival commander, withdrew from the field rather than support him, and Romanos was left with a force too depleted to hold.

Romanos was captured, treated courteously by Alp Arslan, and released under a peace agreement, but a Byzantine coup back in Constantinople replaced him before the terms could hold. The empire's eastern border, largely undefended after the defeat, gave way over the following years as Turkish groups moved into Anatolia's interior, a shift that reshaped the region's population for good.

The Athenians did not wait to be besieged. Seeing the Persian force landed at Marathon in 490 BCE, roughly 10,000 Athenian and Plataean hoplites marched out and struck first, thinning their centre and stacking their flanks so the wings closed around the Persian line once the middle gave way.

The story of a runner named Pheidippides racing 42 kilometres to Athens with news of the victory only appears centuries later, in Plutarch, and does not match Herodotus's own account, in which the army itself marched back to Athens to head off a Persian ships heading for the city. The modern marathon race borrows the distance and the legend, not the history.

On 14 June 1800, an Austrian army under General Melas caught Napoleon's forces by surprise near Marengo in Piedmont and pushed the French back for most of the day, to the point that Austrian couriers had already ridden off to report a victory. Napoleon had scattered part of his army to search for the Austrians elsewhere and had to recall it under fire.

General Louis Desaix arrived with fresh troops in the afternoon and led a counterattack that broke the exhausted Austrian line, but he was shot through the chest early in the assault and died within minutes. The victory secured, French control over northern Italy, briefly lost that spring, and let Napoleon return to Paris having reversed a battle he had been on the verge of losing.

On the evening of 2 July 1644, Parliamentarian and Scottish Covenanter forces launched a surprise attack on the Royalist army holding Marston Moor near York, catching Prince Rupert's men before they expected battle that day. Oliver Cromwell's cavalry on the Parliamentarian left broke Rupert's horse, who had built a reputation as unbeatable in the war's earlier campaigns, and Rupert reportedly hid in a bean field afterward.

Royalist infantry, cut off once their cavalry scattered, took the bulk of the casualties, with roughly four thousand killed against a few hundred on the Parliamentarian side by later estimates. The defeat cost the Royalists control of the north of England and gave Cromwell the reputation that carried him toward command of Parliament's main army.

Thutmose III's own officers argued against the direct route to Megiddo, a track through the Aruna pass so narrow that soldiers had to march single file with the horses trailing behind, warning that an ambush there could cut the army apart. He took it anyway, and found the enemy coalition had massed at the pass's two easier exits, leaving the direct road undefended.

After the rout, Egyptian troops stopped to strip the abandoned camp of chariots and armour instead of chasing survivors through Megiddo's open gates. The delay let the gates close, and Thutmose walled the city in with a moat and a timber palisade, starving it out over seven months. A scribe named Tjaneni kept the field notes, later carved onto the walls at Karnak, that let historians reconstruct the campaign day by day.

American codebreakers had cracked enough of Japan's naval codes to know an attack was coming toward Midway Atoll in June 1942, letting Admiral Chester Nimitz position his three available carriers in ambush rather than in defence. On 4 June, American dive bombers caught Japanese carriers with their flight decks crowded with fuelled and armed aircraft between strikes.

Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu were all sunk within a single day, against the loss of the American carrier Yorktown. Japan lost roughly 3,000 sailors and airmen, including many of its most experienced carrier pilots, a loss of trained personnel the Imperial Navy could not replace as quickly as the aircraft themselves.

Constantine and Maxentius were rival claimants to the western Roman Empire, and by 312 Maxentius controlled Rome itself while Constantine marched south from Gaul with a smaller army. Maxentius chose to fight outside the city, on the far bank of the Tiber, rather than shelter behind Rome's walls, and had a pontoon bridge built alongside the old Milvian Bridge to move his troops across.

Constantine's forces broke Maxentius's line and pushed it back toward the river, where the makeshift bridge collapsed under the retreating soldiers and Maxentius himself drowned. Constantine later told the historian Eusebius that he had seen a sign in the sky before the battle, and his favour toward Christianity, formalised the following year in an edict of toleration, was traced back to that single crossing.

Allied troops attacked German positions around the hilltop monastery of Monte Cassino on 17 January 1944, opening a battle for the road to Rome that would run for four months. The abbey itself, believed by Allied commanders to house German observers, was bombed to rubble in February even though the German defenders had not occupied the building.

Three further assaults followed before a fourth, launched in May with a much larger force, finally broke the Gustav Line. Losses across the whole campaign are estimated at well over 100,000 Allied and German casualties combined, with figures still disputed depending on which surrounding battles, including Anzio, are counted alongside Cassino itself.

The Treaty of Ghent had been signed on 24 December 1814, two weeks before Andrew Jackson's outnumbered force met the British outside New Orleans on 8 January 1815. News crossed the Atlantic by ship, and neither army on the field that morning knew the war was already over on paper.

British regulars advanced across open ground into artillery and rifle fire from behind a canal and earthworks, and lost roughly 2,000 men in under half an hour, including their commander, Edward Pakenham. American losses were counted in the dozens. Jackson's win, useless to the treaty, made him a national figure and carried him toward the presidency.

The Mongol army that took Baghdad in 1258 and Damascus in 1260 seemed unstoppable until Hulagu withdrew much of his force east after the death of the Great Khan, leaving a reduced garrison under Kitbuqa in Syria. The Mamluk sultan of Egypt, Qutuz, marched north to meet it near the spring of Ain Jalut in September 1260.

The Mamluk general Baibars lured Kitbuqa's cavalry into a valley with a feigned retreat, where hidden troops closed in from the flanks. Kitbuqa was killed and his army broken, the first clear defeat of a Mongol field army by a settled Muslim state. Qutuz was murdered by Baibars soon after, who took the sultanate himself and later drove the remaining Crusader footholds from the Levant.

Richard I was marching his army down the coast from Acre toward Jaffa in September 1191, keeping the fleet in sight on one flank to protect his supply line, when Saladin's forces attacked the column near Arsuf on 7 September. Richard kept his infantry and crossbowmen screening the knights until the moment came to counter-charge.

Two of the military orders' commanders reportedly broke ranks early against orders, and Richard had to commit the rest of the cavalry to avoid disaster, but the counterattack broke the Ayyubid lines and drove them from the field. The victory let Richard's army reach and refortify Jaffa, though it did not lead him to retake Jerusalem itself before the crusade ended in a truce.

Antonio Jose de Sucre led roughly 6,000 independence troops against a Spanish royalist army of about 9,000 near Ayacucho in the Peruvian highlands on 9 December 1824. The royalists held far more artillery, but a cavalry charge broke their advantage and captured the wounded viceroy, Jose de la Serna, along with much of his senior command.

Royalist losses have been recorded at around 1,400 dead against roughly 900 on the independence side. The surrender terms, negotiated the next day by the royalist general Canterac since La Serna was too badly hurt to continue, handed over the last major Spanish army remaining in South America and ended three centuries of Spanish rule on the continent.

In March 624, near the wells of Badr on the caravan route from Mecca to Syria, a Muslim force of roughly 300 men from Medina intercepted a much larger Meccan army sent to protect a trading caravan and punish the young community that had raided it. Muhammad's side won despite being heavily outnumbered, and several prominent Meccan leaders were killed or captured.

The victory is described in the Quran itself as a sign of divine help, and it gave Muhammad's followers a standing they had lacked as recent refugees from Mecca. Prisoners were mostly ransomed rather than killed, a choice later Islamic tradition treats as an early model for how Badr's veterans, the badriyyun, were to be honoured within the community.

Edward II marched a large relief army north in June 1314 to break the Scottish siege of Stirling Castle, one of the last English strongholds in Scotland. Robert the Bruce chose the ground near the Bannock burn carefully, digging pits and using boggy terrain to funnel the English cavalry into a narrow front where his massed pikemen, formed in schiltrons, could hold them.

Fighting over 23 and 24 June 1314 broke the English advance, and Edward fled the field as his army collapsed into the marshy ground behind it. The victory did not itself end the war, which dragged on for another fourteen years, but it confirmed Robert's control of Scotland and forced England toward recognising Scottish independence in the 1328 Treaty of Edinburgh Northampton.

On 22 August 1485 Richard III led a charge directly at Henry Tudor's position near Ambion Hill in Leicestershire, hoping to end the battle by killing his rival outright. The charge stalled in marshy ground, Richard was surrounded and killed, and his crown, tradition says, was found afterward in a hawthorn bush and placed on Henry's head on the field.

Richard's naked body was slung over a horse and displayed in Leicester before a hurried burial in a friary that was later demolished; his remains were not identified again until a car park excavation in 2012. Henry married Elizabeth of York the following year, uniting the warring houses of Lancaster and York and opening more than a century of Tudor rule.

King John of England had spent years and a fortune assembling a coalition against Philip II: the Holy Roman Emperor Otto IV, the count of Flanders and other princes, meant to squeeze French territory from two directions at once. John's own southern campaign faltered first, leaving Philip free to face the northern coalition alone near Bouvines on 27 July 1214.

Philip's army broke the coalition's line after hours of close fighting, and Otto fled the field. The count of Flanders and other leading nobles were captured. John returned home to a baronial revolt that forced Magna Carta on him the following year, while Philip's victory secured Normandy and Anjou for the French crown and weakened Otto's hold on the empire.

The armies that met near modern Chalons-en-Champagne in 451 were both coalitions rather than single nations. Aetius commanded Romans, Visigoths under King Theodoric I, and Franks, Burgundians and Alans, while Attila led Huns alongside Ostrogoths, Gepids and other subject peoples he had gathered on his march into Gaul.

The sixth-century historian Jordanes, working from an earlier lost account, describes fighting so fierce that a stream running through the field ran red. Theodoric was killed, but his Visigoths held their ground, and Attila withdrew to his camp rather than press on. Roman and Gothic losses were heavy enough that Aetius let the Huns retreat rather than risk a second day.

James IV crossed into England in September 1513 in support of France under the terms of the Auld Alliance, and met an English force under the Earl of Surrey at Flodden on the 9th. Rather than hold the ridge he had chosen, James led his own charge into the English line, and estimates of the Scottish dead range from about 10,000 to 17,000, English losses far fewer.

The chronicler George Buchanan later listed James's illegitimate son the Bishop of St Andrews, ten earls, thirteen lords and a French ambassador among the dead, alongside the king himself, the last British monarch killed in battle. It remains the heaviest single-day loss in Scottish military history, and the country's regency government was left to a one-year-old king, James V.

A force of Flemish townsmen and guildsmen, mostly weavers and other tradesmen from Bruges and Ghent, had no cavalry of their own and instead dug ditches and channelled streams into the marshy ground before Courtrai to break up a French cavalry charge. On 11 July 1302 the French knights, sent to punish Flanders for an earlier revolt, rode straight into the trap.

Horses foundered in the mud and the Flemish infantry, fighting on foot with pikes called goedendags, cut down knights who could not manoeuvre. Roughly 500 pairs of gilded spurs were reportedly stripped from dead French knights and hung in a Courtrai church, giving the battle its name. It was an unusual defeat of mounted nobility by commoners on foot.

On 15 July 1410, near the villages of Grunwald and Tannenberg in Prussia, the combined army of King Wladyslaw II Jagiello of Poland and Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania met the Teutonic Knights under Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen. The Grand Master was killed along with much of the Order's senior leadership, and the Knights' field army was effectively destroyed in a single afternoon.

The Order kept its capital at Marienburg through a subsequent siege that Jagiello failed to press home, so Grunwald did not end the Teutonic state outright. It broke the Order's capacity to expand at Polish and Lithuanian expense, and the loss of so many knights and officials in one battle left it dependent on mercenaries for its defence for the rest of its existence.

Tariq ibn Ziyad had crossed from North Africa into southern Spain with a mostly Berber force, and the Visigothic king Roderic marched south to meet him rather than let the invaders advance unopposed. The two armies met somewhere near a river the sources call the Guadalete in 711, though its exact location is still disputed among historians.

Roderic's own nobles reportedly deserted him mid battle, whether from resentment at a contested succession or simple opportunism, and his army broke apart; he is believed to have died in the rout, though his body was never confirmed. With the Visigothic king gone and his kingdom leaderless, Tariq's forces pushed on to Cordoba and then Toledo, opening the peninsula to Umayyad rule that lasted for centuries.

Harold's army had just marched roughly 250 miles south from Stamford Bridge, where it had crushed a separate Norse invasion days earlier, and reached Senlac Hill near Hastings exhausted. William's Norman force landed unopposed while Harold was still in the north, and on 14 October 1066 the two armies fought from morning until dusk on a single ridge.

Norman chroniclers later claimed an arrow struck Harold in the eye, but the Bayeux Tapestry's evidence is ambiguous and near-contemporary accounts disagree on how he died, only that he fell near the standard late in the battle. His death broke the English shield wall, and William was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day, replacing much of the English aristocracy with Norman lords within a generation.

Guy of Lusignan marched the Crusader army out of Acre in July 1187 to relieve Tiberias, away from reliable water, and Saladin's forces harried the column across dry hills near the Horns of Hattin until it collapsed from thirst and exhaustion rather than being simply outfought. Saladin had spent years unifying Muslim Syria and Egypt precisely to bring a force this large against the kingdom.

The Crusader army was nearly wiped out and its king captured along with the relic of the True Cross carried into the battle. Saladin reportedly executed the captured military orders' knights but spared Guy, and with the kingdom's field army gone, city after city fell to him within weeks, leaving Jerusalem itself open.

On 15 June 1389 the army of Sultan Murad I met the forces of Serbian Prince Lazar Hrebeljanovic on the Field of Blackbirds near modern Pristina. Both leaders died in the fighting, Murad reportedly stabbed by a Serbian noble who had gained access to his tent under pretence of surrender, and Lazar captured and executed shortly after.

The battle itself was closer to a mutual bloodletting than a decisive rout, and Serbian principalities kept a shrunken independence for decades afterward under Ottoman pressure. What outlasted the tactics was the story: epic poetry and church commemoration turned Lazar's death into a founding sacrifice, and the date became a fixture of Serbian memory centuries before nationalism gave it a modern use.

Frederick Barbarossa had spent nearly two decades trying to force the cities of northern Italy back under direct imperial control, sacking Milan in 1162 and rebuilding it to his own design. The cities answered by banding together as the Lombard League, and on 29 May 1176, near the town of Legnano, their militia infantry and cavalry met Barbarossa's army in the field.

The League's carroccio, an ox-drawn wagon carrying its banners, anchored a defensive core of foot soldiers that held against repeated imperial cavalry charges until fresh League horsemen struck the emperor's flank. Barbarossa was unhorsed and briefly reported dead, and the defeat forced him to negotiate. The 1183 Peace of Constance recognised the cities' self-government within the empire.

A Mongol force under Baidar and Kadan, sent west as a diversion while the main army struck Hungary, met a combined Polish and Moravian army led by Duke Henry II of Silesia near Legnica on 9 April 1241. The Mongols used feigned retreats and smoke to break up the European formation before closing in.

Henry's army was destroyed and Henry himself was killed, his head reportedly carried on a spear before the town's gates. The defeat, coming days before a separate Mongol victory over the Hungarians at Mohi, left much of central Europe undefended and spread reports of the invasion as far as England, though the Mongols withdrew from the region within the year.

On 13 and 14 September 1515, near Marignano south of Milan, a newly crowned Francis I of France fought a Swiss army that had until then been considered nearly unbeatable in open battle. French artillery and heavy cavalry ground down the Swiss pike formations over two days of fighting so costly that survivors on both sides called it a battle of giants.

Milan fell to France soon after, and Francis used the victory to open his reign with a claim on Italian glory his predecessors had chased for decades. The Swiss cantons, having lost heavily for the first time in living memory, signed a permanent peace with France the following year and largely withdrew from offensive wars on the peninsula, turning instead to supplying mercenaries.

Muhammad sent roughly three thousand men toward the town of Mu'ta in Byzantine-controlled Transjordan under the command of Zayd ibn Harithah, a freedman he had adopted as a son. The force met a much larger Byzantine and Arab Christian army near the settlement.

Zayd was killed in the fighting, and the next two commanders named in advance, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, were killed in turn before Khalid ibn al-Walid took charge and withdrew the remaining Muslims rather than risk annihilation. Muslim tradition treats the retreat as a defensible outcome against overwhelming numbers, and the battle marked the first direct clash between Muhammad's followers and Byzantine forces.

Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, had been besieging Nancy since October 1476 when a relief force of Swiss and Lorrainer troops under Rene II caught his army outside the walls on 5 January 1477. Charles's men broke and fled, and Charles himself was cut down in the retreat, his identity unrecognised by whoever struck him.

His mutilated body was found two days later, frozen in a marsh outside the town, one eye gone to wolves or ravens and his skull split open. He left no son, only a daughter, Mary, and the great duchy he had spent his reign expanding was carved up within months: Louis XI of France annexed the Burgundian heartland, and the Habsburgs took the rest through Mary's marriage.

Admiral Edward Codrington sailed into Navarino Bay on 20 October 1827 meaning to pressure the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet into a truce during the Greek war of independence, not to fight it. A shot fired at a British boat sent to deliver terms set off four hours of close-range gunnery inside the anchorage, with ships often too near each other to manoeuvre.

Roughly 3,000 Ottoman and Egyptian sailors were killed against 177 allied dead, and most of the Ottoman fleet, some sixty vessels by later counts, was sunk or burned. No allied ship was lost. The action crippled Ottoman naval power in the Aegean and is generally reckoned the last fleet battle fought without a single steam engine present.

Edward III crossed the English Channel in June 1340 with an invasion fleet and found the French navy anchored in three tight lines off the Flemish port of Sluys, chained together for defence rather than manoeuvre. That formation let the English close in and fight the battle almost as a land engagement fought from ship to ship.

English and Welsh longbowmen cleared the French decks with volleys before boarding parties finished the fighting hand to hand. Chroniclers put French losses in the thousands and most of the fleet was captured or sunk. The disaster left France without a navy able to challenge English crossings for years, shaping the early Hundred Years' War.

Harald Hardrada landed near York in September 1066 with his own claim to the English throne, backed by Harold's estranged brother Tostig, and beat the local earls at Fulford. Harold Godwinson force marched his household troops roughly 185 miles from London in four days to catch the Norwegians unprepared at Stamford Bridge on 25 September.

The Norwegian army had left much of its armour with the ships and was cut down before it could properly form up; Hardrada and Tostig were both killed. Harold had barely two weeks to march south again before William landed on the Sussex coast, meeting him at Hastings with an army already worn down by the earlier fighting.

In 751, near the Talas river in what is now Kyrgyzstan, an Abbasid army reinforced by Tibetan and Karluk allies met a Tang Chinese expeditionary force under Gao Xianzhi that had pushed deep into Central Asia to police its client states. A defection by Karluk troops fighting alongside the Chinese broke the Tang line, and Gao's army was routed far from any hope of reinforcement.

Among the Chinese prisoners taken were skilled craftsmen, including papermakers, who were reportedly put to work in Samarkand. Papermaking had already been spreading westward along trade routes, but captives from Talas are widely credited with establishing the craft directly in Abbasid territory, from where it reached Baghdad and eventually, centuries later, Europe.

On 1 July 1690, William III's army forced a crossing of the River Boyne near Drogheda against the forces of his father in law and rival, the deposed James II. William himself was grazed by a cannonball the day before the battle, an injury that did not stop him leading part of the crossing on horseback under fire.

James's army broke and withdrew south, and James left Ireland for France within days, effectively abandoning his campaign to recover the English throne by force. The battle secured William and Mary's Protestant settlement in Britain, and it became, and remains, the central commemorative event of Ulster Protestant loyalist tradition, marked each July by the Orange Order.

Japan committed nine carriers to stop the American invasion of the Mariana Islands in June 1944, but its pilots were largely inexperienced replacements rushed through shortened training after the losses at Midway and the Solomons. American radar picked up incoming raids well before they arrived, letting Hellcat fighters intercept them at altitude and range.

US pilots later joked about the lopsided result, and one gunner reportedly compared it to a turkey shoot back home. Japan lost around 600 aircraft against a few dozen American planes, along with three carriers, two to submarine attack and one to air strikes. The Imperial Navy's carrier air arm never recovered enough pilots or planes to fight another major battle.

On 10 November 1444, near the Black Sea port of Varna, Sultan Murad II's Ottoman army met a crusading force led by the young King Wladyslaw III of Poland and Hungary. Wladyslaw, only twenty, ignored his commanders and led a charge straight at the sultan's bodyguard in an attempt to kill Murad and end the battle at a stroke.
