The charge failed. Wladyslaw was cut down and, by some accounts, his severed head was later displayed on a spear. The papal legate Julian Cesarini also died in the collapse that followed. Chroniclers put crusader losses near five thousand and Ottoman losses higher still. The defeat ended the last major Christian effort to drive the Ottomans from the Balkans before Constantinople fell nine years later.

By 507 the Visigoths held most of Iberia and southern Gaul under King Alaric II, while Clovis had already united the Frankish tribes and converted to Catholic Christianity, giving him a religious pretext against Alaric's Arian kingdom. Clovis marched south from Paris toward Poitiers to confront him.

The two armies met near Vouille, where Clovis reportedly killed Alaric himself in personal combat, though the sources for that detail are later and not fully reliable. The defeat cost the Visigoths almost all their territory in Gaul, and their court withdrew across the Pyrenees into Spain, leaving Toulouse and the old Gothic heartland in Frankish hands.

In 133 BC a merchant named Nie Yi proposed a trap: he would pretend to betray the border town of Mayi to the Xiongnu, luring their chanyu and his army into Han territory, where Emperor Wu had hidden more than 300,000 soldiers. It was the largest force the Han had committed against the Xiongnu, built entirely around deception rather than a battle at Wei Qiao.

The plan fell apart before a single Han soldier engaged the enemy. Advancing toward Mayi, the chanyu grew suspicious of grazing cattle left with no herdsmen in sight, and his scouts captured a Han officer who confessed the scheme under interrogation. The chanyu withdrew at once. No battle was fought, but the failed ambush ended a long peace and opened sustained wars between Han China and the Xiongnu.

Over six days in August 636, along the Yarmouk river gorge on the border of modern Syria and Jordan, an Arab Muslim army under Khalid ibn al-Walid fought a Byzantine force that Emperor Heraclius had gathered from across the empire's eastern provinces. A sandstorm on the final day is described in Arab accounts as blinding the Byzantine line at the moment Khalid's cavalry pressed its attack.

Byzantine losses were heavy enough that Heraclius withdrew from Syria altogether rather than risk another field army, reportedly bidding the province farewell as he left for Constantinople. Damascus and the rest of the Levant fell to Arab forces within a few years, and Byzantium never recovered the territory it lost at Yarmouk.

General Douglas Haig launched the Third Battle of Ypres, better known as Passchendaele, on 31 July 1917 to break through Belgian lines and reach German submarine bases on the coast. Heavy shelling had destroyed the drainage of the low-lying ground, and weeks of unusually wet weather turned the battlefield into a swamp deep enough to drown wounded men and horses alike.

Fighting dragged on until November, when Canadian troops finally took the shattered village of Passchendaele itself, a few miles beyond where the advance had started. Estimates of combined casualties run from roughly 250,000 to over 500,000 depending on which losses are counted, figures still argued over by historians. The ground gained was largely lost again to a German offensive the following spring.

Pompey commanded roughly twice the infantry Caesar had at Pharsalus in 48 BC, and a cavalry force meant to sweep around Caesar's right flank and finish the battle quickly. Caesar had read that plan in advance and hid a fourth line of picked infantry behind his own cavalry, with orders to use their spears like javelins against Pompey's mounted men rather than fight them as foot soldiers normally would.

Pompey's cavalry broke under that unexpected attack and exposed his own flank, and his larger army collapsed within hours, forcing him to flee the camp he had left half packed for a victory celebration. He escaped to Egypt, where he was murdered on arrival, leaving Caesar the master of Rome's civil war and its Senate with no army left to oppose him.

Robert Clive brought roughly 3,000 East India Company troops against Siraj ud Daulah's army of tens of thousands on 23 June 1757, north of Calcutta. The numbers mattered less than the arrangement Clive had already made with Mir Jafar, the nawab's own commander, who he had secretly promised the throne of Bengal in exchange for holding his troops back from the fight.

Most of Siraj's army never engaged. Mir Jafar's contingents stood aside, the nawab fled, and he was captured and killed within days. Clive installed Mir Jafar as the new nawab and, with him, effective Company control over Bengal's revenue. It was less a battle than a bribe that ended in one, and it opened the way to British rule over a subcontinent.

Near Poitiers on 19 September 1356, Edward the Black Prince's outnumbered force met a French army that chroniclers put at several times its size. English and Gascon men at arms and archers had spent the campaign raiding through Aquitaine before John II caught them; the English formed on rising ground behind hedges that broke up the French cavalry charges before they closed.

John II fought on foot with his household and was taken prisoner along with his son Philip, seventeen great lords and a hundred other knights, by one contemporary count. His ransom, first set at three million gold ecus, drained the French crown for years and left France governed by a regent while its captured king lived in England.

Charles XII of Sweden had spent nine years marching through eastern Europe when his army, weakened by a Ukrainian winter and reduced in numbers, met Peter the Great's larger Russian force near Poltava on 8 July 1709. Charles himself could not lead from the field: a Cossack's bullet had shattered his foot weeks earlier, and he directed the battle from a litter.

The Swedes broke within hours, and thousands of survivors who fled south were trapped and forced to surrender days later at Perevolochna on the Dnieper. Charles escaped with a few hundred men into Ottoman territory, but the army that had terrorised Denmark, Poland and Russia for a decade was gone. Sweden never regained its standing as a great power, and Russia's did not stop rising.

Ten days after his crossing of the Delaware and the strike on Trenton, George Washington moved his army toward Princeton on 3 January 1777, circling British forces sent to intercept him. A chance encounter with a British regiment on the Post Road turned into a running fight through the town rather than the surprise Washington had planned.

American troops broke a British stand in an orchard near Nassau Hall, and the fighting spilled onto the grounds of the College of New Jersey itself, where a cannonball reportedly struck a portrait of King George II inside. The victory, following Trenton, revived an American cause that had looked close to collapse only weeks before and pushed British forces out of most of New Jersey for the winter.

The Macedonian phalanx that met Rome at Pydna in 168 BC was, on open ground, close to unstoppable, a wall of overlapping spears that Roman writers admitted they had no answer for in a frontal clash. The Roman commander Lucius Aemilius Paullus instead let the phalanx advance onto broken ground, where gaps opened between its units as they tried to keep their long spears level.

Roman legionaries pushed into those gaps with short swords, where the phalanx's own spears became a liability at close quarters, and King Perseus's army broke within roughly an hour. Perseus fled and was later captured, the Antigonid kingdom that Alexander's general Antigonus had founded was dissolved, and Macedonia was carved into four Roman-administered republics.

General James Wolfe had spent weeks failing to draw the French out of Quebec when, on the night of 12 September 1759, he moved thousands of troops up the Saint Lawrence and had them climb a barely guarded cliff path onto the Plains of Abraham above the city. The Marquis de Montcalm chose to meet them there rather than wait for reinforcements.

The battle itself lasted under an hour. Both commanders were mortally wounded, Wolfe on the field and Montcalm the following day, and the city surrendered days later. The loss did not end France's presence in North America immediately, but the war's outcome in 1763 handed Canada to Britain, closing the long contest for the continent between the two crowns.

Themistocles, not the Spartans, planned the fight at Salamis in 480 BCE. He lured Xerxes's larger fleet into the narrow strait between the island and the Attic coast, where its numbers became a liability, ships jamming against each other while the lighter Greek triremes rammed at will.

Xerxes reportedly watched the battle from a hillside throne, expecting to see his navy finish the war in an afternoon. Instead the Persian fleet broke apart in the strait, and Xerxes withdrew much of his army from Greece soon after, leaving a smaller force under Mardonius to fight on without him.

On 1 September 1870 Prussian and Bavarian artillery ringed the town of Sedan on high ground and shelled a French army trapped in the valley below. Napoleon III had ridden to the front himself, hoping a show of resolve might steady his generals, and instead watched his last field army pinned against the Meuse with no way out.

The next morning he surrendered along with roughly 100,000 troops, the single largest capitulation of the war. News of the emperor's capture reached Paris within two days, and crowds took to the streets to proclaim a republic before his train had even left French soil, ending the Second Empire he had ruled since 1852.

British and French forces attacked German lines along the Somme river on 1 July 1916 after a week of artillery bombardment that failed to cut the barbed wire or destroy the German dugouts as planned. British troops advanced in the open toward machine guns that had survived intact, and the army recorded around 57,000 casualties on that single first day.

The offensive continued into November, gaining a strip of ground a few miles deep at a combined cost historians put at over one million dead, wounded and missing on both sides. The battle also saw the first use of tanks in combat, at Flers-Courcelette in September, though too few and too unreliable to break the deadlock they were built for.

Arminius had served in the Roman army and won Roman citizenship before he led an alliance of Germanic tribes against his former commanders. In the autumn of the year 9 he lured Publius Quinctilius Varus and roughly 20,000 men of three legions into a forested, marshy route through the Teutoburg Forest on a false report of a local uprising.

Strung out in a narrow column, the legions were ambushed over several days and effectively destroyed. Varus killed himself rather than be captured. The defeat pushed Rome's frontier back to the Rhine, and it never again attempted a permanent conquest of Germany east of that line.

Leonidas did not have 300 men. His Spartans were the core of a much larger Greek force, several thousand strong, holding the narrow coastal pass at Thermopylae against Xerxes's army in 480 BCE for two days before a local shepherd named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain track around the position.

With the pass outflanked, Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed to cover the retreat with his Spartans, some Thespians, and a group of enslaved Thebans he reportedly kept by force. All of them were killed. The delay bought Athens time to evacuate the city before Xerxes burned it later that year.

An Umayyad raiding force under Abd al Rahman al Ghafiqi pushed north from Iberia into Aquitaine and toward the wealthy abbey of Saint Martin at Tours. Charles Martel, the Frankish leader who held no royal title of his own, gathered infantry and met the raiders somewhere between Tours and Poitiers in October 732.

Frankish troops formed a dense defensive square that held through a day of cavalry charges, and al Ghafiqi was killed as his own men began to withdraw at nightfall. Arab chroniclers describe it as a limited setback in a much larger raid rather than a catastrophe, and Muslim forces kept raiding across the Pyrenees for decades afterward, but Charles's reputation from the day helped his family's rise to the Frankish throne.

On 21 October 1805, off Cape Trafalgar in southern Spain, Admiral Nelson broke with standard naval tactics by sailing his fleet directly into the combined French and Spanish line in two columns rather than forming a parallel line to trade broadsides. It exposed his lead ships to concentrated fire but let him split and overwhelm the enemy fleet piece by piece.

Not a single British ship was lost, while the French and Spanish lost around twenty. Nelson was shot by a French marksman during the battle and died below deck that afternoon, having lived long enough to learn the fleet was won. The victory ended any serious threat of a French invasion of Britain by sea and left the Royal Navy without a rival for the rest of the war.

Russia's Baltic Fleet had sailed roughly 18,000 nautical miles from the Baltic Sea, around Africa, to relieve Port Arthur, only to find it had already fallen. Admiral Togo Heihachiro intercepted the exhausted fleet in the Tsushima Strait on 27 May 1905, crossing its line to bring more guns to bear at once.

The battle destroyed the Russian force almost completely: contemporary accounts put Russian losses at around eleven battleships sunk or captured and roughly 5,000 sailors dead, against a few hundred Japanese casualties and no capital ships lost. It was the first time an Asian navy had beaten a European great power's battle fleet, and the defeat helped push Russia toward the peace talks that ended the war that September.

German chief of staff Erich von Falkenhayn opened the attack on the fortress city of Verdun on 21 February 1916 with a plan built around attrition rather than a breakthrough: hold ground the French could not abandon and force them to feed men into it until the army broke. The battle lasted nearly ten months.

France held Verdun, rotating most of its army through the sector on a supply road nicknamed the Voie Sacree, but the cost on both sides ran into the hundreds of thousands of dead and wounded, with figures from contemporary reports varying widely and never fully reconciled. Falkenhayn was replaced before the year was out, and Verdun became shorthand in French memory for endurance bought at a nearly unbearable price.

Ottoman forces under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha had besieged Vienna for two months by 12 September 1683, when a relief army under the Polish king John III Sobieski attacked from the wooded hills above the city. Sobieski commanded the largest cavalry charge of the century, a mass assault by Polish and German heavy cavalry that broke through the Ottoman lines late in the day.

The Ottoman army abandoned its siege equipment and withdrew in disorder, and Kara Mustafa was executed on the sultan's order months later over the defeat. The failure ended sustained Ottoman campaigns to expand further into central Europe, and it began a series of Habsburg advances that pushed Ottoman control out of Hungary over the following decades.

Napoleon had escaped exile on Elba and returned to power in March 1815, rebuilding an army to face the coalition forming against him. He struck first into Belgium, aiming to defeat Wellington's Anglo allied army and Blucher's Prussians separately before they could combine.

Near the village of Waterloo on 18 June, Napoleon attacked Wellington's line through a long afternoon of infantry and cavalry assaults, including the failed advance of his Imperial Guard late in the day. Blucher's Prussians arrived on the field that evening, and the combined counterattack broke the French army, ending Napoleon's rule days later.

Cornwallis withdrew his army to Yorktown, Virginia, in the summer of 1781 expecting the Royal Navy to keep it supplied and free to move by sea. Instead, a French fleet under de Grasse defeated the British navy off the Chesapeake in September, sealing the harbour, while Washington marched a combined American and French force south from New York to besiege the town.

Trapped between the siege lines and the sea, Cornwallis surrendered his roughly 8,000 men on 19 October 1781. He did not attend the surrender ceremony himself, sending a deputy in his place. Fighting continued elsewhere for two more years, but the loss of a second full British army in America broke Parliament's appetite for the war and led to peace talks.

Scipio had studied Hannibal's tactics for years before facing him directly. At Zama in 202 BCE he left lanes open in his infantry lines so Hannibal's war elephants would charge straight through without breaking the Roman formation, then relied on cavalry, borrowed from the Numidian king Masinissa, who had switched sides from Carthage to Rome.

That cavalry, once it scattered Hannibal's own horsemen, swung around and hit the Carthaginian infantry from behind, mirroring the encirclement Hannibal had used against Rome at Cannae fourteen years earlier. Carthage sued for peace within the year, giving up its navy, its war elephants, and its overseas territory.

The CIA had trained around 1,400 Cuban exiles in Guatemala under a plan begun during the Eisenhower administration and inherited by John F. Kennedy. On 17 April 1961 the brigade landed at the Bay of Pigs on Cuba's southern coast, intending to spark a general uprising against Castro's government.

The plan assumed Cuban air cover that never arrived after Kennedy scaled back the supporting air strikes, and Castro's forces, already alerted, were waiting. Within three days the invaders were killed or captured; roughly 1,200 were taken prisoner and later ransomed back to the United States for food and supplies. The failure humiliated Kennedy and pushed Castro further toward Moscow, which led to the missile crisis eighteen months later.

Just after six in the morning on 23 October 1983, a truck loaded with explosives drove past sentries and into the lobby of a US Marine barracks near Beirut's airport before detonating, collapsing the four storey building into rubble within seconds. A second truck struck a French paratrooper barracks about two kilometres away minutes later. Both were part of the multinational peacekeeping force stationed in Lebanon after the 1982 Israeli invasion.

241 American servicemen and 58 French troops were killed. Islamic Jihad, a name later linked to the group that became Hezbollah, claimed responsibility; investigators later concluded Iran had helped fund and direct the operation. President Reagan withdrew the remaining US Marines from Lebanon within four months of the bombing.

Belisarius landed in Sicily in 535 with a force numbering only a few thousand men, small for the task Justinian had set him, and took Naples the following year before the Ostrogoths abandoned Rome without a fight in December 536. The Goths had not expected so modest an army to threaten their hold on Italy at all.

Rome's population, swollen by refugees, endured a Gothic siege lasting over a year once King Vitiges regrouped and marched back. Belisarius held the city and pushed north to Ravenna by 540, but the Gothic kingdom he thought broken revived under new leadership within a few years, dragging the war on for another decade.

An East German official misread a press statement on 9 November 1989 and announced the border would open immediately, when the plan had actually intended a delayed, orderly process. Crowds gathered at checkpoints within the hour, and confused guards, with no clear orders and unwilling to fire on them, simply opened the gates that night.

Berliners climbed onto the wall and began chipping pieces away with hammers within days, and demolition crews finished the job over the following months. Germany formally reunified less than a year later, on 3 October 1990, and the wall's fall is generally treated as the moment the Cold War's division of Europe ended.

Armed Chechen and Ingush militants seized School Number One in Beslan, North Ossetia, on 1 September 2004, the first day of the school year, taking more than 1,100 hostages, most of them children, and wiring the gymnasium with explosives. They demanded Russian withdrawal from Chechnya.

The siege ended in chaos on 3 September when explosions inside the gym triggered a battle between the hostage takers and Russian security forces. More than 330 people were killed, including 186 children, and hundreds more were wounded. Russian officials were later criticised for using tanks and heavy weapons against a building still full of hostages.

Biafra's army surrendered on 12 January 1970, after Nigerian forces closed in on the secessionist enclave's last strongholds in the southeast. The two and a half year war had shrunk Biafran territory to a fraction of its original size, and its government under Odumegwu Ojukwu had already fled into exile in Ivory Coast rather than negotiate terms.

The fighting itself killed a fraction of the war's dead. Most of the estimated one to two million deaths came from starvation, after federal forces blockaded food and medicine from reaching the enclave. Photographs of emaciated Biafran children reached newspapers worldwide and pushed relief agencies to fly in supplies, but the blockade held until the surrender ended the famine along with the war.

Two dozen US Navy SEALs flew by helicopter from Afghanistan into Abbottabad, Pakistan, on the night of 1 May 2011 and raided a walled compound where intelligence analysts had tracked a courier believed to serve Osama bin Laden. The raid lasted under forty minutes, and bin Laden was shot and killed inside.

He had lived at the compound, less than a mile from a Pakistani military academy, for as long as five years without detection, which strained American trust in Pakistan's cooperation. His body was flown to a US aircraft carrier and buried at sea within hours, a decision meant to leave no grave site behind.

War broke out in October 1899 between Britain and the Boer republics of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, whose farmers had spent the 1890s watching British mining interests grow rich off the gold and diamonds under their land. Boer commandos, mounted and lightly equipped, inflicted early defeats on conventional British columns before Britain poured in reinforcements.

As the war turned into a guerrilla campaign after 1900, British forces burned Boer farms and interned civilians in camps where overcrowding and disease killed roughly 26,000 people, mostly women and children. The tactic later gave the term concentration camp its first widespread use in English, well before its far worse twentieth century meaning.

Two pressure cooker bombs went off twelve seconds apart near the finish line on Boylston Street on 15 April 2013, as runners were still crossing after four hours of racing. Brothers Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, ethnic Chechens who had lived in the Boston area for years, built the devices using instructions the FBI traced to an al-Qaeda affiliated online magazine. One of the dead was an eight-year-old boy.

The brothers killed an MIT police officer three days later while fleeing, then fought police in Watertown, where Tamerlan was killed. Dzhokhar hid in a boat in a resident's backyard and was found after the city lifted a daylong shelter-in-place order covering the metropolitan area. He was convicted in 2015 and sentenced to death, reinstated by the Supreme Court in 2022.

Eight British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street on the night of 5 March 1770, after townspeople pelted them with snowballs, ice and oyster shells. A musket was knocked from one soldier's hand, a shot went off, and the rest of the line fired without a clear order. Crispus Attucks, an escaped slave working as a dockworker and sailor, was among the first to fall.

Within weeks, silversmith Paul Revere issued an engraving of the shooting copied almost line for line from a drawing by Henry Pelham, and sold it before Pelham's own reached print, crediting no one. That December, John Adams, later a president, defended the soldiers and won acquittals for six of them; the other two were convicted of manslaughter and branded on the thumb instead of hanged.

On the night of 16 December 1773, members of the Sons of Liberty, some thinly disguised as Mohawk warriors, boarded three ships in Boston Harbour and threw 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water over roughly three hours. The tea itself was not the grievance: Parliament's Tea Act had actually lowered its price, but it also confirmed Parliament's right to tax the colonies without their consent.

Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts, closing Boston's port until the tea was paid for and stripping Massachusetts of much of its self-government. Rather than isolating Boston, the punishment pushed the other colonies toward it, and delegates convened the First Continental Congress in Philadelphia within a year.

A society calling itself the Righteous and Harmonious Fists rose against Christian missionaries and foreign influence across northern China from 1899, and the Qing court, under the empress dowager Cixi, threw its own troops behind them in 1900. Together they besieged the foreign legation quarter in Beijing for fifty-five days.

An eight-nation coalition, including Japanese, Russian, British, American and German troops, marched on Beijing and broke the siege in August 1900. The relief force and its allies then looted the capital and imposed an indemnity on China so large it took decades to pay off, part of which the United States later redirected to fund Chinese students studying abroad.

On 23 June 2016, voters across the United Kingdom were asked a single question: remain in the European Union or leave. Turnout ran above 72 percent, and the result split the country by nation and generation, with England and Wales voting to leave while Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain.

Leave won by 51.9 percent to 48.1, a margin of about 1.3 million votes out of more than 33 million cast. Prime Minister David Cameron, who had campaigned for remain, resigned the next morning. The formal exit did not happen until January 2020, after more than three years of negotiation over the terms of departure.

Budi Utomo was founded in Yogyakarta on 20 May 1908 by students at the Dutch run medical school in Batavia, prompted by a retired doctor, Wahidin Soerjoningrat, who had been touring Java arguing that Javanese culture needed organised support to survive colonial rule. Its early meetings drew mostly aristocrats and civil servants rather than the wider population.

The organisation itself stayed cautious, focused on education and Javanese cultural revival rather than confronting Dutch authority directly, and its membership never grew as large as its founders hoped. Its significance lay less in what it achieved than in the fact of it existing at all: a formally structured, Java wide association of natives that later, more overtly political groups would treat as a starting point.

Burma and Siam had fought intermittently since the sixteenth century over control of the Tenasserim coast and rival claims to Lan Na, but the wars of the 1760s were fought with new intensity under the expanding Burmese Konbaung dynasty. King Hsinbyushin sent two armies converging on the Siamese capital in 1765.

The siege of Ayutthaya dragged on for more than a year while Burma fought off a simultaneous Chinese invasion in the north. Ayutthaya fell in April 1767 and was burned, but Burmese occupation proved brief: within months Siamese forces under Taksin had regrouped and begun driving the occupiers back out of the country.

Khmer Rouge forces entered Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975 and within days ordered the entire city emptied, marching its residents into the countryside on foot. Pol Pot's government abolished money, closed schools, and sent the population to forced labour on collective farms as part of an attempt to rebuild the country as an agrarian state.

Researchers who later exhumed mass grave sites, documented in what became known as the killing fields, estimate that around 1.7 million people died under the regime between 1975 and 1979, from executions, overwork and starvation. Educated professionals, ethnic minorities and anyone linked to the previous government were targeted specifically, and the Vietnamese invasion that removed the Khmer Rouge from power came in January 1979.

On 6 January 2021, thousands of supporters of outgoing President Donald Trump gathered in Washington to hear him repeat false claims that the election had been stolen. A crowd then marched to the Capitol, broke through barricades and police lines, and forced its way into the building while Congress was certifying Joe Biden's victory.

Lawmakers and Vice President Mike Pence were evacuated as rioters occupied the Senate chamber and offices; five people died in connection with the events of that day, including a Capitol police officer who died the next day. Congress resumed and certified the result overnight. More than 1,400 people were later charged, and Trump was impeached a second time within the week.

The First Crusade's army had marched from western Europe for three years, through famine and disease that killed far more of it than any battle, before it reached Jerusalem in June 1099. The siege lasted barely five weeks; crusaders finally breached the walls on 15 July using siege towers built from timber scavenged and shipped in from Genoese vessels at Jaffa.

Chroniclers on both sides describe the killing that followed as extensive, with Muslim and Jewish residents slaughtered in the streets and in the al-Aqsa mosque, though the specific numbers given by medieval writers are not considered reliable. Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen to rule the new Christian kingdom, and Jerusalem stayed under Latin control for most of the next eighty-eight years.

Early medieval lords had defended themselves with earthworks and timber palisades, structures fast to raise but vulnerable to fire and to years of rot. Stone keeps, first common in France and Norman England from around the tenth and eleventh centuries, cost far more in quarried material and skilled masons but could withstand a siege lasting months rather than days.

A stone castle also let a small garrison hold a wide territory, since a fortified point commanding a river crossing or a road junction was expensive for an attacker to reduce and cheap for its lord to defend. That arithmetic reshaped feudal power: a baron who controlled a strong keep could resist his own king for years, a leverage timber forts had rarely offered.

Byzantium hired the Catalan Company in 1303 to fight the Ottoman Turks in Anatolia, paying them in Almogavar mercenary tradition: campaign wages plus whatever plunder they could take. The arrangement soured within two years. When the Byzantines tried to withhold pay and disband the force, the Catalans turned on their employers instead of going home.

At the Battle of Halmyros in March 1311, the Company killed Walter of Brienne, the Frankish Duke of Athens who had hired them next, along with most of his knights. They then seized Athens and Thebes outright, ruling the duchy under the Crown of Aragon until 1388, a stranger outcome for a hired army than anyone in Constantinople had anticipated.

Chain mail was made by drawing iron wire, cutting it into rings, and riveting each ring closed through four neighbours, a method already old by the time Frankish and Norse smiths spread it across early medieval Europe. A single hauberk covering torso and arms could take tens of thousands of rings and weeks of a smith's labour, which made it a mark of wealth as much as a piece of equipment.

Unlike stiff plate, mail flexed with the wearer's movement, letting a mounted soldier swing a sword or couch a lance without the armour binding at the joints. It absorbed cuts well but did little against a concentrated blow from a mace or a bodkin arrow, weaknesses that plate armour was developed over the following centuries to address.

Champa, strung along the coast of what is now central and southern Vietnam, fought Dai Viet over the border region for generations, each side raiding the other's capital when it had the advantage. The rivalry gave both kingdoms battle-hardened forces, but neither could hold the other's territory for long.

That balance broke when Kublai Khan's fleet tried to use Champa as a route into Dai Viet in 1282 and 1283, and both kingdoms found themselves fighting the same invader instead of each other. Champa's forces under King Indravarman V drew the Mongols into jungle terrain and outlasted them, forcing a withdrawal that weakened Yuan ambitions in Southeast Asia.

An ambiguous order from Lord Raglan on 25 October 1854, delivered by an aide who pointed at the wrong guns, sent the Light Brigade's roughly 670 cavalrymen down a valley at Balaclava directly into a battery of Russian artillery rather than the retreating guns Raglan had actually meant. Cannon fired on the brigade from three sides as it advanced.

The brigade reached the guns and briefly scattered their crews before being forced back, having lost around a third of its men and nearly as many horses in about twenty minutes. Alfred Tennyson's poem, published within weeks, fixed the charge in British memory as heroic disaster rather than the command failure the army's own inquiry later described.

On Christmas Day in 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor during mass at Saint Peter's in Rome. According to his biographer Einhard, Charlemagne later claimed he had no idea the crowning was planned and would not have attended had he known, a claim historians treat sceptically since his court was in Rome for weeks beforehand.

The title revived a western imperial claim that had lapsed since 476, and it irritated Constantinople, which still considered itself the sole Roman empire. Charlemagne already ruled most of western Europe through decades of campaigning; the coronation gave that rule a Roman title, and it set a precedent later German kings would keep reviving for centuries as the Holy Roman Empire.

Charlemagne opened his campaign against the pagan Saxons in 772 by destroying the Irminsul, a sacred wooden pillar the Saxons revered, at Eresburg. What followed was not one battle but eighteen separate campaigns over three decades, punctuated by Saxon uprisings that undid earlier Frankish gains almost as soon as troops withdrew.

The Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae made death the penalty for refusing baptism, for eating meat during Lent, or for cremating the dead in pagan fashion. At Verden in 782, Frankish sources record several thousand Saxon prisoners executed after a revolt led by Widukind, a massacre still debated by historians who question the figure's reliability. Saxony was not fully absorbed into Charlemagne's empire until 804.

Parliament put Charles I on trial in January 1649 on a charge of treason against his own people, a novel accusation for a king who claimed he answered to God alone. Charles refused to plead, denying the court's authority to try him at all, and the commissioners convicted him regardless on 27 January.

He was beheaded on a scaffold outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649, wearing two shirts against the cold so that he would not shiver and be seen to show fear. England abolished the monarchy days later and was governed as a republic, the Commonwealth, until Charles's son was restored to the throne in 1660.

On the morning of 7 January 2015, brothers Said and Chérif Kouachi forced their way into the Paris offices of Charlie Hebdo during the magazine's weekly editorial meeting and shot twelve people dead, including four leading cartoonists and a police officer outside. The gunmen shouted that they belonged to al-Qaeda in Yemen and were avenging the magazine's cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad.

The brothers were killed two days later after a siege at a printing works northeast of Paris. An associate, Amedy Coulibaly, took hostages at a kosher supermarket in Paris the same day and killed four before police stormed the store. Roughly four million people marched across France that weekend under the slogan Je Suis Charlie.

Che Guevara had left Cuba in 1966 to organise a guerrilla campaign in Bolivia, hoping to spread revolution across South America as he had helped Fidel Castro do in Havana. His small band never grew past a few dozen fighters and never won the peasant support it needed. Bolivian army rangers, trained with CIA assistance, cornered his group in the Yuro ravine on 8 October 1967 and captured him wounded.

He was held overnight in a schoolhouse in the village of La Higuera and shot the following afternoon on orders that came from the Bolivian high command rather than from any battlefield decision. His hands were severed and preserved to confirm his identity before his body was buried in a secret location, not found and identified until 1997.

In 1212 a shepherd boy named Stephen of Cloyes in France, and separately a boy called Nicholas in the German Rhineland, began gathering followers with claims that God had chosen the young and poor to win back the Holy Land where armed knights had failed. Neither movement was made up mainly of children; medieval chroniclers used the Latin pueri to describe the poor and landless generally, and most participants were probably young adults.

Stephen's group dispersed before reaching the sea. Nicholas led his followers across the Alps to Genoa and other Italian ports expecting the waters to part; when they did not, the crowd scattered, and later, unreliable accounts claim some were sold into slavery by ship captains who had promised passage. No group from either movement reached the Holy Land.

On the morning of 11 September 1973, Chilean armed forces under General Augusto Pinochet moved on the presidential palace, La Moneda, while jets bombed it from the air. Salvador Allende, the elected socialist president, gave a final radio address refusing to resign and died inside the palace that afternoon; an official inquiry decades later confirmed he had shot himself rather than be captured.

The United States had worked for years to undermine Allende's government, and the CIA had contact with plotting officers beforehand, though the extent of direct American involvement in the coup itself remains disputed. Pinochet's junta suspended the constitution and ruled by decree, and the National Stadium in Santiago was turned into a detention centre within days of the takeover.

Mao Zedong's Communist forces had spent decades building support in the countryside, through land reform and guerrilla warfare against both Japanese occupiers and Nationalist rivals, before a renewed civil war after 1945 turned decisively against Chiang Kai-shek's government. Nationalist forces, weakened by inflation and corruption scandals, lost city after city through 1948 and 1949 despite American aid.

Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China from the gate of the Forbidden City on 1 October 1949 in Beijing. Chiang and roughly two million Nationalist supporters retreated to the island of Taiwan, where his government continued to claim to be China's legitimate ruler, a dispute over recognition that has never been formally resolved.

A mutiny by army engineers in Wuchang in October 1911, triggered by the accidental detonation of a bomb they were preparing, set off province after province declaring against the Qing dynasty within weeks. The revolt spread faster than the court could respond, and by December most of southern and central China had broken away.

Sun Yat-sen, who had spent years abroad organising and raising money for exactly this outcome, was named provisional president of a new Republic of China in January 1912. The six-year-old emperor Puyi abdicated the following month, ending more than two thousand years of dynastic rule, though the republic that replaced it soon splintered under regional warlords.

Rajaraja I sent his fleet against Anuradhapura, the Sinhalese capital, around 993, sacking the city and annexing northern Sri Lanka as a Chola province he named after himself. Buddhist monasteries there were looted and Shiva temples raised in their place, and a permanent Chola garrison was installed on the island rather than a raiding force that simply withdrew.

By 1014 the same navy, based at the port of Nagapattinam, had subdued the Maldives, described in Chola inscriptions as the twelve thousand old islands of the sea. Control of these waters put the spice and silk routes linking Arabia, East Africa and Southeast Asia under Chola oversight, a reach his son Rajendra I extended further with a fleet sent against Srivijaya.

President Jacobo Arbenz's 1952 land reform law expropriated unused acreage from large plantations, including land held by the United Fruit Company, offering compensation at the value the company itself had declared for tax purposes. United Fruit lobbied Washington heavily, and the Eisenhower administration, whose officials had personal and professional ties to the company, approved a covert CIA operation code named PBSUCCESS.

A CIA backed force under exiled colonel Carlos Castillo Armas crossed from Honduras in June 1954, backed by psychological warfare broadcasts and a handful of air strikes on the capital that exaggerated the invasion's real strength. Arbenz resigned within two weeks. Castillo Armas took power and reversed the land reform, opening decades of military rule and a civil war that lasted into the 1990s.

Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh had nationalised the Anglo Iranian Oil Company in 1951, cutting off a major source of British oil revenue and prompting London to seek American help after Washington refused an earlier British-only plan. The CIA, working with Britain's MI6 under an operation code named Ajax, funded street protests, paid off military officers and spread propaganda against Mosaddegh through August 1953.

An initial attempt to arrest Mosaddegh on the Shah's order failed and the Shah briefly fled the country, but a second wave of paid demonstrators and army units loyal to the plot overran the capital on 19 August 1953. Mosaddegh was arrested and later given a suspended sentence, while the Shah returned to rule with strengthened security services for the next 26 years.

Syagrius, the man Clovis defeated at Soissons in 486, was not a Roman emperor but a local strongman, the son of a Roman general, ruling the last unattached Roman territory in northern Gaul after the empire's collapse in the west. Clovis was still a pagan king in his twenties leading one of several Frankish groups rather than a single unified people.

The victory gave him the core territory around Paris and Soissons from which he absorbed rival Frankish kings over the following years, sometimes by war and reportedly sometimes by having relatives assassinated. His later conversion to Catholic Christianity, and the Merovingian dynasty he founded, grew directly out of the base he secured that day.

Belgium granted the Congo independence on 30 June 1960 having trained almost no Congolese officers or administrators to run the country it left behind. Within days the army mutinied against its remaining white officers, the mineral-rich province of Katanga declared secession under Moise Tshombe, and Belgium flew paratroopers back in, ostensibly to protect its citizens.

Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba appealed to the United Nations and then to the Soviet Union for help suppressing the secession, which drew the crisis directly into the Cold War. He was dismissed, then arrested, and killed in January 1961 with Belgian and American involvement in the plot against him. UN peacekeepers and mercenary armies fought on for years afterward, and Colonel Joseph Mobutu eventually seized power in a coup in 1965.

Muhammad marched on Mecca in January 630 at the head of a force numbering in the thousands, after a truce with the city's Quraysh leaders had broken down. The city's defenders, aware they were badly outmatched, largely chose not to fight, and Muhammad entered the city he had fled eight years earlier without the mass killing that ancient tribal custom might have expected.

He granted amnesty to almost everyone who had opposed him, including men who had once ordered his followers hunted down. Inside the Kaaba he had the idols that had stood there for generations destroyed, and the shrine was rededicated as the central sanctuary of the religion he had founded, which it has remained since.

Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople for fifty three days before his forces broke through the Theodosian Walls on 29 May 1453. His army, put by later accounts at tens of thousands against perhaps seven thousand defenders, relied on huge bronze cannon built by a Hungarian founder named Orban, who had first offered his services to the Byzantines and gone to the Ottomans when Constantine XI could not pay him.

Constantine XI, the last Byzantine emperor, refused offers of escape by sea and reportedly died fighting near the walls, his body never conclusively identified afterward. The city's fall ended an empire that traced itself back to Rome and gave the Ottomans a capital they renamed Istanbul, from which they governed a realm stretching across three continents.

Unmarked Russian soldiers, known locally as little green men, took control of Crimean airports, government buildings and military bases in late February 2014, weeks after protests had driven Ukraine's president from office in Kyiv. Moscow denied at first that the troops were Russian, though Vladimir Putin later admitted they were.

A referendum held under military occupation on 16 March 2014 reported over 96 percent support for joining Russia, a result the United Nations General Assembly declared invalid. Russia formally absorbed the peninsula days later. Most of the world continues to recognise Crimea as Ukrainian territory, and the annexation set the pattern for Russia's fuller invasion eight years later.

Russia's expansion at Ottoman expense, and its claimed right to protect Orthodox Christians inside the empire, alarmed Britain and France enough that both declared war on Russia in March 1854, joining the Ottomans who had already been fighting since the previous October. Most of the fighting settled around the Russian naval base at Sevastopol in the Crimea.

The siege dragged on for nearly a year, and disease killed far more soldiers than combat did on both sides. Florence Nightingale's work reorganising military hospitals during the siege changed nursing practice afterward, and Sevastopol finally fell in September 1855, ending a war that left roughly half a million dead and Russia's Black Sea ambitions checked for a generation.

A crossbow's mechanical trigger let a soldier draw and hold the string under load, then release it at will, unlike a longbow which demanded years of practice to draw at full strength. This meant a garrison or a levy of peasants with no archery training could be armed with a weapon capable of punching through mail at close range within weeks rather than a lifetime.

The Church tried to ban the crossbow's use against Christians at the Second Lateran Council in 1139, calling it too lethal and unchivalrous, a prohibition largely ignored by the armies that kept using it. Its slower reload compared to a bow made it better suited to sieges and defensive positions than to the open field, which shaped how medieval commanders deployed crossbowmen for the next several centuries.

On the night of 31 December 406, groups of Vandals, Suebi and Alans crossed the frozen Rhine near Mainz, a river the Roman army had held as a defensive line for centuries. A Frankish force allied to Rome tried to stop them at the riverbank and reportedly killed the Vandal king Godigisel before being overwhelmed by the sheer number of people crossing behind him.

Rome's Rhine garrisons had already been thinned to fight civil wars elsewhere in the empire, leaving too few troops to seal the breach once it opened. The tribes moved on through Gaul largely unopposed for the next two years, and the crossing is remembered as the moment the Rhine frontier, long treated as a solid boundary, stopped functioning as one at all.

Roman law barred a general from bringing an army into Italy proper, and the Rubicon, a minor stream in the north, marked that boundary. When the Senate ordered Caesar to disband his command in January 49 BCE, he led a single legion across it instead, reportedly telling his officers the die was cast.

The phrase survives better than the stream itself, whose exact course is no longer certain. Caesar's move triggered immediate civil war against Pompey and the Senate's loyalists, a conflict Caesar won within four years, after which he was made dictator for life, a title that lasted less than twelve months.

Fidel Castro had landed with fewer than 20 surviving fighters in the Sierra Maestra mountains in December 1956, after the yacht Granma ran aground and Batista's army ambushed most of the group on the beach. From that remnant his forces built a guerrilla campaign that spread across the island over the next two years, joined by columns led by Che Guevara and Camilo Cienfuegos.

Batista's army largely stopped fighting rather than defending a government few believed could survive; he flew into exile in the Dominican Republic on New Year's Eve 1958. Castro's forces entered Havana on 8 January 1959. The new government nationalised American-owned businesses within two years, prompting a United States trade embargo that has lasted, in modified form, ever since.

Allied planners spent over a year assembling the ships, landing craft and deception operations behind the invasion of Normandy, including a fictitious army group under General Patton meant to convince German command the real target was Calais. Poor weather forced a one-day postponement before General Eisenhower committed to 6 June 1944 on a narrow forecast of clearing skies.

Roughly 156,000 troops landed across five beaches, codenamed Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, supported by airborne drops inland the night before. Casualties at Omaha Beach were especially heavy, where American troops faced well-sited German defences on high ground, but by nightfall the Allies held a foothold that would not be dislodged.

Damietta sat on a Nile branch behind a chain-guarded tower and a floating barrier, and it took the Fifth Crusade a year and a half of siege, from 1218 into November 1219, to break through. Disease killed far more of the besieging army than combat did during that time, including the papal legate's own troops.

With the port finally in hand, the Crusaders pushed south toward Cairo the following summer, but the annual Nile flood trapped their army between rising water and the Egyptian forces of al-Kamil. Surrounded and cut off from supply, the Crusaders surrendered Damietta back in exchange for safe passage out of Egypt in 1221.

Denmark declared war on Sweden in 1657 hoping to catch it exhausted from campaigns in Poland, but Swedish king Charles X Gustav turned his army north instead and marched it straight through Jutland. In January 1658 a hard freeze let his troops cross the frozen Great Belt strait on foot and horse, a route no army had used before.

The surprise crossing brought Swedish forces within reach of Copenhagen and forced Denmark to sign the harsh Treaty of Roskilde that February, ceding Scania and other provinces it never recovered. Charles tried to seize the rest of Denmark within months anyway, breaking the treaty he had just won.

In early 2003, rebel groups in Sudan's western Darfur region took up arms against a government they accused of neglecting non-Arab communities. Khartoum answered by arming Janjaweed militias drawn from Arab herding tribes, who burned villages, poisoned wells and killed civilians alongside government forces. The campaign targeted Darfur's Fur, Zaghawa and Masalit populations specifically, not the rebels alone.

The United States government formally called it genocide in 2004, and the International Criminal Court later indicted President Omar al-Bashir. Estimates of the dead range widely because so much of Darfur was inaccessible to observers, but the United Nations and aid agencies put the figure at roughly 300,000, with several million more driven from their homes into camps.

Franklin Roosevelt was sitting for a portrait at his retreat in Warm Springs, Georgia, on 12 April 1945 when he complained of a terrific headache and collapsed; a cerebral haemorrhage killed him within hours. He was 63 and had begun a fourth term as president just ten weeks earlier, his health already failing from years of heart disease he had kept largely hidden from the public.

Vice President Harry Truman, who had met with Roosevelt only a handful of times and knew nothing of the atomic bomb project, was sworn in that evening. Germany surrendered less than a month later, and Roosevelt did not live to see either that victory or the defeat of Japan he had spent years planning for.

Soviet troops were fighting street by street through central Berlin when Adolf Hitler, holed up in the concrete bunker beneath the Reich Chancellery, married his longtime companion Eva Braun on 29 April 1945. The next afternoon, 30 April, the couple killed themselves; Hitler is generally believed to have shot himself while biting a cyanide capsule, and Braun took poison.

Aides carried the bodies into the Chancellery garden and burned them with petrol, following instructions Hitler had left to prevent his corpse from being displayed. Soviet forces later recovered charred remains they believed to be his. Germany's unconditional surrender followed within a week, and the war in Europe ended on 8 May.

Qin Shi Huang spent his final years sending expeditions to find an elixir of immortality and touring his empire in secret, fearful enough of assassination that his ministers hid his death from the army for weeks after it happened on tour in 210 BC. Court records say he may have died from mercury poisoning, having swallowed pills that alchemists sold him as the cure for death itself.

His tomb complex near Xian had been under construction for decades and held a buried army of terracotta soldiers, each face reportedly individual, arranged to guard him in the afterlife the way real legions had guarded his conquests. The tomb mound itself remains unopened, and the workforce that built it, said by ancient historians to number in the hundreds of thousands, left almost no other trace of who they were.

Mughal forces captured Sambhaji, Shivaji's son and successor as Maratha king, near Sangameshwar in February 1689 and brought him before Aurangzeb. Sambhaji was tortured and executed within weeks after refusing to convert to Islam and surrender Maratha forts, a punishment meant to end Maratha resistance outright.

It did not. Maratha commanders scattered into the hills and kept fighting as a guerrilla force under Sambhaji's brother and later his widow, denying the Mughals any lasting hold on the territory they claimed. The campaign that was supposed to finish the Marathas instead bled Mughal resources for another two decades.

Demak grew out of a small port on Java's north coast that had accepted Islam while Majapahit's Hindu Buddhist court, inland to the south, was losing its grip on the coastal trade that fed it. Its founding ruler, Raden Patah, is remembered in Javanese tradition as a Majapahit prince who converted, though the surviving accounts of his ancestry conflict with each other.

Demak used its fleet and its alliance with coastal Muslim traders to eclipse Majapahit's remaining authority within a generation, and its mosque, built with help from other coastal states, became a centre for spreading Islam further along Java's shore. The sultanate itself proved short lived, splintering into rival successor states within a century of its founding.

Greek tradition remembered a wave of Dorian-speaking Greeks entering the Peloponnese from the north after the Mycenaean palaces had already collapsed, a movement Greeks later called the Return of the Heraclidae. Archaeology has found no clear invasion layer matching a single migration, and many historians now treat the story as a later explanation for a dialect boundary rather than a recorded conquest.

What is better attested is the result: by the time Greek writing resumes with Homer and Hesiod, Doric dialects dominate Sparta, Corinth and much of the Peloponnese, while Ionic and Aeolic speakers held Attica, the islands and Asia Minor's coast. Whatever process produced that split, it reshaped which cities spoke which Greek for the rest of antiquity.

Over three raids between 13 and 15 February 1945, British and American bombers dropped roughly 3,900 tonnes of bombs and incendiaries on Dresden, a city packed with refugees fleeing the advancing Red Army. The resulting firestorm generated hurricane-force winds that pulled oxygen from air raid shelters and melted tram tracks in the streets above.

A German historians' commission convened in 2004 spent five years cross checking city archives, cemetery and registry records against wartime reports, concluding that around 18,000 people died and that the true toll almost certainly did not exceed 25,000, far below the hundreds of thousands claimed at various points by Nazi propaganda and later by neo Nazi groups.

Operation Dynamo began on 26 May 1940 with planners hoping to save perhaps 40,000 men before the port fell. Royal Navy destroyers worked the harbour moles while hundreds of civilian craft, fishing boats and pleasure launches among them, ferried soldiers from the open beaches to ships waiting offshore, all under Luftwaffe bombing that sank dozens of vessels.

By the time the operation ended on 4 June, roughly 338,000 British and French troops had reached England, far more than anyone had planned for. They came home without their tanks, trucks and heavy guns, which were abandoned on the sand, and Churchill warned Parliament that wars are not won by evacuations even as the rescue was being celebrated.

Dutch nobles and townspeople rose against Spanish rule in 1568, driven by heavy taxation, the presence of Spanish garrisons and the persecution of Protestants by the Duke of Alba's tribunals. William of Orange, a nobleman who had served the Spanish crown before breaking with it, became the revolt's leading figure, raising forces and appealing to foreign Protestant allies for support.

The fighting dragged on for decades, splitting the Low Countries roughly along the line that still separates the Netherlands from Belgium: the northern provinces, more Protestant, held out and effectively governed themselves from the 1580s, while the south stayed under Spanish control. Spain did not formally recognise Dutch independence until the Peace of Munster in 1648, after eighty years of intermittent war.

Taizong came to the Tang throne in 626 after killing two brothers in a succession struggle, and within four years turned his new dynasty's army against the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, which had dominated the northern steppe and once forced tribute out of the Tang court itself.

A harsh winter in 627 had already weakened the Turkic herds and split their leadership, and Tang generals exploited the disorder to shatter the khaganate by 630, taking its khan prisoner. The victory opened the trade routes of Central Asia to Tang control and let Taizong's court claim the additional title of Heavenly Khan over the steppe peoples who submitted afterward.

Construction workers on East Berlin's Stalinallee walked off the job on 16 June 1953 over a government order raising production quotas by ten percent without extra pay. The strike spread overnight to factories and towns across East Germany, and by the next day hundreds of thousands of workers in over 700 towns had joined marches and strikes demanding free elections and lower quotas.

The East German government could not control the scale of the unrest on its own, and Soviet tanks and troops moved into East Berlin on 17 June, opening fire on crowds and declaring martial law. Estimates of the dead range from around 55 to over 100, with many more arrested. The Soviet garrison remained the ultimate guarantor of the regime for the rest of its existence.

On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, around 1,200 Irish Volunteers and Irish Citizen Army members occupied the General Post Office and other buildings in Dublin. Patrick Pearse read a proclamation declaring an independent Irish Republic from the GPO steps. Most Dubliners that morning were bewildered rather than supportive, and the rebels held out for less than a week against British artillery and reinforcements.

The fighting killed around 485 people, many of them civilians caught in the crossfire, and left much of central Dublin in ruins. British courts martial executed sixteen of the rising's leaders, including Pearse and James Connolly, over the following weeks. The executions, more than the rising itself, shifted Irish public opinion toward the republican cause that fought the War of Independence three years later.

Edward of York was proclaimed king in London on 4 March 1461, but the crown was not secure until his Lancastrian rivals were beaten in the field. That fight came three weeks later at Towton in Yorkshire, fought in a snowstorm on Palm Sunday. Heralds who counted the dead afterward gave a figure near 28,000, a toll later chroniclers pushed even higher.

The scale came partly from a royal order that no quarter be given to fleeing Lancastrians, so men were cut down in the retreat and while crossing a swollen river. Edward, eighteen years old, was crowned formally that June. He would rule twice, losing the throne briefly to the restored Henry VI in 1470 before retaking it the following year.

President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed the Philippine-American War over on 4 July 1902, a date chosen for its symbolism rather than any single Filipino surrender. By then Emilio Aguinaldo had already been captured the previous year and had sworn allegiance to the United States, and most organised resistance in Luzon had collapsed.

The proclamation did not stop the fighting. Moro communities in the southern islands and scattered guerrilla bands elsewhere kept resisting American rule for years afterward, in campaigns the US government simply declined to call a war. Civil governance under William Howard Taft had already begun replacing military rule in areas judged pacified before the official end date arrived.

Charles I raised his standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642, after years of disputes with Parliament over taxation, religion and the extent of royal authority had broken down into open preparation for war. Both sides had spent the preceding months securing arms, garrisons and the loyalty of local militias across England before the first serious fighting began that autumn.

The war split families, towns and counties rather than following any simple regional line, and it ran through several distinct campaigns over the next several years. It ended with Charles's capture, trial and execution in 1649, and with England governed for the only time in its history without a monarch, first under Parliament and then under Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector.

Haile Selassie had ruled Ethiopia since 1930, and famine, army mutinies over unpaid wages and student protests over land reform brought his government down in 1974. A committee of military officers, the Derg, arrested him in September and abolished the monarchy he had headed for forty-four years.

The Derg executed dozens of former ministers and nobles that November without trial, and within three years Mengistu Haile Mariam had eliminated his rivals within the committee to take sole control. Haile Selassie died in custody in August 1975; the Derg said it was natural causes, though later investigations found evidence he was killed.

Argentine forces landed on the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982, acting on a long standing claim to territory Britain had held since 1833. Britain's ruling military junta in Buenos Aires had hoped an unopposed seizure would rally a population angry over economic collapse, and expected London to accept the loss of a distant, sparsely populated colony.

Britain sent a naval task force over 8,000 miles to retake the islands instead, and the war turned on the sinking of the Argentine cruiser Belgrano and, days later, the British destroyer Sheffield. Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June after seventy four days of fighting that killed around 900 people combined, and the junta's defeat helped bring down the government in Buenos Aires within a year.

The Han court had already been hollowed out by eunuch factions, warlords and the Yellow Turban uprising decades before its formal end. In 220 the general Cao Pi forced the last emperor, Xian, to abdicate, ending four centuries of Han rule and installing his own state of Wei in its place.

Two rival claimants, Shu Han and Wu, refused to recognise Wei, and China split into the Three Kingdoms, a division that lasted roughly sixty years before reunification under the Jin. Novelists and playwrights returned to that period for over a thousand years afterward, drawn to generals and strategists whose loyalties shifted as the old empire came apart.

Soviet forces under Zhukov and Konev closed on Berlin in April 1945, fighting through suburbs and then through the city itself street by street against a defence of regular troops, Hitler Youth boys and old men drafted into the Volkssturm. Artillery bombardment reduced much of central Berlin to rubble before the fighting even reached the Reichstag.

German garrison commander Helmuth Weidling surrendered the city on 2 May 1945, two days after Hitler's suicide in the Fuhrerbunker nearby. Soviet casualties in the assault on the city are estimated at over 80,000 dead, a toll the Soviet high command accepted in order to take the capital before its Western allies could reach it.

German forces crossed the Meuse at Sedan on 13 May 1940, bypassing the Maginot Line's fortifications through the Ardennes forest, ground French planners had judged too dense for tanks. Panzer divisions under commanders including Guderian and Rommel then raced for the Channel coast rather than pausing to consolidate, splitting the Allied armies in two within days.

Paris fell without a fight on 14 June, and Marshal Philippe Petain, the aging hero of Verdun, asked for an armistice rather than continue resistance. France signed on 22 June in the same railway carriage at Compiegne where Germany had accepted defeat in 1918, and the country was split into an occupied north and a nominally independent Vichy south.

The rupiah lost most of its value during the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and by early 1998 prices for basic goods had climbed so far that riots broke out in cities across Indonesia. In May, security forces shot and killed four student protesters at Trisakti University in Jakarta, which triggered days of wider rioting in which over a thousand people died, many in fires set during looting.

Thousands of students occupied the parliament building demanding Suharto's resignation, and one by one his own cabinet ministers and military allies withdrew their support. On 21 May 1998 Suharto announced his resignation on television after 31 years in power, handing the presidency to his vice president, B.J. Habibie, and opening the period Indonesians call Reformasi.

The siege that ended the Aztec Empire lasted roughly ten weeks, from May to 13 August 1521. Hernan Cortes's small Spanish force could not have taken the lake city alone; it depended on tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other indigenous allies who had their own reasons to break Aztec dominance, and on brigantines built to cut off Tenochtitlan's causeways and canoe traffic.

Smallpox, introduced by earlier contact with Europeans, had already killed the emperor Cuitlahuac and weakened the city's defenders before the final assault under his successor Cuauhtemoc. The Spanish razed much of Tenochtitlan and built Mexico City on its ruins, using its stones in the new capital's churches and government buildings.

Finland had declared independence from Russia in December 1917, and within weeks the new state split along its existing class divide. Fighting began on 27 January 1918 between the socialist Red Guards, based in the industrial south, and the White Guards, a conservative force under General Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim backed by the rural north and later by German troops.

The war lasted about three and a half months and ended with a White victory in May 1918. Roughly 36,000 people died, a large share of them Red prisoners who died in internment camps from disease and starvation after the fighting stopped rather than in combat itself. The war left a bitterness in Finnish society that outlasted the independence it had settled.

Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon sent troops into Palestine within a day of Israel's declaration of independence on 14 May 1948, expecting the fledgling state's militias to collapse quickly against regular Arab armies. Fighting had already been under way for months between Jewish and Arab paramilitaries as British forces withdrew from the mandate.

Israeli forces held the line through the first weeks and, once armed with weapons smuggled in from Czechoslovakia and elsewhere, pushed beyond the 1947 UN partition boundaries during a series of truces and renewed offensives into 1949. Armistice agreements left Israel holding roughly 78 percent of former Mandatory Palestine, while hundreds of thousands of Palestinians fled or were expelled and became refugees.

Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro formed the Balkan League in 1912 with backing from Russia, then declared war on the Ottoman Empire that October while it was still recovering from the loss of Libya to Italy the year before. Bulgarian forces pushed toward Constantinople while Serbian and Greek armies cleared Ottoman garrisons from Macedonia and much of the remaining European territory.

By the armistice in December 1912 the Ottomans held little more than a strip around the capital and a few besieged fortresses; the Treaty of London in May 1913 confirmed the loss of nearly all remaining Ottoman land in Europe. The victors then fell out almost immediately over how to divide Macedonia, setting up the second war within weeks of the first one ending.

By early September 1914 the German First Army had swung so close to Paris that the French government evacuated to Bordeaux. Military governor Joseph Gallieni requisitioned around six hundred Paris taxicabs to rush reinforcements to the front along the Marne river, a detail that became legend even though most troops still moved by rail.

The battle involved more than two million men along a front stretching roughly 250 kilometres. General Alexander von Kluck's decision to wheel his army east of Paris exposed his flank, and the combined French and British counterattack forced a German retreat to the Aisne river, where both sides dug in. Neither army broke through again for four years.

Britain had annexed the Transvaal in 1877 with the promise of self-government to follow, but by December 1880 Boer farmers, angry at broken assurances and new taxes, declared the republic restored and besieged British garrisons at Potchefstroom and elsewhere. Boer commandos fought as mounted riflemen using cover and marksmanship rather than formal lines.

The decisive clash came at Majuba Hill in February 1881, where British troops occupying the summit at night were routed the next morning by Boers climbing the slopes and picking them off from below; General Sir George Colley was killed. London chose negotiation over reinforcement, and the Pretoria Convention that followed restored Transvaal self-rule under nominal British oversight.

Pope Urban II spoke at the Council of Clermont in November 1095, urging western knights to march east and aid Byzantine Christians against Seljuk advances while also freeing Jerusalem from Muslim rule. Accounts of the speech vary in wording since none were recorded verbatim at the time, but chroniclers agree crowds reportedly shouted 'Deus vult', it is God's will.

Tens of thousands set out the following year, a mix of trained knights and poorly organised bands of commoners. The expedition took Antioch after a long siege and reached Jerusalem in June 1099, capturing the city after weeks of assault. It established four Crusader states in the Levant, none of which lasted longer than two centuries.

The uprising traces to 9 December 1987, when four Palestinians died after an Israeli army truck collided with a car in Gaza, an incident many Palestinians believed was deliberate. Protests spread within days across the Gaza Strip and West Bank into strikes, boycotts of Israeli goods and stone throwing that Israeli soldiers struggled to contain without live fire.

The uprising ran for roughly six years and drew international attention to images of soldiers confronting stone throwing youths, shifting sympathy that Israel's earlier military victories had not generated. It also returned the Palestine Liberation Organization to diplomatic relevance, and the Madrid and Oslo talks followed in the early 1990s.

The war began after rebels angry over favouritism toward Uthman's own clan broke into his house in Medina in 656 and killed him while he read the Quran. Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin and son in law, was named caliph in his place, but Uthman's kinsman Muawiyah, governor of Syria, refused to accept him without first punishing the killers.

The two sides fought to a stalemate at Siffin in 657, and when Ali agreed to arbitrate the succession rather than fight it out, a faction within his own camp, the Kharijites, judged that decision a betrayal of God's law and later assassinated him. Muawiyah went on to found the Umayyad dynasty, and the dispute over rightful leadership hardened into the Sunni-Shia split.

Chinese officials had been seizing and destroying British opium stocks at Canton through 1839, acting on orders from the commissioner Lin Zexu, who had over a thousand tonnes of the drug dumped and dissolved with lime. British merchants demanded compensation and their government sent a naval expedition rather than pay it.

Steam gunboats and Royal Navy ships outmatched Qing coastal defences along the Chinese coast over the next three years. The 1842 Treaty of Nanking ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain, opened five ports to foreign trade and set the terms other Western powers would copy in later treaties with China.

Rome had almost no navy when the First Punic War began in 264 BCE over the Sicilian city of Messana. Roman engineers are said to have copied a captured Carthaginian warship plank by plank to build their first fleet, and added a boarding device called the corvus that let legionaries fight the way they knew, on foot.

The war ran for 23 years, mostly at sea, and cost both sides heavily in ships lost to storms as much as to battle. Carthage sued for peace in 241 BCE and ceded Sicily, Rome's first province outside the Italian mainland and the opening move in a rivalry that produced two more Punic Wars.

On 22 January 1905, troops guarding the Winter Palace fired on unarmed workers marching to petition the tsar for better conditions, killing well over a hundred in what became known as Bloody Sunday. The killing detonated strikes, mutinies and peasant uprisings across the empire for the rest of the year.

Facing a general strike that had shut down the railways and much of industry, Nicholas II issued the October Manifesto, promising an elected parliament, the Duma, and basic civil freedoms he had never conceded before. The concessions were real but narrow: the tsar retained the power to dissolve the Duma and rule by decree, and he used both within two years.

Both Qing China and Japan had troops in Korea in 1894, ostensibly to help suppress a peasant rebellion, but the rivalry over influence there tipped into open war that August. Japan's modernised army and navy, rebuilt on European models over the previous two decades, outperformed Qing forces on land in Korea and Manchuria and destroyed China's Beiyang fleet at the Battle of the Yalu River.

The Treaty of Shimonoseki in April 1895 forced China to recognise Korean independence, cede Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, and pay a large indemnity. Russia, France and Germany then pressured Japan into giving up Liaodong, a humiliation Japan remembered. The war marked the first time a modern industrial power in Asia had defeated an older regional one, unsettling the balance across the region.

The Fourth Crusade was meant for Egypt, not Constantinople. Debt to Venice for the fleet, and a deposed Byzantine prince offering payment and troops for his own restoration, pulled the army instead to the walls of the Byzantine capital in 1203 and again, after the promised money failed to appear, in April 1204.

The second assault broke through, and Crusaders spent three days looting churches, palaces, and the imperial treasury, sending bronze statues to be melted for coin and relics back to Western cathedrals. A Latin emperor was crowned in Hagia Sophia, and the Byzantine state that re-formed in exile at Nicaea never recovered its former reach before Constantinople fell for good in 1453.

Pope Innocent III issued his call for a new crusade in 1198, aiming, as his predecessors had, to recover Jerusalem, lost to Saladin over a decade earlier. Recruitment ran slowly, and the crusaders who gathered at Venice in 1202 owed the Venetians more money for transport ships than they could pay, a debt that shaped everything the expedition did next.

To settle it, the crusaders were diverted first to attack the Christian city of Zara on the Adriatic, then drawn into a succession dispute in Constantinople itself. The campaign never reached Jerusalem at all; it ended instead with the sack of Constantinople in 1204, an outcome Innocent had not called for and tried, too late, to disown.

Louis XIV crossed the Rhine in May 1672 with an army far larger than anything the Dutch Republic could field, and his forces took town after town along the eastern approaches within weeks. The Dutch call the year rampjaar, the disaster year: the government of Johan de Witt collapsed under the shock, and a mob later killed de Witt and his brother in The Hague.

With the army routed, the Dutch opened the sluices and broke the dikes around Amsterdam, flooding the polders to create a barrier of water the French could not cross. William of Orange, raised to stadtholder amid the crisis, built a coalition with Spain and the Holy Roman Emperor against France, turning a near collapse into a war that dragged on for six more years.

Prussia's chancellor Otto von Bismarck goaded Paris into declaring war on 19 July 1870 over a Spanish succession dispute, after leaking an edited telegram that made a routine diplomatic exchange at Bad Ems read as a French humiliation. French public opinion, already primed to see Prussia as an upstart rival, demanded war before Berlin had to ask for one.

Within six weeks Prussian and allied German armies had encircled and destroyed the main French field force at Sedan.
