The war dragged on through a siege of Paris into early 1871, and its settlement, a huge indemnity and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, left a grievance the French carried into the next war with Germany forty-three years later.

Frederick II inherited the Prussian throne in May 1740 and, within months, marched into the Austrian province of Silesia, exploiting a succession crisis after Emperor Charles VI's death without a male heir. The seizure violated Austria's guarantees and drew much of Europe into the War of the Austrian Succession.

On the battlefield Frederick favoured the oblique order, massing infantry and cavalry against one flank of an enemy line rather than attacking it evenly. Prussia kept Silesia through two further wars, and its rich textile and mining industries roughly doubled the state's tax revenue, funding the army that later fought the Seven Years' War.

France had returned to reoccupy Vietnam after Japan's defeat, and negotiations with Ho Chi Minh's government collapsed after a French cruiser shelled Haiphong harbour in November 1946, killing hundreds of Vietnamese civilians. Viet Minh forces attacked French positions in Hanoi on 19 December 1946, and Ho Chi Minh withdrew his government to the mountains to fight a guerrilla war.

The conflict dragged on for nearly eight years, with France relying increasingly on American funding as the Cold War reframed the fighting as a front against communism. Viet Minh commander Vo Nguyen Giap besieged a French garrison at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, and its surrender that May ended French rule and split Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

Paris crowds stormed the Bastille fortress on 14 July 1789, seeking gunpowder rather than the small handful of prisoners held inside, and killed the governor after he surrendered. The building's fall, more symbolic than militarily decisive, followed weeks of crisis after King Louis XVI's finance minister was dismissed and rumours spread of a royal crackdown on the newly formed National Assembly.

Within weeks the Assembly abolished feudal privileges and adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, dismantling the legal basis of the old order faster than anyone had predicted that summer. The monarchy survived in a weakened form for three more years, but the direction of events, toward a constitutional and then a republican France, was set almost immediately.

Allied troops had landed on the Gallipoli peninsula in April 1915 aiming to force open the Dardanelles and knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war. Eight months of trench fighting in the hills above the beaches gained almost no ground against Ottoman forces under Mustafa Kemal, later known as Ataturk. British commanders finally accepted the position was hopeless and began withdrawing troops from Anzac Cove and Suvla Bay in December 1915.

The last men left Cape Helles on 9 January 1916, and the entire evacuation was carried out without a single casualty, unlike almost everything that had preceded it. The campaign had cost roughly 130,000 dead on both sides for no strategic gain. For Australia and New Zealand the landings became a founding national memory, marked every year on Anzac Day.

Mahatma Gandhi was walking to an evening prayer meeting in the grounds of Birla House in New Delhi on 30 January 1948 when Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for concessions to Muslims and for the partition of India, pushed through the crowd and shot him three times at close range. Gandhi died within minutes.

Godse and a co-conspirator were tried, convicted and hanged the following year; several accomplices received prison terms. Gandhi's death came less than six months after independence and partition had already killed hundreds of thousands, and it briefly stilled the communal violence still convulsing the new republic he had spent his final weeks trying to calm.

Temujin spent decades building alliances and defeating rival Mongol and Tatar clans before a council of chieftains, a kuriltai, declared him Genghis Khan, ruler of all, in 1206. He had survived enslavement as a young man and the killing of allies who betrayed him, and he rebuilt the steppe's fractured clans into a single military structure organised around loyalty to him rather than lineage.

He reorganised Mongol society into units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, breaking older tribal loyalties and promoting commanders on merit. Within a few years this new army turned outward against the Western Xia and Jin states in China and the Khwarazmian empire in Central Asia, beginning the conquests that would make the Mongol empire the largest contiguous land empire in history.

Fighting broke out in the early hours of 8 August 2008 when Georgian forces moved into South Ossetia, a breakaway region backed by Russia since the 1990s, and Russia responded within hours with a large armoured and air counteroffensive that pushed deep into undisputed Georgian territory.

The war lasted five days before a French-brokered ceasefire took hold, but Russian troops remained in South Ossetia and the second breakaway region, Abkhazia, both of which Russia formally recognised as independent states days later. Most of the world still regards them as Georgian territory under Russian occupation.

The uprising began in the summer of 1524 in the Black Forest and Upper Swabia, where peasants refused to pay dues that in some places included counting geese laying enough eggs to feed a landlord's household. Their grievances, gathered into the Twelve Articles the following year, asked for an end to serfdom, the right to choose their own pastors and relief from new taxes and tithes.

Martin Luther, whose ideas the peasants invoked, condemned the revolt once it turned violent and urged princes to crush it without mercy. By the time the fighting ended in 1525, the aristocracy's armies, far better equipped than the peasant bands, had killed an estimated 100,000 of roughly 300,000 who had risen up, and none of the Twelve Articles were granted.

On 18 January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at the captured palace of Versailles, the assembled German princes proclaimed King Wilhelm I of Prussia as emperor of a new German Reich. Holding the ceremony inside a French royal palace, while Paris itself was still under siege by German guns, was a deliberate humiliation that France did not forget.

Bismarck had spent the previous decade manoeuvring Prussia through wars with Denmark, Austria and now France to bring the smaller German states under Prussian leadership rather than Austrian. The empire he built was a federation of kingdoms and duchies dominated by Prussia, with a parliament, the Reichstag, that had limited power over the chancellor.

Lincoln spoke for around two minutes at the dedication of a soldiers' cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania on 19 November 1863, four and a half months after the battle. He was not the day's main speaker; the orator Edward Everett had already spoken for roughly two hours, and some newspapers barely mentioned Lincoln's remarks at the time.

The speech survives in five manuscript copies in Lincoln's own hand, none identical, so historians cannot fix its exact wording with certainty. Its opening line, invoking a nation conceived in liberty, and its closing call for government of the people, by the people, for the people, have since become the most quoted words in American political history.

English Protestant nobles invited William of Orange, ruler of the Dutch Republic and husband of James II's daughter Mary, to intervene after James's Catholicism and his moves toward absolute rule alarmed Parliament. William landed with a Dutch army at Brixham in November 1688, and support for James collapsed so quickly that he fled to France before any major battle was fought on English soil.

Parliament declared the throne vacant and offered it jointly to William and Mary in 1689, on terms set out in a Bill of Rights that limited royal power over taxation, standing armies and the calling of Parliament. The near bloodless outcome in England let contemporaries call it glorious, though fighting over the same succession continued for years in Ireland and Scotland.

Emperor Taizong of Tang, who had already broken the Eastern Turks and Gaochang, led a huge army into Goguryeo territory in 645, expecting the same swift result. His forces took several fortified towns quickly but stalled at Ansi, a fortress whose garrison held out through repeated assaults and an enormous earthen siege ramp built against its walls.

Winter closed in before Ansi fell, and Taizong withdrew his army rather than risk it in the Manchurian cold, later admitting the campaign had failed to achieve its aim. Goguryeo survived this invasion by decades, though the kingdom would eventually fall in 668 to a combined Tang and Silla assault that Ansi's defenders were no longer there to resist.

The Gokturks began as ironworking vassals of the Rouran Khaganate on the Mongolian steppe. Under their leader Bumin, they rebelled and in 552 defeated the Rouran outright, killing their khan and taking over the confederation that had ruled the eastern steppe for over a century.

Bumin's brother Istemi then pushed the new empire's reach west, allying with the Sasanians and later the Byzantines against shared rivals, until Gokturk authority stretched from Manchuria to the Black Sea's northern shore. It was the first steppe empire to leave its own written records, in a runic script carved into stone monuments, rather than being known only through the accounts of settled neighbours.

The fleet that landed in East Anglia in 865 was unlike the raiding parties England had faced for decades: a coalition of Danish and Norwegian warbands under leaders including Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan, come to conquer land rather than take plunder home. Within a few years it had toppled the kingdoms of Northumbria and East Anglia and installed puppet rulers in Mercia.

Only Wessex held out, under Alfred, who paid off part of the army in 871 and finally broke the remaining Danish force at Edington in 878. The treaty that followed split England along a rough line, leaving Danish law and settlement across the north and east under what became known as the Danelaw. The invasion reshaped English political geography for generations.

Mao Zedong ordered China's peasants organised into vast communes in 1958 and set wildly inflated grain and steel targets, encouraging local officials to report harvests far above what fields actually produced. Backyard furnaces meant to boost steel output instead melted down usable tools and cookware into worthless pig iron, while farmland went untended as labour was diverted to construction and industry.

Local cadres, afraid to report shortfalls, exported grain and requisitioned what little remained from villages already starving, and officials who tried to warn Mao were purged as rightists. Historians using census and demographic records now estimate between 30 and 45 million excess deaths from famine between 1959 and 1961, among the deadliest events of the twentieth century.

Denmark, Saxony Poland and Russia declared war on Sweden within months of each other in 1700, each hoping to seize territory from a young Swedish king, Charles XII, they judged inexperienced. Charles knocked Denmark out of the war within weeks, then crossed to Estonia and, on 20 November 1700, routed a much larger Russian army besieging Narva during a blinding snowstorm.

Believing Russia broken, Charles spent the next six years campaigning against Saxony and Poland instead of finishing off Tsar Peter I, who used the time to rebuild his army and navy along Western lines. That decision let Russia recover, and Sweden's early dominance gave way over the following two decades to a war that stripped it of most of its Baltic empire and left Russia the region's rising power.

Fighting broke out in the spring of 1821 as Greek bands attacked Ottoman garrisons across the Peloponnese, following a rising planned by the secret society Filiki Eteria and led into Moldavia by Alexander Ypsilantis, a general in the Russian army. Both sides committed massacres in the opening months, at Tripolitsa and on the island of Chios.

The war dragged on for most of a decade before Britain, France and Russia intervened, destroying the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet at Navarino in 1827. Byron's death at Missolonghi in 1824 had already drawn wide European sympathy, and the London Protocol of 1830 recognised an independent Greek state under a monarchy chosen by the powers.

US forces landed on Grenada on 25 October 1983, six days after a faction within the island's Marxist government had executed Prime Minister Maurice Bishop and several of his ministers. President Reagan cited the safety of American medical students on the island and the risk of a Cuban military build up as the justification for the invasion.

Nearly 8,000 US troops, alongside a small Caribbean force, met resistance mainly from Cuban military advisers rather than Grenada's own army, and organised fighting was over within days. The operation restored a pro Western government but drew condemnation at the United Nations, where a General Assembly resolution described it as a flagrant violation of international law.

Hugo Grotius wrote De Jure Belli ac Pacis while in exile in Paris, having fled the Dutch Republic in 1621 after being smuggled out of a fortress prison in a book chest. Published in 1625, the three volume work argued that certain laws bind states even without a shared sovereign or a shared faith, because they arise from reason and from nature rather than from any single ruler's command.

Grotius drew on Roman law, scripture and recent European wars to set out when a war could be considered just, and how prisoners, property and neutral parties should be treated once fighting began. The book circulated widely among diplomats and lawyers within his lifetime, and later writers on international law treated it as a founding text for the field, though Grotius himself never used that name for his subject.

A US led coalition of 35 nations began bombing Iraqi forces on 17 January 1991, five months after Saddam Hussein's army had invaded and annexed Kuwait. The air campaign ran for over a month before a ground offensive began, targeting Iraqi command structures, air defences and the occupying forces dug into Kuwait itself.

The ground war lasted barely a hundred hours once it started on 24 February, and Kuwait was declared liberated within days as Iraqi troops retreated, setting oil wells alight behind them. President Bush ordered a ceasefire on 28 February rather than pursue the war into Baghdad, leaving Saddam Hussein in power for another twelve years.

Chinese alchemists had recorded gunpowder's ingredients, sulphur, saltpetre and charcoal, since at least the ninth century, warning that mixing them carelessly could burn a house down. By around 1000 the Song military had turned that hazard into weapons: fire arrows carrying small powder charges, thrown bombs packed in ceramic or iron shells, and early rocket-propelled arrows launched from tubes.

A Song court official, Tang Fu, is credited with presenting fire-arrow designs to the throne in 1000, and manuals of the following century describe dozens of gunpowder devices in military use. These weapons were incendiary and explosive rather than a true firearm, but the same mixture and casings would develop over the following three centuries into cannon and hand guns that spread westward along trade routes.

Gunpowder reached Europe from China by the thirteenth century, likely carried along trade routes through the Islamic world, and European written references to gunpowder recipes appear from the 1260s onward. Early cannon were slow, unreliable and prone to bursting, but by the mid fourteenth century armies including the English at Crecy in 1346 were bringing primitive guns onto the battlefield alongside older weapons.

The technology spread unevenly: castles built for centuries to resist siege engines and battering rams began to need thicker, lower walls to survive cannon fire, and the cost of founding guns and buying powder shifted military power toward states wealthy enough to afford them. Handheld firearms took another century to become reliable enough to challenge the longbow and crossbow on open ground.

By the mid fifteenth century, cannon capable of breaching stone walls had become standard siege equipment across Europe, and mounted knights increasingly faced infantry carrying handguns or crossbows that could pierce plate armour at close range. The French crown's use of mobile artillery trains against English held fortresses in the 1450s was widely studied by other rulers.

Fortress design changed in response, moving toward lower, angled bastions that deflected cannon fire rather than tall towers that offered an easy target. Knighthood as a battlefield role did not vanish overnight, but the cost of keeping pace with gunpowder tipped military advantage toward states that could afford standing artillery corps rather than feudal levies.

Cannon had been used sporadically in Europe since the early 1300s, but by the 1380s they were common enough in sieges that town walls began to be redesigned around them, lower and thicker rather than tall for scaling ladders. Early handguns, little more than a metal tube on a stick lit by a match cord, spread through infantry ranks alongside crossbows rather than replacing them outright.

The change was gradual rather than a single breakthrough: armoured knights and stone castles remained militarily relevant for another century, and gunpowder weapons of this period were slow to load, inaccurate and prone to misfiring. Their real advantage was against masonry, and siege warfare changed faster than fighting in the open field did.

Students in Gwangju began protesting martial law on 18 May 1980, after General Chun Doo hwan seized power and shut down the National Assembly. Paratroopers sent to suppress the demonstrations beat protesters in the street, and the violence pulled ordinary residents into the uprising, who armed themselves from police stations and pushed the troops out of the city for several days.

The army retook Gwangju on 27 May, killing residents in the final assault on the provincial office where the citizen militia made its last stand. The government's official count put the dead at under 200, but later investigations have put the toll well over that, and the massacre became a founding grievance of South Korea's democracy movement through the 1980s.

Enslaved people on the French colony of Saint Domingue had been in open revolt since 1791, and the war that followed passed through French, Spanish and British intervention and years of fighting under Toussaint Louverture before Jean Jacques Dessalines, his former lieutenant, finished it. Napoleon's attempt to restore slavery and French control in 1802 and 1803 cost tens of thousands of French soldiers to combat and yellow fever.

Dessalines declared independence on 1 January 1804 and renamed the colony Haiti, an indigenous Taino word for the island. It became the first state in the Americas founded by formerly enslaved people and the only one born from a successful slave revolt, at a cost France and its allies never came close to matching in the fighting itself.

Emperor Wu took the Han throne as a teenager in 141 BC and ruled 54 years, turning a dynasty that had paid tribute to the Xiongnu into one fighting on every frontier. Han armies pushed into the Tarim Basin and Central Asia, annexed the northern Korean peninsula, and marched south into what is now Vietnam and Guangdong, more than tripling Han territory.

The campaigns were financed by state monopolies on salt and iron and by a debased currency, burdens that fell on peasant farmers rather than the court. Zhang Qian's mission west, sent to find allies against the Xiongnu, instead mapped trade routes linking China to Central Asia and Rome. Wu's wars left the treasury exhausted and the population smaller than when he began.

Hannibal set out from Iberia in 218 BCE with an army that ancient writers put at close to 40,000 men, plus cavalry and a small number of war elephants, and crossed the Alps in autumn through snow, hostile Gallic tribes, and terrain steep enough that pack animals slid off the paths. Polybius, writing decades later using veterans' accounts, is the main source for the march.

Most of the elephants died in the mountains or soon after, and Hannibal's army arrived in Italy badly reduced by the crossing. It was still enough. Within months he had beaten Roman forces twice, at the Trebia and Lake Trasimene, before the disaster at Cannae two years later.

Peroz I had already been captured once by the Hephthalites in 481 and released only after handing over his son Kavadh as a hostage and paying a large ransom. Rather than accept the loss, he raised a second army and marched northeast toward Balkh to settle the matter directly.

The Hephthalites learned of his approach and prepared an ambush, reportedly digging a trench across his line of march and concealing it. Peroz was killed in the battle in 484 and much of his army with him. The defeat left the Sasanian treasury drained by tribute payments and its eastern frontier exposed for decades afterward.

By 626 Sasanian armies under Chosroes II held Egypt, Syria and Palestine and had camped within sight of Constantinople itself, while Heraclius's own empire was so drained he had reportedly melted church plate to pay his troops. Rather than defend the capital directly, he shipped his army across the Black Sea and struck into Persian territory from the north in 627.

He pushed deep into Mesopotamia, and near the ruins of ancient Nineveh his forces broke a Persian army in a battle fought partly at night. Chosroes fled toward his capital, Ctesiphon, and was overthrown and killed by his own nobles soon after, forcing his successor to make peace and return the territories Persia had seized years earlier.

German colonial authorities in South-West Africa answered a Herero uprising over land seizures with a policy of extermination rather than reconquest. On 2 October 1904 General Lothar von Trotha issued an order stating that every Herero found within German-controlled territory, armed or not, with cattle or without, was to be shot on sight.

Troops drove survivors into the Omaheke desert and sealed off waterholes behind them, leaving thousands to die of thirst, while others were confined in camps such as Shark Island where forced labour, disease and malnutrition killed many more. Estimates put Herero deaths at 40,000 to 80,000, a large majority of the population, with several thousand Nama also killed. Germany did not formally acknowledge the killing as genocide until 2021.

An American B-29, the Enola Gay, dropped an atomic bomb nicknamed Little Boy on Hiroshima on the morning of 6 August 1945. The blast and firestorm that followed killed tens of thousands of people within the first hours, and by the end of that year deaths from injuries and radiation sickness are estimated to have reached roughly 140,000, out of a city population of around 350,000.

Hiroshima had been chosen partly because it had escaped earlier conventional bombing, making it possible to measure the new weapon's effects against a mostly intact city. Three days later a second bomb, Fat Man, was dropped on Nagasaki, and Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, ending the war without the invasion of the Japanese home islands that Allied planners had been preparing.

No party had a majority in the German parliament after the November 1932 election, and the Nazis, though the largest single party, held under a third of the seats. President Paul von Hindenburg had refused Hitler the chancellorship twice before, but conservative advisers convinced him that Hitler could be controlled inside a coalition cabinet where non Nazis held most posts. He was sworn in on 30 January 1933.

Within weeks the Reichstag fire gave the government a pretext to arrest communist opponents, and the Enabling Act of March 1933 let Hitler's cabinet pass laws without parliament at all. The men who thought they could contain him were sidelined or dead within eighteen months. By the summer of 1934 Germany had become a one party dictatorship with no legal opposition left standing.

At Castillon in July 1453, French artillery dug into a fortified camp shattered an English relief force before it could properly deploy, killing the English commander John Talbot in the rout. It was one of the earliest major battles decided largely by cannon fire rather than by cavalry or archers.

No formal peace treaty followed; English resistance in Gascony simply collapsed afterward, and Bordeaux surrendered that October. England kept only Calais on the French mainland, and the war's end let the French crown turn its enlarged standing army and taxation powers toward consolidating royal authority at home.

Edward III of England claimed the French throne in 1337 through his mother, a Capetian princess, after French nobles instead chose Philip of Valois as king under a rule barring inheritance through women. Philip's seizure of the English held duchy of Gascony that same year gave Edward's claim a practical grievance to attach to.

The conflict that followed ran with long truces and resumptions across more than a century, well beyond either king's lifetime, and drew in Flanders, Castile and Brittany at various points as allies were pulled into the two crowns' quarrel. It was fought largely on French soil, and its name, coined by nineteenth century historians rather than contemporaries, describes a span of roughly 116 years rather than a single continuous war.

Students and workers in Budapest began the revolution on 23 October 1956 by marching on the radio building to demand the broadcast of their reform demands; secret police fired on the crowd, and the protest turned into an armed uprising within hours. For a few days the new government under Imre Nagy negotiated a Soviet withdrawal and announced plans to leave the Warsaw Pact.

Soviet tanks returned to Budapest on 4 November 1956, this time to crush the uprising rather than negotiate with it. Fighting in the streets killed an estimated 2,500 Hungarians and around 700 Soviet soldiers over the following days. Nagy was arrested, later tried in secret and executed in 1958, and roughly 200,000 Hungarians fled across the border into Austria as refugees.

The wars began after reformer Jan Hus was burned at the stake in 1415 despite a promise of safe conduct, and his Czech followers rose against both the Catholic church and the Holy Roman Emperor. Bohemian commander Jan Zizka organised peasant fighters into disciplined units defended by farm wagons chained together into mobile forts.

These wagenburgs carried early cannon and gave lightly armed infantry a fortified position they could drag across a battlefield, letting Hussite forces beat several larger crusading armies sent against them through the 1420s. The wars ended in 1434 with a negotiated compromise that allowed Bohemia limited religious autonomy inside the empire.

Around 1650 BCE, groups from the Levant who had already been settling in the eastern Nile Delta for generations took formal control of Lower Egypt and set up a capital at Avaris. Egyptian sources later called them Hyksos, a Greek rendering of a phrase meaning rulers of foreign lands, and treated their rise as an invasion, though modern evidence suggests a gradual migration rather than a single conquest.

The Hyksos kings adopted Egyptian royal titles and worship of Egyptian gods alongside their own, and their courts brought the horse-drawn war chariot and composite bow into regular use in the Nile valley. Egyptian rulers based in Thebes drove them out around 1550 BCE, and later pharaohs cited that period of foreign rule to justify their own campaigns into the Levant.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi, having unified Japan under his own rule, sent an invasion force of well over a hundred thousand men across to Korea in April 1592, intending to use the peninsula as a route to conquer Ming China. Japanese armies took Seoul within weeks and pushed north rapidly against a Korean army that had not fought a major war in generations.

The invasion stalled at sea, where Admiral Yi Sun sin's fleet, built around ironclad turtle ships, cut Japanese supply lines along the southern coast and won repeated victories, including at Hansan Island in August 1592. Ming China intervened on Korea's side, and years of grinding, inconclusive campaigning followed until Hideyoshi's death in 1598 let Japan withdraw its remaining forces.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched a second army into Korea in 1597 after peace talks with Ming China collapsed, sending roughly 140,000 men back across the strait. Fighting bogged down around fortified Japanese strongholds on the southern coast, and Yi Sun sin's fleet, restored to command after a disgrace, broke a Japanese squadron at Myeongnyang that autumn with a handful of ships.

Hideyoshi died in Kyoto in September 1598 without ever returning to Japan, and his commanders withdrew the remaining forces within weeks. No later ruler of Japan tried to conquer the mainland again for three centuries, and the withdrawal left Korea devastated but nominally intact under the same dynasty.

Korean admiral Yi Sun sin's ships at Sacheon in 1592 were roofed in iron spikes and planking to stop boarders, with a dragon's head at the bow that could vent smoke to blind the enemy. Contemporary accounts describe the hulls as low, broad and hard to grapple, built for ramming and cannon fire rather than the sword fights Japanese crews favoured.

Korea had almost no navy worth the name when the invasion began, and Yi's early wins cut the supply line feeding Japanese armies on land. He kept detailed war diaries, later published as the Nanjung Ilgi, which is most of what is known about how these battles were actually fought.

Huayna Capac died without clearly settling the succession, leaving the empire split between Huascar, ruling from Cusco, and Atahualpa, based in Quito with the seasoned army their father had used to conquer the north. What followed was years of campaigning, executions of rival nobles and the destruction of provincial administration across the Andes.

Atahualpa's generals eventually captured Huascar, but the victory came only shortly before Francisco Pizarro's small expedition landed on the coast in 1532. The exhausted, divided empire he found had already fought itself into a state that made a handful of Spaniards seem worth negotiating with rather than simply crushing.

Atahualpa arrived at Cajamarca fresh from winning the civil war against his brother Huascar, bringing thousands of soldiers to meet a Spanish party of under two hundred men. Pizarro's force ambushed the unarmed royal procession in the town square, killing large numbers of Atahualpa's attendants and seizing the emperor himself within the space of an hour.

Pizarro held Atahualpa for months, collecting an enormous ransom in gold and silver from across the empire before having him garrotted anyway on charges including treason. The killing removed the one figure who might have rallied a unified Inca response, leaving Spanish forces to fight the empire's remaining factions piecemeal.

Topa Inca Yupanqui took the Inca throne around 1471 and turned his father's conquests in the highlands into a much larger empire stretching along the Andes. His forces defeated the Chimor kingdom on Peru's northern coast, absorbing a rival state that had its own long tradition of irrigation engineering and metalworking.

Campaigns under Topa Inca also pushed north into what is now Ecuador and south toward Chile, using a network of roads and way stations that let armies and messages move quickly across difficult terrain. By the time of his death around 1493, the empire he left stretched further than any state South America had previously known.

The Aymara kingdoms around Lake Titicaca, including the Lupaqa and Colla, ran their own irrigated farming and llama herding economies before Inca armies moved against them in the 1470s. Some accounts describe Inca rulers securing alliances through marriage before resorting to outright conquest, though the sequence of diplomacy and war for each kingdom is not always clearly recorded.

Once absorbed, the Altiplano became a major source of llama and alpaca herds and of skilled weavers for the empire's textile economy. The region's fertile shoreline and established roads also gave the Inca a secure route toward the silver producing lands further south that later empires would fight over as well.

Indonesian special forces had already been crossing into East Timor for weeks, and on 16 October 1975 troops killed five foreign television journalists at the border town of Balibo, an attack Indonesia later described as crossfire but which a 2007 New South Wales coroner's inquest found was a deliberate killing by Indonesian soldiers. Fretilin declared independence on 28 November, six days before the main invasion.

Indonesian forces launched a full airborne and seaborne assault on the capital, Dili, on 7 December 1975, days after Portugal withdrew without transferring authority to any government. The occupation that followed lasted 24 years and, by most demographic estimates examined by a later truth commission, killed well over 100,000 East Timorese through violence, forced displacement and famine.

On 4 November 1979, a few weeks after the United States admitted the deposed shah for cancer treatment, several hundred Iranian students loyal to the revolution scaled the walls of the US Embassy in Tehran and took the staff inside captive. Ayatollah Khomeini, who had returned from exile that February, backed the takeover rather than ordering it ended, and it became state policy overnight.

A rescue attempt in April 1980, Operation Eagle Claw, was aborted in the Iranian desert after mechanical failures brought down a helicopter, killing eight American servicemen and embarrassing the Carter administration further. The remaining 52 hostages were released on 20 January 1981, minutes after Ronald Reagan was sworn in as president, ending a captivity that had lasted 444 days.

Iraqi forces crossed into Iran on 22 September 1980, after Saddam Hussein renounced a 1975 border agreement and sought to seize the oil rich province of Khuzestan while Iran's military was still in disarray following its revolution. Iraq's initial gains stalled within months against fiercer resistance than Baghdad had expected.

The war settled into static trench fighting reminiscent of the First World War, with Iraq using chemical weapons against Iranian troops and Iranian commanders sending waves of young volunteers, some of them teenagers, against fortified lines. A ceasefire took effect in August 1988 with the border largely unchanged from where it had started, after a conflict researchers estimate killed several hundred thousand people on each side.

Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, and the war that followed settled into trench warfare reminiscent of the First World War, with static front lines, human wave assaults and repeated use of chemical weapons by Iraqi forces against both Iranian troops and Kurdish civilians. Both sides also attacked oil tankers in the Gulf, drawing in foreign navies to protect shipping.

United Nations Security Council Resolution 598 called for a ceasefire in July 1987, but fighting continued for another year before Iran, exhausted and facing renewed Iraqi gains, accepted its terms on 20 August 1988. The border returned to roughly where it had been before the invasion. Estimates of the dead on both sides run into the hundreds of thousands, with some accounts putting the combined toll over a million.

Mass protests against Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi grew through 1978 into general strikes that shut down Iran's oil industry, and he left the country on 16 January 1979, never to return. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who had directed the movement from exile in France, flew back to Tehran on 1 February to crowds estimated in the millions.

A referendum that April approved an Islamic republic, and Khomeini was installed as its supreme leader under a new constitution finalised that December. The revolution's second shock came in November 1979, when militants seized the US embassy in Tehran and held American staff hostage for 444 days, a crisis that defined Iran's relationship with Washington for a generation.

American and British forces invaded Iraq on 20 March 2003, opening with air strikes on Baghdad and a ground advance from Kuwait, on the claim that Saddam Hussein held stockpiles of chemical and biological weapons. No such stockpiles were ever found, and the intelligence behind the claim was later discredited by official inquiries in both countries.

Baghdad fell within three weeks, but the swift military victory gave way to an insurgency, sectarian civil war between Sunni and Shia militias, and years of occupation that killed far more people than the invasion itself. American combat troops did not fully withdraw until December 2011.

On 21 January 1919, the same day Ireland's newly elected Sinn Fein members convened their own parliament, Dail Eireann, in Dublin, Irish Volunteers ambushed and killed two Royal Irish Constabulary officers at Soloheadbeg in County Tipperary. The killing was not ordered by any central command; the local Volunteers, led by Dan Breen and Sean Treacy, acted on their own initiative, but the date is generally treated as the war's start.

What followed was fought less as open battle than as ambush, assassination and reprisal, waged by small IRA flying columns against police barracks and, from 1920, against the paramilitary Black and Tans brought in from Britain. The violence killed around 2,000 people over two and a half years before a truce in July 1921 led to the Anglo-Irish Treaty and the creation of the Irish Free State.

The rising began on the night of 22 October 1641, when Catholic gentry in Ulster, aiming to seize Dublin Castle and force concessions from Charles I, attacked instead across the province after their plot was betrayed. Settlers were driven from their homes in the cold, and in some districts, notably around Portadown, groups of them were killed outright, feeding wildly inflated pamphlet accounts back in England.

Those pamphlets, printed in London within weeks and claiming tens of thousands dead, shaped English opinion for a decade and hardened Oliver Cromwell's resolve when he arrived in Ireland in 1649. His campaign there, including the storming of Drogheda and Wexford, killed thousands more and confiscated land on a scale that reshaped Irish landholding for generations.

The Society of United Irishmen, founded by Protestant and Catholic radicals including Theobald Wolfe Tone, drew on the language of the French Revolution to demand an Ireland free of British rule and of sectarian division between its members. Their planned rising broke out in May 1798 in Leinster and reached its fiercest fighting at Vinegar Hill in County Wexford, where rebel forces held out for weeks before being driven back.

A small French force under General Humbert landed in County Mayo in August to support the rising but arrived too late and was defeated within weeks. Wolfe Tone was captured aboard a French ship and died in custody before he could be executed. The government's response was the Act of Union of 1800, which abolished the separate Irish Parliament and brought Ireland directly under Westminster rule.

A rider without a stirrup fights from the saddle at a disadvantage, unable to brace for a lance strike or stand to shoot. When iron stirrups reached the Sahel through trans-Saharan trade routes, they let West African horsemen fight mounted rather than merely ride to battle and dismount.

Kingdoms including Mali and later Songhai built armies around this cavalry, using horses bred or imported across the desert since the region's own climate was poor for breeding them. Cavalry became the visible mark of Sahelian state power, and later travellers such as Ibn Battuta described the mounted retinues of Mali's rulers with particular attention.

On 29 June 2014, in the city of Mosul which its fighters had seized weeks earlier, the Islamic State's spokesman Abu Muhammad al-Adnani announced that the group's leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, was now caliph over a state spanning captured territory in Iraq and Syria. Baghdadi appeared soon after at Mosul's Great Mosque to claim the title in person.

The declared caliphate demanded allegiance from Muslims worldwide and imposed its own courts, currency and school curriculum on roughly eight million people at its peak. Iraqi and Syrian forces, backed by an international coalition, retook Mosul in 2017 and Raqqa the same year, and Baghdad's prime minister declared the group's territorial defeat in December 2017.

Italian troops entered Rome in September 1870 and annexed the city the following year, taking the last piece the new kingdom needed. Pope Pius IX, stripped of the Papal States he had ruled for over a thousand years, refused to recognise the seizure and shut himself inside the Vatican, a standoff that outlasted his own papacy.

Rome became the capital of a kingdom stitched together over the previous decade from Piedmont, Lombardy, the Two Sicilies and a string of smaller states, mostly under the diplomacy of Camillo Cavour and the campaigns of Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteers. The pope and the Italian state remained formally unreconciled until the Lateran Treaty of 1929.

Charles VIII of France crossed the Alps in 1494 to press a dynastic claim on the kingdom of Naples, marching an army equipped with mobile bronze siege cannon that reduced Italian fortresses far faster than the older stone towers had been built to withstand. His initial advance through Florence and Rome met little resistance.

Spain, the Holy Roman Empire and several Italian states soon combined against him, and Charles was forced to withdraw within a year without keeping Naples. The fighting he started continued intermittently for over sixty years, drawing in most of Western Europe's major powers and leaving Italy's smaller states as battlegrounds for foreign armies rather than independent actors.

Italian and Allied negotiators secretly signed an armistice at Cassibile in Sicily on 3 September 1943, days after Allied troops had landed on the Italian mainland. King Victor Emmanuel III and the government of Marshal Pietro Badoglio, who had replaced Mussolini in a palace coup two months earlier, kept the deal hidden until it was made public on 8 September.

German forces, expecting exactly this, moved quickly to disarm Italian units and occupy Rome and the north, rescuing Mussolini from captivity and installing him as head of a puppet state at Salo. Italy went on to declare war on Germany the following month, leaving the peninsula fighting itself for the remainder of the war.

Between August and November 1888, five women working as prostitutes in the impoverished Whitechapel district, Mary Ann Nichols, Annie Chapman, Elizabeth Stride, Catherine Eddowes and Mary Jane Kelly, were killed and mutilated within a small radius of streets. Scotland Yard investigated hundreds of suspects and received hoax letters, including one signed 'Jack the Ripper' that gave the killer his name in the press.

No one was ever charged, and the case file was formally closed decades later with the killer unidentified. The murders drew national attention to the slum conditions of the East End and to the vulnerability of women working the streets there, and the unsolved identity has since generated more amateur and professional theorising than perhaps any other Victorian crime.

Charles Edward Stuart, grandson of the deposed James II, landed in the Hebrides in July 1745 with seven companions and almost no money, hoping to raise Scotland for his father's claim to the British throne. Highland clans rallied to him faster than either side expected, and by September he held Edinburgh and had beaten a government army at Prestonpans.

His army marched as far south as Derby before its commanders, wary of thin French support and English indifference, turned back. The retreat ended at Culloden in April 1746, where Cumberland's forces destroyed the Jacobite army in under an hour. Charles fled disguised, eventually reaching France, and the rising's failure brought harsh reprisals against the Highland clan system that had supported him.

The revolt took its name from Jacques Bonhomme, a mocking nickname the nobility used for peasants, and it began in the Beauvaisis region north of Paris in May 1358. Bands of rural labourers, angry at taxes raised to pay ransoms after the disastrous defeat at Poitiers, burned manor houses and killed nobles and their families, in some accounts including women and children.

The rebels found an ally in Etienne Marcel, the Paris merchant leader, but their army had no real military structure. Charles of Navarre led the nobility's counterattack, luring the peasant captain Guillaume Cale to a parley under truce and then seizing and beheading him. Noble reprisals across the countryside killed thousands of peasants within weeks, ending the revolt by late June.

By the summer of 1192 Richard I had already agreed peace terms in principle when Saladin's nephew stormed Jaffa's citadel garrison out. Richard sailed down from Acre and landed on the beach with a small party, wading ashore before his main force disembarked, and drove the Ayyubid troops back out of the town in a single afternoon.

Days later Saladin's army counterattacked in the open ground outside Jaffa. Richard is said to have fought bareheaded on foot with a handful of knights and held the line until reinforcements arrived. The engagement pushed both sides toward the treaty signed that September, which left Jerusalem under Muslim rule but allowed Christian pilgrims access to the city.

On 13 April 1919, Brigadier General Reginald Dyer marched about fifty riflemen to the single exit of Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden in Amritsar where thousands had gathered for a spring festival and a banned political meeting. He ordered them to fire into the crowd without warning and kept them firing for roughly ten minutes, stopping only when ammunition ran low.

The Hunter Commission that investigated set the toll at 379 dead; a Congress inquiry that Gandhi helped organise counted nearly 1,200. Dyer told the commission he had fired to, in his words, strike terror throughout Punjab. The Commons voted 247 to 37 to condemn him in 1920; the Lords voted 129 to 86 to back him instead.

Jan Palach, a 20-year-old philosophy student, walked to the fountain in front of Prague's National Museum on 16 January 1969, poured petrol over himself and set it alight. He ran flaming toward Wenceslas Square before collapsing; bystanders put out the fire, but he had suffered burns over most of his body and died in hospital three days later.

He left a letter, addressed to fellow students and signed Torch Number One, protesting the Soviet-led invasion that had crushed the Prague Spring the previous August and calling for renewed resistance. His funeral drew a huge silent crowd through Prague and became one of the last open demonstrations before Czechoslovak authorities tightened control again. Two more young men set themselves on fire in the following months.

Japanese forces landed on Java in March 1942 after weeks of fighting across the archipelago's oilfields and outer islands, and the Dutch colonial army, hopelessly outmatched, surrendered within days. Dutch and other European civilians were interned in camps for the rest of the war, while many Indonesians initially welcomed troops who promised liberation from centuries of colonial rule.

That welcome soured quickly under forced labour drafts, known as romusha, and requisitioning that produced famine in parts of Java. The occupation also trained and armed Indonesian youth militias and gave nationalist leaders like Sukarno a public platform they had been denied under the Dutch, groundwork that let independence be declared within days of Japan's surrender in August 1945.

Diponegoro, a Yogyakarta prince passed over for the throne, went to war in 1825 after Dutch surveyors ran a road through land holding his mother's grave, a grievance on top of years of resentment at Dutch interference in the sultanate. He fought as a guerrilla, claiming the religious authority of a coming Javanese ruler, and for two years the campaign badly strained Dutch resources.

The Dutch answer was a network of fortified posts that boxed in his forces and starved the countryside supplying them. Diponegoro was captured in 1830 during talks he had been promised would be safe conduct, and exiled to Manado and then Makassar, where he died in 1855. Dutch military records and later historians put Javanese deaths, mostly from famine and disease rather than combat, at over 200,000.

Roman taxation and a governor's seizure of temple funds set off open revolt in Judea in the year 66, after years of smaller clashes between Jewish communities and Roman authority. A Roman garrison in Jerusalem was overwhelmed early on, and a relief force under the Syrian governor Cestius Gallus was driven off, an early setback that encouraged the rebellion to spread.

Rome responded with a sustained campaign under Vespasian and then his son Titus, who took Jerusalem in the year 70 after a months-long siege and destroyed the Second Temple. Fighting continued in isolated strongholds for three more years, ending at Masada in 73.

President Kennedy was riding in an open convertible through Dealey Plaza in Dallas on 22 November 1963 when shots were fired from the Texas School Book Depository. He was struck in the head and neck and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital shortly after 1pm. Lee Harvey Oswald, a former Marine and warehouse employee at the depository, was arrested that afternoon.

Vice President Lyndon Johnson took the oath of office aboard Air Force One before it left Dallas. Oswald was shot dead two days later by Jack Ruby while being transferred between jails, an act broadcast live on television. The Warren Commission concluded in 1964 that Oswald acted alone, a finding that opinion polls have shown much of the American public has never fully accepted.

Joan was around seventeen when she arrived at the besieged city of Orleans in 1429, having convinced the dauphin Charles at Chinon that she carried instructions from God to save France. On 8 May, after several days of fighting, the English abandoned the siege, and Joan rode with the army that escorted Charles to Reims to be crowned Charles VII within two months.

Burgundian soldiers captured her at Compiegne in May 1430 and sold her to the English, who put her before a church court at Rouen on charges of heresy rather than treason, since only a church court could execute her without French royal sanction. Convicted, she was burned at the stake on 30 May 1431, still not twenty years old. A later trial cleared her name in 1456, and she was canonised in 1920.

Joan of Arc was burned at the marketplace in Rouen on 30 May 1431. She had been captured by Burgundian troops the previous year and sold to the English, who put her on trial not for military resistance but for heresy, focusing much of the questioning on her decision to wear men's clothing.

She was nineteen. Her ashes were thrown into the Seine so no relics could be kept, though an eyewitness account describes an English soldier watching the burning who declared they had killed a saint. A retrial ordered by the Pope in 1456 annulled the conviction, and Joan was canonised in 1920, nearly five centuries after the fire.

On the evening of 8 December 1980, John Lennon returned to the Dakota, his apartment building on Manhattan's Upper West Side, after a recording session for the album Double Fantasy. Mark David Chapman, who had asked Lennon for an autograph outside the building hours earlier and received one, was waiting near the entrance and shot him four times in the back as he walked toward the door.

Lennon was rushed to Roosevelt Hospital but was already dead on arrival. Chapman made no attempt to flee and was found reading The Catcher in the Rye when police arrived at the scene. He pleaded guilty to second degree murder and has been denied parole at every hearing since becoming eligible in 2000.

A group of senators, including men Caesar had pardoned and promoted, stabbed him to death at a meeting of the Senate on 15 March 44 BCE. Ancient sources put the number of wounds at 23, and Suetonius says a physician later judged only one of them fatal.

The killing was meant to restore the Republic by removing a man the conspirators believed intended to make himself king in fact if not in name. It did the opposite. Caesar's death triggered another round of civil war, and within thirteen years his adopted heir Octavian had become Rome's first emperor.

Caesar arrived in Gaul in 58 BC not as a conqueror by mandate but as a governor chasing a war he needed, deeply in debt and facing prosecution once his term ended. He found his pretext when the Helvetii tribe migrated through Roman allied territory, then used that campaign to justify pushing further into Gaul, fighting tribes that had made no move against Rome at all.

His own account, the Commentarii de Bello Gallico, is the main surviving source for the war and was written partly to keep his political standing in Rome intact. Roman writers later put the campaign's death toll above a million, though ancient figures like that cannot be verified. The wealth and veteran army Caesar brought home from Gaul let him cross the Rubicon in 49 BC and seize control of Rome.

Justinian had already retaken North Africa from the Vandals in 533 with a comparatively small force under Belisarius, and he sent Belisarius to Italy in 535 with similar confidence that the Ostrogothic kingdom would fall quickly. It did not. The war dragged on for nearly two decades against a succession of Gothic kings.

Sieges of Rome, Naples and Ravenna, plague, famine and repeated changes of Byzantine commander ground the peninsula down far worse than the barbarian settlement it replaced ever had. Procopius, who served under Belisarius and wrote the fullest account, describes whole regions of Italy left depopulated by the fighting before Justinian's forces finally secured it around 554.

Kublai Khan sent a second invasion fleet against Japan in 1281, far larger than the one repelled in 1274, carrying a combined Mongol, Chinese and Korean force said to number well over a hundred thousand. The Japanese had spent seven years building stone walls along the likely landing beaches at Hakata Bay, and the invaders were held to a narrow coastal strip for weeks.

A typhoon struck the anchored fleet in August, sinking a large part of it and drowning many of the troops still aboard. Japanese chroniclers later called the storm kamikaze, divine wind, and the term was revived seven centuries later for the suicide pilots of the Second World War. No further Mongol invasion of Japan followed.

Mai Idris Alooma built his reputation on organisation rather than novelty weapons alone: fixed fortified camps, scorched earth tactics and boat crews recruited from Kotoko fishermen along Lake Chad. Into this system he added imported muskets and, by his chronicler Ibn Fartuwa's account, Ottoman-trained musketeers who taught local soldiers to load and fire them.

The chronicle credits the acquisition directly to God's favour on the ruler, which says something about how unusual the guns seemed at court. Iron-helmeted musket infantry became one part of a wider, deliberately modernised army that also used armoured horses, and it helped Bornu dominate the Lake Chad basin for decades afterward.

Three southern Chinese generals who had helped the Qing conquer the Ming rose against Beijing in 1673, controlling territory that stretched from Yunnan to the coast, and Kangxi's forces spent eight hard years grinding that rebellion down province by province. Taiwan followed in 1683, when a Qing fleet defeated the Ming loyalist regime still holding out there under Koxinga's descendants.

Kangxi then turned north, personally leading armies against the Dzungar Mongol leader Galdan through the 1690s. The fighting stretched Qing supply lines across the Gobi and forced Galdan into repeated retreats before his death ended that threat, leaving Kangxi's reign as the period when Qing borders reached their furthest extent yet.

In March 1940 the Soviet Politburo, at Stalin's signature and those of the rest of the leadership, ordered the NKVD to shoot Polish officers and officials held since the 1939 invasion of eastern Poland. NKVD records logged 21,857 executions carried out that spring at Katyn Forest near Smolensk and at sites in Kalinin and Kharkiv, most victims shot in the back of the head.

Germany discovered the mass graves in 1943 and publicised them to split the Allies, but Soviet authorities blamed the killings on the Nazis and maintained that lie for nearly five decades. Moscow admitted NKVD responsibility only in 1990, and in 1992 released the original execution order under Boris Yeltsin, confirming what Polish exile groups had argued since the war.

Jamal Khashoggi, a Washington Post columnist and former Saudi royal court insider turned critic of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, walked into the Saudi consulate in Istanbul on 2 October 2018 to collect papers for his upcoming marriage. His fiancee waited outside; he never came out. Turkish intelligence had bugged the building and recorded a team of Saudi agents waiting inside.

Turkish officials leaked details of an audio recording in which Khashoggi was heard being beaten and dismembered with a bone saw, though his remains have never been found. Saudi Arabia denied involvement for weeks, then admitted he had been killed inside the consulate, blaming a rogue operation. A CIA assessment concluded the crown prince had approved the operation, a finding Riyadh rejected.

Fighting broke out in June 1675 after Plymouth Colony executed three Wampanoag men for the murder of a colonist, and Metacom, known to the English as King Philip, led an alliance of Wampanoag, Narragansett and other peoples against the New England colonies. Villages on both sides were burned through 1675 and 1676, reaching deep into what is now Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut.

Against a colonial population of roughly 52,000, several hundred English settlers died. Native losses were worse still: entire communities were killed, sold into slavery or driven from the region, and the Wampanoag and Narragansett as functioning polities in southern New England never recovered. Metacom was killed in August 1676 and his body dismembered.

The violence in Kishinev began on Easter Sunday, 19 April 1903, after local newspapers ran fabricated stories accusing Jews of ritually murdering a Christian boy found dead nearby. Crowds moved through Jewish neighbourhoods over two days, wrecking homes and shops while police and troops largely stood by until the second day.

Estimates settle around 47 to 49 Jews killed, roughly 500 injured, and around 1,500 homes and businesses damaged or destroyed. Leo Tolstoy and other prominent figures condemned the attack, and the scale of press coverage abroad, together with the tacit official tolerance behind it, accelerated Jewish emigration from the Russian Empire in the years that followed.

Korean Air Lines Flight 007, a Boeing 747 flying from New York to Seoul with a stop in Anchorage, drifted roughly 300 kilometres off its planned route on 1 September 1983 because of an autopilot set incorrectly to a fixed heading. It entered Soviet airspace over Sakhalin Island, an area also used by American reconnaissance flights, and a Soviet interceptor pilot fired two missiles after tracking it for over two hours.

All 269 people aboard were killed, including a sitting US congressman. The Soviet Union initially denied shooting the plane down and only admitted it days later, insisting it had been mistaken for a spy plane. The incident deepened Cold War distrust at a tense moment and pushed the United States toward opening its GPS satellite system to civilian aviation, to prevent a repeat of the navigational error.

Negotiators signed the armistice at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953, after more than two years of talks that had stalled repeatedly over the fate of prisoners who did not want to be repatriated. Neither Syngman Rhee, the South Korean president, nor any South Korean official signed the document; it was agreed between the United Nations Command, North Korea and China alone.

The line it fixed ran close to the pre-war border, cutting through territory that had changed hands several times during three years of fighting. It created the Demilitarised Zone, a strip about four kilometres wide that is still patrolled and mined. Because the armistice only stopped the shooting, the two Koreas remain technically at war, governed by a truce rather than a treaty neither side ever replaced.

North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel in a coordinated attack on 25 June 1950, quickly overrunning South Korean defences and taking Seoul within days. Korea had been divided along that line only since 1945, when Soviet and American forces had accepted the surrender of Japanese troops on either side of it without either government intending a permanent border.

The United Nations Security Council, with the Soviet delegate absent in protest over China's UN seat, voted to authorise a multinational force to defend South Korea. American troops under General MacArthur were committed within days, turning a civil conflict between two Korean governments into the first major military confrontation of the Cold War.

NATO began bombing Yugoslav targets on 24 March 1999 without a United Nations mandate, the alliance's first sustained air campaign against a sovereign state, after talks at Rambouillet over Serbian actions against Kosovo Albanians collapsed. The campaign struck bridges, power plants and government buildings across Serbia for eleven weeks.

Slobodan Milosevic agreed to withdraw Yugoslav forces from Kosovo on 10 June 1999, and NATO suspended its bombing the same day. A UN administration and a NATO-led peacekeeping force, KFOR, took over the province, whose Albanian majority had by then seen hundreds of thousands displaced during the fighting. Kosovo declared independence in 2008.

On the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, Nazi paramilitaries and civilians attacked Jewish owned businesses, homes and synagogues across Germany and Austria, using the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris by a Jewish teenager as pretext. Police and fire services were ordered not to intervene unless a fire threatened non Jewish property. Around 1,400 synagogues were burned or damaged, giving the pogrom its name, meaning night of broken glass.

At least 91 Jews were killed that night, and roughly 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps in the days after. The German government fined the Jewish community for the damage and used the pogrom to accelerate laws stripping Jews of property and livelihoods. Kristallnacht marked a visible shift from legal discrimination toward open, organised violence.

On 3 March 1991, Los Angeles police officers had beaten motorist Rodney King with batons more than fifty times after a high speed chase, an assault filmed by a bystander from a nearby balcony. On 29 April 1992, a jury in suburban Simi Valley acquitted four officers of nearly all charges related to the beating. Unrest began within hours, first in South Central Los Angeles and then across much of the city.

Rioting, arson and looting continued for six days before National Guard troops and federal forces restored order. More than fifty people were killed and thousands injured, and property damage was estimated at over a billion dollars, making it the costliest urban unrest in modern US history. Two of the four officers were later convicted on federal civil rights charges.

Israel launched Operation Peace for Galilee on 6 June 1982, sending forces across the Lebanese border after the attempted assassination of its ambassador in London and continued PLO rocket fire from southern Lebanon. Israeli troops advanced as far as Beirut within days and besieged the city through the summer, shelling PLO positions in west Beirut for weeks.

The siege ended in August when Yasser Arafat and thousands of PLO fighters were evacuated from Beirut by sea under an internationally brokered agreement. Israeli forces largely withdrew from most of Lebanon by 1985 but kept a self-declared security zone in the south under occupation until 2000, a presence that fed the growth of Hezbollah as an armed resistance movement.

Soviet troops of the 1st Ukrainian Front entered Auschwitz on 27 January 1945 and found around 7,000 prisoners still alive, most too sick or weak to have joined the death march the SS had forced roughly 60,000 others onto days earlier as the front approached. Soldiers also found storerooms of clothing, hair and personal belongings taken from people who had been gassed.

Soviet military photographers and journalists documented the camp's gas chambers, crematoria and mass graves, producing some of the first images the wider world saw of the Holocaust's mechanics. Auschwitz had killed more than a million people, most of them Jews, over the four and a half years it operated. 27 January is now marked internationally as Holocaust Remembrance Day.

Parisians rose against the German garrison on 19 August 1944 as Allied armies approached from Normandy, and French Resistance fighters seized police stations and government buildings while barricades went up across the city. General Dietrich von Choltitz, the German commander, held Hitler's order to burn the city but chose not to carry it out.

General Philippe Leclerc's Free French 2nd Armoured Division entered Paris on 24 August, followed by American troops, and von Choltitz surrendered the next day at the Hotel Meurice. Charles de Gaulle led a march down the Champs-Elysees on 26 August to reassert French sovereignty, even as isolated gunfire from snipers continued around the crowd.

Protests against Muammar Gaddafi's four decades of rule began in Benghazi in mid February 2011, inspired by the uprisings already underway in Tunisia and Egypt, and were met with lethal force that quickly turned the unrest into an armed rebellion controlling much of eastern Libya within days.

A United Nations resolution authorising action to protect civilians led NATO to begin air strikes on Gaddafi's forces in March 2011. Rebel fighters captured Tripoli that August, and Gaddafi was killed by fighters near Sirte in October after his convoy was struck from the air. Rival militias and governments have since divided the country.

John Wilkes Booth, an actor and Confederate sympathiser, shot Abraham Lincoln in the back of the head at Ford's Theatre in Washington on the evening of 14 April 1865, five days after Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Booth had been plotting for months, first to kidnap Lincoln and later to kill him alongside the vice president and secretary of state on the same night.

Lincoln was carried across the street to a boarding house and died the next morning without regaining consciousness, the first American president assassinated. Booth escaped through Maryland and Virginia for twelve days before Union cavalry cornered him in a Virginia barn, where he was shot and died on 26 April 1865.

In February 1655 Mapuche forces across southern Chile launched coordinated attacks on Spanish forts and estates, angered by the enslavement of indigenous people in violation of earlier royal decrees. The uprising swept Spanish settlement back north toward the Maule river, destroying farms and missions as far south as the lake country around Llanquihue.

It was the worst crisis Spanish Chile had faced in decades and opened a further decade of intermittent war known to historians as the Arauco conflict. Afterward the colonial government leaned more on negotiated parliaments with Mapuche leaders, an approach that outlasted outright conquest for the rest of the century.

Four suicide bombers detonated homemade explosives on three London Underground trains and a double decker bus during the morning rush hour on 7 July 2005, a day after London had won its bid to host the 2012 Olympics. The attacks killed 52 people and the four bombers, and wounded more than 700.

All four bombers were British-born men from West Yorkshire, radicalised without any direct al-Qaeda handler at the scene, which unsettled investigators who had expected foreign operatives. The attacks led to a major expansion of surveillance powers in the United Kingdom and to renewed scrutiny of homegrown extremism within British Muslim communities.

Welsh archers using long yew bows had already given Edward I's armies trouble as opponents before he began recruiting them as allies. English commanders adopted the weapon during the Welsh campaigns of the 1270s and 1280s, valuing a draw weight and range that outmatched the shorter bows used across most of continental Europe.

Training took years rather than months, since drawing a heavy longbow repeatedly required strength built up from boyhood, and English law later required regular archery practice to keep the supply of skilled archers coming. Massed volleys from a few thousand archers, delivered at a rate no crossbow could match, became the tactic that shaped English battles for the next century and a half.

Nationalist forces under Chiang Kai-shek had surrounded the Communists' Jiangxi Soviet with blockhouses and encirclement campaigns, forcing roughly 86,000 troops and party cadres to break out on 16 October 1934 rather than be destroyed where they stood. Mao Zedong was not yet in overall command; he took control of Communist strategy only at the Zunyi Conference the following January, after early defeats under other leaders.

The retreat covered around 6,000 miles of mountains, rivers and marsh over roughly a year, ending in Shaanxi province in late 1935. Only about 8,000 to 10,000 of the original marchers reached the destination, the rest lost to combat, hunger, cold and desertion along the way. The survivors formed the core leadership of the Communist Party that eventually won China's civil war in 1949.

Norse shipwrights built longships from overlapping oak planks fastened with iron rivets, a clinker technique that gave the hull enough flex to twist over open-ocean swells without cracking. A shallow draught, often under a metre, let the same vessel cross the North Sea and then be rowed miles up a narrow river, far past where a deeper-hulled ship would run aground.

A single mast carrying a square woollen sail could be raised or lowered quickly, letting crews switch between sail and oar depending on wind and the need for surprise. The Gokstad and Oseberg ships, both excavated from Norwegian burial mounds, show the design in enough detail to have been sailed again in replica across the Atlantic in the twentieth century.

Louis XIV claimed the Spanish Netherlands in 1667 on the argument that his wife, a Spanish princess, was owed a share of her father's inheritance under a regional law called the right of devolution. French troops under Marshal Turenne took towns across Flanders faster than Spain could reinforce them.

A Triple Alliance of the Dutch, English and Swedes forced Louis to give back most of his gains by treaty in 1668, keeping only a handful of frontier towns. The episode taught him that European coalitions would form against him quickly, a lesson he answered five years later by attacking the Dutch Republic directly.

Louis XVI was guillotined in Paris's Place de la Revolution on 21 January 1793, having been convicted of treason by the National Convention after a trial in which he was addressed only as Citizen Louis Capet. He was permitted a last meeting with his family the night before and reportedly tried to speak to the crowd from the scaffold before drums drowned him out.

His execution removed any possibility of a negotiated return to constitutional monarchy and pushed France's remaining monarchies into open war against the Republic. Marie Antoinette followed him to the guillotine nine months later. The killing of an anointed king, rather than his deposition, was the point at which several European courts stopped treating the Revolution as an internal French matter.

On 20 April 1914 the Colorado National Guard, backed by the coal company's own guards, opened fire on a tent colony of striking miners at Ludlow and kept up the assault through the day. In the evening they set the tents alight. Two women and eleven children died in a pit dug beneath one tent for shelter, suffocated by smoke as the fire above burned off their air.

Twenty five people died in total, including three guardsmen, at the end of a strike the United Mine Workers had called against the Rockefeller-owned Colorado Fuel and Iron Company over pay, safety and company-run towns. News of the deaths, especially the children, turned public opinion against the company more forcefully than any earlier account of the strike had managed.

Patrice Lumumba, the Congo's first elected prime minister, was flown under guard to the breakaway province of Katanga on 17 January 1961, beaten by soldiers during the flight and again on arrival. That evening he and two colleagues, Joseph Okito and Maurice Mpolo, were driven to a clearing and shot by a Katangan firing squad in the presence of Belgian officers.

Belgium's government had pushed for Lumumba's removal after he turned to the Soviet Union for support against the Katanga secession, and a Belgian officer supervised the disposal of the bodies, which were dissolved rather than buried to prevent any grave becoming a shrine. Belgium's parliament acknowledged a share of moral responsibility in 2002, and a Belgian court sent a former diplomat to trial over the killing decades later.

The German submarine U-20 torpedoed the Cunard liner off the coast of Ireland on 7 May 1915, and a second explosion, likely coal dust or steam rather than a hidden arms cache as Germany claimed at the time, sent the ship down in under twenty minutes. Germany had published warnings beforehand that ships flying Allied flags in the area were fair targets.

Most of the roughly 2,000 people aboard had no time to reach the lifeboats before the ship rolled and sank. American outrage over the dead citizens did not bring the United States into the war immediately, Woodrow Wilson kept the country out for nearly two more years, but the sinking became one of the war's most effective pieces of Allied propaganda long before that.

Ten bombs hidden in gym bags and backpacks exploded on four crowded commuter trains during the Madrid morning rush hour on 11 March 2004, three days before a general election. The attack killed 193 people and wounded around 2,000, the deadliest terrorist act in Spain's history.

The government initially blamed the Basque separatist group ETA, but investigators soon traced the bombings to a cell inspired by al-Qaeda, most of them Moroccan immigrants. Several of the suspects blew themselves up when police cornered their flat weeks later. The governing party lost the election that followed, a result widely tied to public anger over the initial handling of the attack.

Madura was one of the earlier Islamic sultanates to take root on Java, at a time when most of the island's ruling courts still followed Hindu-Buddhist tradition. Its rise put it in the path of Majapahit, the Hindu-Buddhist empire then expanding to dominate Java and reach into much of the wider archipelago.

Majapahit forces overthrew the sultanate, and the region came under Majapahit's authority for generations afterward. Records from this period of Javanese history are thin and often contradictory, pieced together from later court chronicles rather than contemporary documents, so many details of the campaign itself have not survived.

On 21 February 1965, Malcolm X was about to address a crowd at the Audubon Ballroom in Manhattan when a disturbance broke out near the front rows. As attention turned toward it, three men rushed the stage and shot him at close range. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital within the hour, at the age of 39.

He had left the Nation of Islam less than a year earlier, publicly breaking with Elijah Muhammad and receiving death threats afterward. Two of the three men convicted in 1966 were later exonerated in 2021, after prosecutors acknowledged that the FBI and New York police had withheld evidence pointing to other Nation of Islam members as the actual gunmen.

Mansa Musa's wealth and pilgrimage had made Mali famous abroad, but the empire's succession was never settled by a fixed rule, and rival claimants from his family fought for the throne after his death. Provincial governors, some appointed decades earlier, found room to act as independent rulers while the capital argued over who held it.

Gao and other eastern provinces broke away during this unrest, laying the ground for the Songhai state that would eventually eclipse Mali entirely. The empire did not collapse in a single defeat; it lost territory piece by piece over the following century as neighbouring powers absorbed what the central court could no longer hold.

Maori iwi that gained early access to European traders, particularly Ngapuhi in the north under leaders such as Hongi Hika, acquired muskets and used them to raid tribes still fighting with traditional weapons. Hongi Hika's campaigns from 1818 carried Ngapuhi war parties as far south as the Bay of Plenty and Waikato.

The imbalance triggered a scramble among rival iwi to obtain their own firearms, often trading land, flax or preserved heads to coastal traders for muskets and powder. Fighting continued into the 1830s, displacing entire communities and shifting territorial boundaries across the North Island before missionary influence and a rough balance of arms brought the worst of the raiding to an end.

A pa was not a single design but a family of fortified sites, ranging from small refuges to terraced hilltop towns holding hundreds of people. Builders cut ditches and banks into ridgelines, then raised palisades of timber stakes lashed with flax, sometimes in two or three concentric rings to slow an attacking party before it reached the inner enclosure.

Archaeologists have mapped several thousand pa sites across the North Island alone, most dated from the fourteenth century onward as competition for land and resources sharpened between tribes. Their earthworks survive today as terraced hillsides, still visible without excavation, and remain one of the clearest physical records of pre European Maori settlement and conflict.

Spanish expeditions pushing south from the newly founded settlements around Santiago met organised Mapuche resistance almost as soon as they crossed the Bio Bio river. Rather than fighting one decisive battle, Mapuche fighters adapted quickly to Spanish tactics and weapons, learning to use captured horses and steel to fight on more even terms.

No single campaign settled the conflict.
