Spanish forts were built, besieged and abandoned repeatedly over the following decades, and the frontier along the river hardened into something closer to a border between two states than a temporary military line, a pattern of resistance that outlasted most other conflicts of Spain's American conquests.

Thirty three Korean activists gathered in Seoul on 1 March 1919 and publicly read a declaration of independence from Japanese colonial rule, timing the act to coincide with the funeral of the former emperor Gojong, whose death many Koreans believed Japan had caused. Peaceful demonstrations broke out in cities and villages across the country over the following weeks.

Japanese police and troops answered with mass arrests and lethal force; estimates of Korean deaths range from the low hundreds recorded by Japanese authorities to figures above 7,000 claimed by Korean sources, a gap that has never been resolved. Colonial rule continued until 1945, but the movement gave Korean nationalism an organised reference point.

Communities of escaped enslaved people, known as Maroons, had held the mountainous interior of Jamaica since the Spanish period, and by the 1720s two main groups under leaders including Cudjoe were raiding plantations and evading British patrols in terrain the colonial militia could not hold.

Fighting escalated through 1728 as Britain sent additional regiments and even Miskito trackers from Central America, without breaking Maroon resistance. The war ground on until 1739, when treaties granted the Leeward and Windward Maroons their own lands and self-government in exchange for peace, an arrangement that outlasted British rule.

Mayapan, walled and crowded with an estimated 12,000 residents, ruled a league of northern Yucatan cities through the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries rather than through the temple-building of earlier Maya capitals. Its rulers, the Cocom family, kept order by holding rival lords' relatives hostage inside the city itself.

That arrangement collapsed around the 1440s when the Xiu family led a revolt, killed most of the Cocom line, and abandoned Mayapan for good. The city was never resettled, and the region broke into smaller warring provinces that the Spanish found still fighting each other when they arrived a century later.

President Polk sent troops under Zachary Taylor into the disputed strip between the Nueces and Rio Grande rivers in early 1846, land Mexico still considered its own after the loss of Texas a decade earlier. When Mexican cavalry clashed with the Americans near the river in April, Polk told Congress that Mexican forces had shed American blood on American soil.

Congress declared war on 13 May 1846, though a minority, including a freshman representative named Abraham Lincoln, later questioned whether the clash had even happened on undisputed US territory. American forces went on to take Mexico City in 1847, and the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred roughly half of Mexico's territory to the United States.

Francisco Madero called for an uprising against President Porfirio Diaz in November 1910, after Diaz had jailed him for challenging his re-election following more than three decades in power. The revolt spread quickly, drawing in regional leaders like Pancho Villa in the north and Emiliano Zapata, who fought for land reform in the south.

Diaz resigned within months, but the coalition that had removed him fractured almost immediately into a decade of shifting alliances, coups and civil war among Madero, Villa, Zapata, Venustiano Carranza and others. The fighting killed roughly a million people before a new constitution in 1917 gave the country a settled, if still turbulent, government.

As Shaka's Zulu kingdom consolidated power in the early 1820s, defeated and fleeing chiefdoms were pushed outward across southern Africa, colliding with groups already settled on land that could not support the sudden influx. Some historians argue drought and Portuguese slave raiding from Delagoa Bay were driving the upheaval before Shaka's rise, not only after it.

Displaced groups such as the Ndebele, Ngoni and Kololo carried the disruption as far as modern Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia, founding new states along the way. Estimates of the death toll from famine, war and displacement across the region vary widely and remain disputed among historians, with some questioning whether the scale attributed to the period was later exaggerated by colonial writers.

Field Marshal Burkhard Munnich drafted the decree, signed on 29 July 1731, that created Russia's first cadet corps. It opened the following February on Vasilievsky Island, in the former palace of Peter the Great's favourite Alexander Menshikov, with 56 boys enrolled as pupils.

Unlike similar schools elsewhere in Europe, the corps trained cadets for civil service as well as the army, teaching languages, mathematics and law alongside drill. Alumni later included the playwright Alexander Sumarokov and Fyodor Volkov, founder of Russia's first professional theatre, and several officers who would join the Decembrist revolt a century on.

Earlier walls along China's northern frontier had mostly been packed earth, easily eroded and easily breached. From the 1470s the Ming government rebuilt long stretches in fired brick and dressed stone, adding watchtowers, garrison forts and beacon platforms that let defenders signal a raid down the line faster than any rider could carry the news.

The project ran on and off for close to two centuries, absorbing enormous amounts of labour and grain to feed the crews. What tourists walk near Beijing today, with its crenellated parapets and stepped towers, is largely this Ming brickwork rather than anything from the wall's much older, cruder predecessors.

Martin Luther King Jr. had travelled to Memphis to support a strike by sanitation workers and was standing on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel on the evening of 4 April 1968 when he was shot once in the jaw and neck. He was pronounced dead at St Joseph's Hospital just over an hour later, at the age of 39.

James Earl Ray, a fugitive with a long criminal record, was arrested in London two months later and eventually pleaded guilty, though he later recanted and disputes over the case continued for decades. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within days, and Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, which had been stalled for years, exactly one week after King's death.

Francisco de Almeida's fleet arrived off Mombasa on its way to India, and the town's ruler refused the terms Almeida demanded. The Portuguese responded by storming the island city, burning much of it and killing a large share of its population before sailing on toward the real prize further east.

Mombasa itself was not kept as a permanent Portuguese base at this stage, but the attack announced how the Portuguese meant to treat East African ports that resisted them. Swahili coast cities from Kilwa to Malindi drew the lesson and adjusted their dealings with Lisbon's captains accordingly in the years that followed.

Hulagu Khan besieged Baghdad in January 1258 after the Abbasid caliph al Mustasim refused to submit or send sufficient tribute. The city's walls fell within two weeks, and Mongol troops killed much of the population over the following days while the caliph himself was executed, ending an Abbasid line that had held the caliphate for five centuries.

Contemporary chroniclers gave death tolls running into the hundreds of thousands, with the Persian historian Hamdallah Mustawfi citing 800,000; modern historians consider such figures inflated but agree the toll was immense. The House of Wisdom's libraries were destroyed and, by later tradition, so many books were thrown into the Tigris that its water ran black with ink, a detail no contemporary source records firsthand.

Genghis Khan crossed into the territory of the Jin dynasty in 1211 with an army that, unlike the settled Jin forces, moved as fast in winter as in summer. Jin generals who had fought Mongol raiders before found this campaign different: entire garrison towns were bypassed rather than besieged, cutting off the capital before a formal siege even began.

Zhongdu, near modern Beijing, fell in 1215 after its Jin garrison had already been starved through a long blockade. The Jin court fled south and held on for two more decades, but the campaign set the pattern the Mongols repeated against the Song further south: encirclement first, siege engines and captured artisans second.

Genghis Khan first tried trade, not war, sending a caravan of merchants to open relations with the Khwarezmian Empire. The governor of Otrar had the caravan seized and its merchants killed, and when Genghis Khan sent envoys to demand redress, the shah Muhammad had them executed too.

The Mongol response, from 1219, dismantled the empire city by city: Otrar, Bukhara, and Samarkand were stormed and their populations killed or deported to work as labourers and craftsmen for the Mongol army. Shah Muhammad fled west and died, reportedly of pleurisy, on an island in the Caspian Sea, and his son Jalal ad-Din kept fighting a losing campaign for several more years.

Bela IV had gathered nearly the whole of the Hungarian nobility's fighting strength into one camp near the Sajo River when Subutai's forces attacked on 11 April 1241. Mongol siege engines, unusual for a supposedly mobile army, bombarded the camp before the cavalry closed in, and the Hungarian force broke apart in the retreat rather than the battle itself.

Modern estimates put overall population loss in the kingdom during the invasion and the famine that followed at roughly a fifth to a quarter of Hungary's people, concentrated on the open plains where villages had nowhere to shelter. Bela himself escaped west, and Hungary spent the following years building the stone castles the invasion had shown it lacked.

Batu Khan led Mongol forces across the Volga into the fractured Rus principalities in the winter of 1237, choosing the frozen season deliberately so his cavalry could cross rivers that would have blocked them in summer. Ryazan fell first after a short siege, and the campaign moved on to Vladimir and other cities the following year, with Kiev itself destroyed in 1240.

The Rus principalities never united against the invasion, each falling in turn while rivals elsewhere failed to send help. What followed was two and a half centuries of tribute paid to the Mongol successor state known as the Golden Horde, with local princes confirmed in office only after travelling to receive a patent from the khan. Moscow's rise began partly from its role collecting that tribute on the Horde's behalf.

Batu Khan split his army in 1241 and sent both halves west at once. One column under Baidar and Kadan struck Poland, killing Duke Henry II the Pious at Legnica on 9 April, while the main force under Batu and Subutai crossed into Hungary and destroyed Bela IV's army at the Sajo River two days later.

The Polish attack was a deliberate diversion, meant only to stop reinforcements reaching Hungary rather than to conquer Poland itself. Both campaigns succeeded within days of each other, and Mongol raiders reached the outskirts of Vienna before the death of the Great Khan Ogedei that December pulled the armies back east to take part in choosing his successor.

By March 1279 the Southern Song court had been reduced to a fleet anchored off Yamen, on China's south coast, with the seven year old emperor Zhao Bing aboard. The Yuan admiral Zhang Hongfan attacked the chained-together Song ships directly rather than waiting them out, and broke the formation after a day of close fighting.

As the fleet collapsed, the chancellor Lu Xiufu took the boy emperor in his arms and jumped into the sea; accounts describe hundreds of officials and their families following rather than surrender. The battle ended three centuries of Song rule and left Kublai Khan in control of the whole of China as the first Yuan dynasty emperor.

Kublai Khan's fleet, carrying an estimated 900 ships and around 30,000 Mongol, Chinese, and Korean troops, landed at Hakata Bay in November 1274. Samurai forces, unfamiliar with the coordinated volley tactics and gunpowder bombs the invaders used, fell back inland after the first day of fighting.

A storm struck the anchored fleet that night and forced the invasion force to withdraw, ending the campaign before it could push further into Kyushu. Japanese chroniclers later called such storms kamikaze, divine wind, and the near miss prompted the shogunate to build stone defensive walls along the bay ahead of the larger invasion Kublai sent seven years later.

A Mongol rider trained from childhood on horseback could shoot a composite bow accurately at a full gallop, something the stirrup made possible by letting him stand and brace rather than grip with his legs alone. Genghis Khan, elected khan of the united Mongol tribes in 1206, organised these riders into units of ten, drilled to wheel and regroup on signal.

Each warrior carried spare horses and travelled light, letting Mongol armies cover far greater distances than settled kingdoms expected of any force. That combination of range, discipline, and firepower let a population of perhaps a million or so eventually hold territory from Korea to Hungary within a single generation.

Baldwin IV had leprosy severe enough that he could no longer grip a sword without a strap, and he was sixteen when he rode out from Ascalon on 25 November 1177 with a force William of Tyre put at roughly 500 knights. Saladin, believing the truce with Jerusalem safe, had let his army scatter across the countryside to plunder.

The Templars and Baldwin's knights caught the raiders unassembled near the hill of Montgisard and broke them before they could form up. Saladin escaped on a fast camel with a fraction of his men; William of Tyre's chroniclers put Crusader losses near 1,100 dead against far heavier casualties among the Ayyubid forces.

On 23 October 2002, around fifty Chechen fighters led by Movsar Barayev seized the Dubrovka theatre during a performance of the musical Nord-Ost and wired the auditorium with explosives. For two and a half days they held the audience while demanding Russian troops leave Chechnya; one hostage was shot when negotiations stalled, and officials refused to withdraw troops.

Before dawn on 26 October, special forces pumped an unannounced fentanyl derivative through the theatre's ventilation system, then stormed the building and shot the incapacitated militants. Russian authorities put the toll at around 130 hostages, nearly all killed by the gas itself rather than by gunfire, since ambulance crews were not told what agent to expect. Families of the dead later sued Russia at the European Court of Human Rights.

Akbar was only thirteen when his regent, Bairam Khan, led Mughal forces against the Afghan Hemu at Panipat in 1556, on ground close to where Akbar's grandfather Babur had won the first battle there three decades earlier. Hemu's army briefly seemed to be winning until an arrow struck him, and his retreating troops were routed.

The victory secured Delhi and Agra for a dynasty that had nearly collapsed after Akbar's father died in exile. Over the following decades Akbar expanded Mughal control from Gujarat to Bengal, building an administration that absorbed Hindu Rajput allies and officials alongside Muslim nobles rather than ruling through conquest alone.

Leaders of Britain, France, Germany and Italy met in Munich on 29 and 30 September 1938 to settle Hitler's demand for the Sudetenland, the German speaking border region of Czechoslovakia. Neville Chamberlain and Edouard Daladier agreed to hand over the territory in exchange for Hitler's promise to seek no further conquest. Czechoslovakia's government was not invited to the talks that decided its border.

Chamberlain returned to Britain declaring he had secured peace for our time, a phrase that became a byword for misplaced confidence within a year. Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, breaking the agreement outright, and Britain abandoned appeasement soon after. The Munich Agreement is still cited as a warning against conceding to aggression in hope of avoiding war.

Tens of thousands of Mussolini's Blackshirts marched on Rome in late October 1922, threatening to seize the capital by force. King Victor Emmanuel III, unwilling to risk civil war and unsure the army would fire on the marchers, declined to declare a state of emergency and instead invited Mussolini to become prime minister on 29 October, a legal appointment despite the intimidation behind it.

Mussolini was 39 and led a coalition government at first, holding only a minority of seats in parliament. He spent the next four years dismantling parliamentary opposition, most decisively after the 1924 murder of the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti, until by 1926 Italy was a one party fascist state with Mussolini as Il Duce. His rule became the template other European fascist movements looked to.

Before dawn on 1 February 2021, Myanmar's military detained State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi and President Win Myint hours before parliament was due to open following her party's landslide election win the previous November. The army declared a state of emergency and handed power to commander in chief Min Aung Hlaing, alleging voting fraud that international observers found no evidence for.

Mass protests and a nationwide civil disobedience campaign followed, met with lethal force that killed thousands over the following years according to monitoring groups. Suu Kyi was tried on charges widely seen as politically motivated and sentenced to decades in prison. The coup ended a decade of tentative civilian rule that had begun in 2011.

Nadir Shah's Persian army crushed a much larger Mughal force at Karnal in February 1739 after only a few hours of fighting, and he entered Delhi in March as the guest, nominally, of the emperor Muhammad Shah. The occupation turned violent after a rumour spread that Nadir Shah had been killed, prompting a mob to attack his soldiers and kill several thousand of them.

In retaliation, on 22 March 1739, Nadir Shah ordered a massacre that lasted several hours across the city; estimates for the dead run from roughly twenty thousand to thirty thousand, though bodies were buried in mass pits without any count kept. He left in May with the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Noor diamond and treasure historians have estimated at tens of millions of rupees, wealth the Mughal state never recovered.

Fighting broke out along the Nagorno-Karabakh line of contact on 27 September 2020, three decades after Armenian forces had taken the territory from Azerbaijan in a war fought in the early 1990s. Azerbaijani forces, backed by Turkish military advisers, opened with strikes that destroyed Armenian air defences before ground troops advanced through the south of the enclave, taking the town of Shusha in the war's final week.

Turkish made Bayraktar TB2 drones, cheap compared with the tanks they destroyed, let Azerbaijan pick off Armenian columns from the air with little risk to its own troops. A Russian brokered ceasefire signed on 9 November ended the fighting after 44 days and handed Azerbaijan the districts it had captured, along with further territory still under Armenian control.

Napoleon had been ruling the island of Elba, off the Tuscan coast, since May 1814, with a small pension and a personal guard of about a thousand men that the treaty allowed him to keep. British and French agents were meant to be watching him, but on 26 February 1815 he simply loaded his guard onto a handful of ships and sailed for France.

He landed near Cannes on 1 March and marched north through the Alps rather than the Rhone valley, avoiding towns loyal to the restored monarchy. Troops sent to arrest him instead joined him, and he reached Paris on 20 March without a shot fired, ending Louis XVIII's first restoration after less than a year.

Louis XVIII fled Paris on 19 March 1815, and Napoleon walked into the Tuileries the next evening without having fought a battle since his escape from Elba three weeks earlier. He set about rebuilding an army and drafted a new liberal constitution, the Charte, to soften his image among a public wary of another dictatorship.

The period is named for the roughly hundred days between his return and Louis XVIII's second restoration in July, though the coalition that had already agreed at Vienna to remove him moved fast. Napoleon's army met the British and Prussians at Waterloo on 18 June, and by 22 June he had abdicated a second time.

Napoleon crossed the Niemen River into Russia in June 1812 with over 400,000 troops from across his empire, expecting a short campaign ending in a decisive battle. Russian forces instead retreated for months, burning supplies and villages behind them, and gave real battle only once, at Borodino in September, a brutal but inconclusive fight that left Moscow open.

Napoleon occupied an abandoned, burning Moscow for a month, waiting for a peace offer that never came, then began retreating in October as winter closed in early. Cold, starvation and harassment by Russian forces and Cossack raiders destroyed the army on the road home; only a small fraction of those who crossed the Niemen made it back out of Russia.

The Peace of Amiens between Britain and France collapsed in May 1803 over disputes including Malta, which Britain had promised to evacuate but refused to abandon while Napoleon kept expanding his influence in Italy and the Low Countries. Britain declared war first, and Napoleon responded by massing an invasion force at Boulogne.

Napoleon shelved the invasion once his fleet failed to secure the Channel, turning his army east instead to crush Austria and Russia at Austerlitz in 1805. The conflict drew in one continental coalition after another over the following decade, redrawing borders from Spain to Poland before ending with Napoleon's final defeat in 1815.

Nat Turner had already told followers he saw signs in the sky, including an August 1831 solar eclipse, pointing to a day of reckoning. On 21 August he and a small band began at the household that enslaved him in Southampton County, Virginia, killing the family in their beds, then moved farm to farm through the night gathering more men and more victims.

By the time militia scattered the group the next day, about 55 to 60 white residents were dead. Turner hid for over two months before capture; he was tried, hanged, and reportedly skinned as a warning. Virginia and neighbouring states answered with harsher slave codes and militia patrols, and white mobs killed an unknown number of enslaved and free Black people in reprisal.

The Hyksos had ruled the eastern Delta from Avaris for over a century, a foreign dynasty that Egyptian sources afterward treated as a wound to be avenged rather than a settled fact of history. The Theban king Ahmose finished a war his brother and father had already begun, capturing Avaris and pursuing the Hyksos out of Egypt entirely around 1550 BC.

Ahmose's victory reunified Egypt under Theban rule and opened what modern historians call the New Kingdom, the era of Hatshepsut, Akhenaten and Ramesses II. Freed from a rival power inside its own borders, Egypt pushed its armies into the Levant and up the Nile into Nubia, building the wealth that filled the tombs of the Valley of the Kings.

The war began because a band of Nez Perce refused an order to move onto a reduced reservation in Idaho and instead tried to reach safety in Canada, where Sitting Bull's Lakota had already taken refuge. Roughly 750 men, women and children, trailing horses and household goods, set out under several chiefs including Joseph, Looking Glass and White Bird.

Over about four months they crossed some 1,170 miles of Idaho, Wyoming and Montana, outmanoeuvring army units in several sharp engagements before being caught just short of the border near the Bear Paw Mountains in October 1877. Joseph surrendered there with the words 'I am tired of fighting,' and survivors were sent not home but to reservations in Kansas and Oklahoma.

On the evening of 14 July 2016, a crowd filled the seafront in Nice to watch Bastille Day fireworks when a 19 tonne rental truck swerved onto the pedestrian promenade and accelerated into them. The driver, Mohamed Lahouaiej-Bouhlel, a Tunisian delivery worker with no known ties to any militant group, kept the truck moving for more than a kilometre, killing 86 people before police shot him dead.

Investigators found no evidence Lahouaiej-Bouhlel had pledged loyalty to Islamic State beforehand, though the group claimed him afterward; French prosecutors instead described a man with a history of violence and mental instability. President Francois Hollande extended the state of emergency imposed after the Charlie Hebdo attacks and ordered further airstrikes against Islamic State positions in Syria.

The riot began at the Hippodrome on 13 January 532, when supporters of the Blue and Green chariot factions, usually bitter rivals, united in anger after Justinian refused to pardon convicted rioters from both sides. Within days the crowd was chanting 'Nika', meaning victory, burning parts of Constantinople including the original Hagia Sophia, and demanding the dismissal of the emperor's officials.

The rebels proclaimed a senator named Hypatius emperor in Justinian's place, and Justinian himself reportedly considered fleeing before his wife Theodora and his generals argued against it. Those generals trapped the crowd inside the Hippodrome and killed an estimated 30,000 people there. The revolt collapsed, and Justinian rebuilt the city, Hagia Sophia included, on his own terms.

On 22 July 2011, Anders Behring Breivik detonated a car bomb outside government buildings in Oslo, killing eight people. Dressed as a police officer, he then crossed to Utoya island, where a Labour Party youth camp held several hundred teenagers and young adults. Over roughly ninety minutes he hunted campers across the small island, killing 69 of them, many as they tried to swim to the mainland.

Breivik had written a lengthy manifesto attacking multiculturalism and Islam and told the court he wanted to punish the Labour Party for its immigration policies. He was convicted of terrorism and mass murder in August 2012 and given Norway's maximum sentence, 21 years, extendable if he remains dangerous. A government inquiry found police could have reached Utoya sooner, and the police chief resigned.

The International Military Tribunal opened in Nuremberg on 20 November 1945, trying 22 surviving senior Nazi officials before judges drawn from the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. The city was chosen partly because its Palace of Justice had survived Allied bombing largely intact and had an attached prison, and partly for the symbolism of trying Nazism where it had staged its largest rallies.

The tribunal introduced charges that had no clear precedent in international law, including crimes against humanity, and rejected the defence that officials had merely followed orders. Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, among them Hermann Goring, who took cyanide in his cell the night before his scheduled hanging; others received prison terms or were acquitted.

Barack Obama, a first term Illinois senator who had delivered a widely noticed speech at the 2004 Democratic convention, defeated Republican nominee John McCain on 4 November 2008 with 365 electoral votes to 173. He carried states such as Virginia and North Carolina that had voted Republican in every recent presidential election.

His victory came amid a deepening financial crisis that had crashed markets that autumn, and his campaign's use of small online donations and social media organising reshaped how American campaigns were run afterward. He was inaugurated on 20 January 2009, and Democrats also held both chambers of Congress for the first two years of his presidency.

Nobunaga began his march toward controlling Japan's fractured provinces after installing a shogun of his choosing in Kyoto in 1568, using the appointment as cover for extending his own authority over rival warlords. He built his power on trade income from Sakai and other merchant towns as much as on the battlefield.

His armies became known for organising large numbers of arquebusiers into disciplined firing formations, a break from older samurai tactics built around individual combat. Nobunaga never finished unifying Japan himself, killed by one of his own generals in 1582, but his methods and much of his territory passed to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who completed the process.

A rented truck packed with fertiliser and fuel oil exploded outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City on the morning of 19 April 1995. The blast collapsed a third of the nine storey building, including a day care centre on the second floor, and 168 people died, 19 of them children.

Timothy McVeigh, an army veteran radicalised by anti-government militia ideas, was stopped for a traffic violation less than an hour after the bombing and later convicted and executed for the attack. His accomplice Terry Nichols received life in prison. It remained the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in United States history.

At dawn on 22 June 1941, roughly three million Axis troops crossed into Soviet territory along a front stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, tearing up the non-aggression pact Germany and the Soviet Union had signed less than two years earlier. Joseph Stalin had been warned of the buildup and reportedly disbelieved it until the attack was underway.

German forces advanced hundreds of kilometres in the first weeks, encircling entire Soviet armies, but failed to take Moscow before winter set in. The campaign opened a front on which the German army suffered the bulk of its wartime losses, and Hitler's own planners had assumed the Soviet Union would collapse within a matter of months.

On 12 January 1962, American Army helicopter crews lifted over 1,000 South Vietnamese paratroopers toward a suspected Viet Cong stronghold roughly 16 kilometres west of Saigon. The 32 Piasecki H-21 helicopters, nicknamed the flying banana for their curved twin-rotor shape, had arrived by ship from the United States only a month earlier.

American pilots flew the aircraft and American advisers helped plan the operation, but the troops on the ground were entirely South Vietnamese; officially, the United States was not yet a combatant. The insertion surprised the Viet Cong, who retreated without much of a fight, and the raid captured a radio transmitter. It also proved that helicopters could move large infantry forces quickly, a tactic used through the rest of the war.

In October 1856 Chinese officials boarded the Arrow, a Chinese owned ship flying a British flag under a lapsed Hong Kong registration, and arrested its crew on suspicion of piracy. The British consul in Guangzhou, Harry Parkes, demanded an apology and the men's release. When the governor refused to apologise, British warships shelled the city, and France joined soon after, citing the killing of a French missionary in Guangxi.

The fighting dragged on for four years and ended only when an Anglo-French force occupied Beijing in 1860 and burned the Old Summer Palace. The resulting treaties opened eleven more ports, permitted foreign embassies in the capital and allowed Christian missionaries to travel inland, on top of legalising the opium trade the first war had already forced open.

Oromo pastoralist clans, organised through an age set system known as gadaa that rotated leadership every eight years, began moving out of their homeland in what is now southern Ethiopia during the sixteenth century. Their expansion coincided with a period when the Christian Ethiopian highland kingdom and neighbouring Muslim sultanates had exhausted each other in decades of warfare.

Oromo groups settled across a much wider stretch of the highlands and lowlands than they had previously occupied, absorbing or displacing earlier populations in the process. Their language and gadaa institutions took root widely enough that Oromo speakers remain one of the largest ethnic groups in the Horn of Africa today.

The janissaries had begun centuries earlier as an infantry corps recruited through the devshirme levy of Christian boys from the Balkans, trained from childhood and forbidden to marry or hold outside trades. By the later 1500s the corps was shifting from archers and swordsmen toward firearms, with muskets increasingly issued as standard equipment.

The change came with costs the sultans had not fully anticipated. As musket drill spread, the janissaries grew harder to keep confined to barracks life, took up trades and married in defiance of old rules, and their growing political leverage over the following century made them as dangerous to weak sultans as to any foreign enemy.

Ottoman forces adopted firearms earlier and more systematically than most European rivals, arming Janissary units with matchlock guns while cavalry elsewhere still relied on lance and bow. Sultans invested in foundries capable of casting large bombards, work that drew foreign engineers, including reportedly a Hungarian gun founder later hired for the 1453 siege of Constantinople.

Combining slave soldier infantry with heavy artillery gave the Ottomans an edge in siege warfare that older feudal armies struggled to match, since raising and training gunners took organisation that seasonal levies could not provide. That institutional head start shaped Ottoman campaigns against both Byzantine and European strongholds for the next century.

In June 1422 Sultan Murad II moved against Constantinople itself, not the separate Genoese trading colony across the Golden Horn, after Byzantine emperor Manuel II had backed a rival claimant to the Ottoman throne. Ottoman forces built earthworks and used early cannon called falcons against the city's ancient walls, one of the first times artillery featured in an assault on the capital.

The city held through the summer with only a few thousand defenders against a far larger besieging force, and Murad withdrew in September to deal with a domestic revolt elsewhere in his territory. Constantinople survived another 31 years before the Ottomans returned in far greater strength and finally took it in 1453.

Most sources date the corps to 1363 under Sultan Murad I, built from a levy of one fifth of the prisoners taken in war. Boys were converted to Islam, trained under strict discipline and barred from marrying while in service, producing soldiers whose loyalty ran to the sultan personally rather than to any regional lord.

That arrangement made them Europe's first paid, year round infantry force at a time when most armies still assembled around feudal levies and seasonal campaigns. The corps grew into a political power of its own over the following centuries, strong enough to depose sultans, before it was violently disbanded in 1826.

Oyo sat on savanna country in what is now southwestern Nigeria, terrain open enough to support horses in a region where the tsetse fly made cavalry impractical further south. Rulers imported horses through trade networks reaching north toward the Sahel and built a mounted force that outmatched the infantry armies of neighbouring Yoruba states.

That cavalry let Oyo project power well beyond its own farmland, collecting tribute from client towns and controlling trade routes toward the coast. Horses could not be bred easily in Oyo's own climate, so the empire depended on continued imports to keep its army mounted, a dependency that later weakened it as trade routes shifted.

The United States launched Operation Just Cause on 20 December 1989, sending roughly 27,000 troops into Panama in an assault that opened with airstrikes on Panamanian Defence Force positions overnight. President George H.W. Bush cited the killing of an American serviceman at a checkpoint days earlier, along with drug trafficking indictments already pending against Panama's leader, General Manuel Noriega.

Noriega evaded capture for ten days before taking refuge in the Vatican's embassy in Panama City, where US forces played loud rock music outside around the clock in an attempt to force him out. He surrendered on 3 January 1990 and was flown to Miami to face trial, where he was convicted on drug trafficking and racketeering charges and imprisoned in the United States.

Parisians angered by defeat in the war with Prussia and by a conservative national government elected the Commune in March 1871 and ran the city themselves for ten weeks. It separated church from state, cancelled rents owed during the siege, and gave working women a public role in its assemblies and clubs.

The national army retook Paris street by street between 21 and 28 May, a week remembered as Bloody Week. Estimates of the dead range from about 6,000 to over 10,000, most killed in summary executions after resistance collapsed rather than in the fighting itself, and thousands more were deported to penal colonies.

Armed members of the Symbionese Liberation Army seized Patricia Hearst from her Berkeley apartment on 4 February 1974, beating her boyfriend and firing shots as they dragged her into a car. She was nineteen, a granddaughter of publisher William Randolph Hearst, and the group demanded a ransom of food distribution to the poor before naming a cash sum.

Two months later Hearst appeared in recordings announcing she had joined the SLA under the name Tania, and surveillance footage showed her carrying a rifle during a bank robbery in San Francisco. Arrested in September 1975, she argued she had acted under duress and brainwashing; a jury convicted her anyway, and she served nearly two years before President Carter commuted her sentence.

Delegates from most of Europe's states negotiated for years at Munster and Osnabruck, two Westphalian towns kept separate so Catholic and Protestant parties could each deal with France and Sweden on their own ground. The resulting treaties, signed in 1648, ended the Thirty Years' War within the Holy Roman Empire and the separate Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch, whose independence Spain finally recognised.

The settlement confirmed that hundreds of German princes and free cities could set their own religion and largely run their own affairs within the empire, weakening the emperor's practical authority over them. Later writers used the term Westphalian sovereignty for the resulting idea that states deal with each other as formal equals, though the treaties themselves never used the word sovereignty.

Japanese carrier aircraft struck the US Pacific Fleet at anchor on the morning of 7 December 1941, sinking or damaging eight battleships and killing more than 2,300 Americans in under two hours. The attack aimed to cripple American naval power in the Pacific before Japan expanded into Southeast Asia, and it arrived without a formal declaration of war having reached Washington first.

President Roosevelt called it a date which will live in infamy in his address to Congress the next day, and the United States declared war on Japan within hours. Germany and Italy then declared war on the United States on 11 December, bringing the country into both theatres of a conflict it had spent two years supplying but not joining.

A third poll tax in four years, on top of long-standing grievances over serfdom and labour laws that pinned wages below plague-era market rates, triggered risings across south-east England in May 1381. Bands from Kent and Essex, including one led by Wat Tyler, converged on London in June, opening the prisons and burning the Savoy Palace of John of Gaunt.

The fourteen-year-old Richard II met the rebels at Smithfield on 15 June, where Tyler was killed by the mayor of London during the parley, apparently after some dispute over conduct in the king's presence. Richard promised reforms that were never honoured once the crowds dispersed, and the leaders were hunted down and executed, but the poll tax was not tried again for centuries.

Peisistratos first tried to seize Athens by wounding himself and his mules, then telling the assembly that his enemies had attacked him, a trick that won him a bodyguard he used to occupy the Acropolis. He was driven out twice before he returned for good around 546 BC, this time with mercenaries and an alliance secured through his son's marriage.

Once in power he kept Athens' existing laws and offices in place rather than replacing them, while quietly filling key posts with allies and taxing the wealthy to fund public works and festivals. Farmers received loans and land, poets and sculptors found patronage, and Athens grew steadier and richer under one man's control than it had under the aristocratic infighting he had exploited to take it.

Sparta and its allies declared war on Athens in 431 BCE, provoked by Athenian support for Corcyra and pressure on Megara, but the underlying cause was older: a Spartan-led alliance watching Athens grow into a naval empire funded by tribute from other Greek cities. Thucydides, an Athenian general exiled during the war, wrote its history as it happened.

Athens's own plague, a failed expedition to Sicily that destroyed an entire fleet, and the eventual defeat of its navy at Aegospotami in 405 BCE ended the war the following year with Athens's surrender. Sparta tore down the city's walls, and Greece never again fielded a single power strong enough to unite it.

Napoleon had marched troops through Spain in 1807 with Spanish agreement, aiming at Portugal, but by early 1808 he moved to depose the Spanish Bourbons outright and install his brother Joseph on the throne. Riots in Madrid on 2 May 1808 spread into a nationwide uprising against the occupation.

Spanish and Portuguese guerrillas, backed from 1808 by a British expeditionary force under Arthur Wellesley, tied down hundreds of thousands of French troops in a war of ambush and reprisal rather than open battle. The fighting continued until 1814, and the manpower and supplies it consumed weakened Napoleon's position for his later campaigns elsewhere in Europe.

The Ionian cities on the Aegean coast of Anatolia had been under Persian control for decades when they rose up in 499 BCE, led by Aristagoras of Miletus. Athens sent a small fleet to help, and Athenian and Ionian forces burned Sardis, the regional Persian capital, an act Darius I is said to have taken as a personal insult.

The revolt itself collapsed by 493 BCE, its fleet crushed at Lade and Miletus sacked. Darius did not forget Athens's part in it. He sent envoys around the Aegean demanding earth and water as tokens of submission, and within a decade Persian forces had landed on Greek soil at Marathon, opening a conflict that ran on and off for half a century.

Peter I travelled through the Netherlands and England in 1697 and 1698 disguised in a lower rank, working in Dutch shipyards to study construction firsthand rather than through envoys. He returned to Russia determined to replace its old noble cavalry levies with a standing army drilled, uniformed and armed on Western European models.

He cut short his own tour to rush home and crush a mutiny by the Streltsy guard regiments, whose privileges the coming reforms threatened directly. The new army he built over the following years was tested hard, and initially badly beaten, when Russia went to war with Sweden in 1700.

On 16 August 1819, a crowd estimated at 60,000 or more gathered at St Peter's Field in Manchester to hear the radical speaker Henry Hunt call for parliamentary reform and wider voting rights. Local magistrates, alarmed by the size of the peaceful gathering, ordered the arrest of Hunt and sent mounted yeomanry cavalry into the packed crowd to reach him.

The cavalry, many of them local shopkeepers and businessmen with little training, used sabres against a crowd that included women and children and had nowhere to disperse to. Contemporary records list around eighteen dead and several hundred injured, some from sabre wounds and others crushed in the panic. A journalist covering the event helped found the Manchester Guardian in response.

Filipino revolutionaries under Emilio Aguinaldo had already been fighting Spain and expected independence once Spain lost the 1898 war with the United States. Instead the Treaty of Paris transferred the islands to American control, and fighting broke out in February 1899 when a US sentry shot a Filipino soldier crossing a bridge near Manila.

The war shifted from open battles to a guerrilla campaign that US forces answered with reconcentration camps and, in places such as Samar, orders to kill anyone capable of bearing arms. Estimates for Filipino civilian deaths, mostly from famine and disease in the camps, run into the hundreds of thousands, while American dead numbered around 4,200. Aguinaldo's capture in 1901 broke organised resistance.

Vladimir Lenin saw the newly independent Poland as a bridge for spreading revolution west into a defeated Germany, and by summer 1920 the Red Army under Mikhail Tukhachevsky had pushed to the outskirts of Warsaw. Polish commander Jozef Pilsudski, with French advisor Maxime Weygand assisting, planned a counterattack rather than a static defence of the capital.

In mid August 1920, Polish forces struck the gap between two Soviet army groups south of Warsaw, cutting supply lines and forcing a chaotic Soviet retreat that some Poles later called the Miracle on the Vistula. The 1921 Treaty of Riga fixed a border well east of the ethnically Polish heartland, one that held until the Soviet invasion of 1939.

Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BCE after a three month siege, arriving as an arbiter in a civil war between two Hasmonean brothers, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, and leaving as the city's new master. His troops breached the temple precinct on a Sabbath, and the historian Josephus records that Pompey himself walked into the Holy of Holies, a space normally closed even to most priests, though he reportedly took none of its treasure.

Aristobulus was carried off to Rome in chains to be paraded in Pompey's triumph, and Hyrcanus was left as a client high priest stripped of the royal title his family had held. Judea kept a measure of self-government under Rome for another century, but its independence, gained under the earlier Maccabean revolt, effectively ended with Pompey's entry into the city.

Calicut's ruler, the Zamorin, had welcomed Vasco da Gama a decade earlier but soon found himself at war with the Portuguese over control of the pepper trade his port had run for centuries. Portuguese ships shelled the city repeatedly and fought its Arab and local merchant fleets at sea to choke off rival access to spices.

Unlike Goa, Calicut itself was never permanently occupied, but Portuguese naval pressure forced its trade increasingly through routes Lisbon could tax and licence. The old Indian Ocean pattern of open, competing merchant networks gave way, port by port, to a system built around Portuguese cartazes, or trading passes.

Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate, lost it within months to a counterattack, then retook it later the same year with reinforcements from Cochin. The fighting was brutal on both sides, and Albuquerque's own letters describe ordering the massacre of the Muslim garrison after the second capture.

Goa's deep, defensible harbour and its distance from the main Mughal and Deccan armies made it easy to hold once secured. Albuquerque made it the seat of Portuguese government in Asia, and it stayed under Portuguese rule for over four centuries, longer than almost any other European colonial holding in the region.

Portuguese nobles seized the royal palace in Lisbon on 1 December 1640 and proclaimed the Duke of Braganza king as John IV, ending sixty years of rule from Madrid that had begun when the Portuguese line died out without an heir. Spain, tied down fighting France and the Dutch, could spare only limited forces to answer.

The war dragged on through decisive Portuguese victories at Montes Claros and elsewhere in the 1660s before Spain finally recognised independence by treaty in 1668. Portugal kept its own crown, its overseas empire and, crucially, its separate identity from a union that had never sat comfortably with either kingdom.

The trigger was maggot-ridden meat served to the crew of the battleship Potemkin during gunnery exercises on 14 June 1905. When officers ordered the ship's doctor to declare it fit to eat, sailors refused it, and an argument over the refusal ended with an officer shooting sailor Grigory Vakulenchuk. His comrades then killed several officers, including the captain, and took the ship.

The crew sailed the Potemkin to Odessa, where a general strike was already under way, and brought Vakulenchuk's body ashore for a funeral that drew huge crowds before troops put down the port with heavy loss of life. The mutineers surrendered the ship to Romanian authorities rather than face capture. Sergei Eisenstein's 1925 film made the mutiny, and its Odessa steps sequence, one of cinema's most quoted images.

Alexander Dubcek, elected First Secretary of Czechoslovakia's Communist Party in January 1968, had spent months easing censorship and allowing open debate under a programme he called socialism with a human face. Moscow watched the reforms spread and warned repeatedly that they risked Czechoslovakia leaving the Soviet bloc's orbit entirely.

On the night of 20 to 21 August 1968, roughly 200,000 Warsaw Pact troops and 2,000 tanks crossed into Czechoslovakia from the Soviet Union, Poland, East Germany, Hungary and Bulgaria. Resistance was mostly passive: crowds argued with soldiers and removed street signs, but dozens of civilians were killed in confrontations. Dubcek was flown to Moscow, forced to sign an agreement reversing the reforms, and removed from office the following year.

Frederick William I inherited a small, thinly funded Prussian army when he became king in 1713 and rebuilt it around relentless, repetitive drill, standardised iron ramrods that let infantry fire faster than rival armies, and officers drawn systematically from the Junker landed nobility. He personally inspected regiments and punished sloppy formation drill without exception.

He rarely used the army he built, preferring to hoard troops and treasury rather than fight, which earned him the nickname the Soldier King even though he led few campaigns himself. His son Frederick II inherited a force that was, soldier for soldier, among the best drilled in Europe, and spent it almost immediately after taking the throne.

Hannibal Barca left Iberia in the spring of 218 BC with an army ancient sources put near 100,000, along with dozens of war elephants, and crossed the Alps in early winter, losing perhaps half his men and most of the elephants to cold, landslides and hostile mountain tribes before he reached Italy. He chose the route because Rome expected an attack from the sea, not from the mountains at its back.

Hannibal then destroyed Roman armies at Trebia, Lake Trasimene and, in 216 BC, at Cannae, where he encircled and annihilated a force Roman writers put at around 50,000 men, among the heaviest single day losses Rome ever recorded. He never had the equipment to take Rome itself, and after over a decade campaigning in Italy, Rome carried the war to Africa and forced his recall to defend Carthage.

Kangxi personally led one of two Qing armies converging on the Dzungar leader Galdan in the summer of 1696, while a second force under General Fiyanggu marched north from the Ordos. On 12 June, Galdan's troops stumbled into Fiyanggu's army on the upper Terelj river near modern Zuunmod and were trapped between the two Qing columns with no escape route.

Galdan's wife Anu was killed in the fighting, and the Qing seized tens of thousands of the Dzungars' cattle and sheep. Galdan fled west with only a few dozen men and died the following spring, and Outer Mongolia's Khalkha tribes, who had already sought Qing protection from him, remained under Qing overlordship afterward.

The Dzungar Khanate had controlled the grasslands and oases of Central Asia for decades before internal succession quarrels weakened it in the 1750s. Qing armies under the Qianlong Emperor exploited the split, campaigning across the Tarim Basin and destroying Dzungar power by 1759.

Qing sources describe the campaigns as devastating to the Dzungar population, with survivors scattered or absorbed into neighbouring groups. The conquered territory, renamed Xinjiang, meaning new frontier, was garrisoned and settled by Qing administrators, adding a vast expanse of Central Asia to an empire that already stretched from Tibet to Manchuria.

The two Battles of Tarain, fought near Delhi in 1191 and 1192, decided the same contest twice over. In the first, Prithviraj Chauhan's Rajput coalition drove off Muhammad of Ghor's army and wounded Muhammad himself, who withdrew to Ghazni to rebuild his force.

A year later Muhammad returned with a larger, faster cavalry force and reversed the result, capturing and executing Prithviraj. The defeat broke the Chauhan kingdom and opened the Gangetic plain to the Ghurid armies, whose general Qutb ud-Din Aibak went on to found the Delhi Sultanate within a decade.

Japanese forces entered Nanjing, then China's capital, on 13 December 1937 after a rapid siege. Over the following six weeks soldiers under General Iwane Matsui carried out organised killings of surrendered soldiers and civilians alike, along with mass sexual violence against women and girls. Foreign residents who stayed, including the businessman John Rabe, set up a safety zone that sheltered an estimated 200,000 people from the worst of it.

Estimates of the dead range from around 40,000 by some Japanese scholars to over 300,000 in the figure used by the postwar Nanjing tribunal, a gap that reflects disputed methods of counting rather than doubt that a massacre occurred. Matsui was convicted by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East in 1948 and executed.

The siege of Granada lasted from April 1491 until the city's surrender on 2 January 1492, the last Muslim held territory on the Iberian peninsula after centuries in which Christian kingdoms had steadily pushed south. Emir Muhammad XII, known to Christians as Boabdil, negotiated terms that initially promised religious freedom for Granada's Muslim population.

Those terms were not honoured for long. Within a decade, forced conversions and expulsions followed, and Boabdil himself went into exile in North Africa. Ferdinand and Isabella financed Columbus's first voyage that same year, so 1492 closed one long frontier in Spain's history while opening another across the Atlantic.

The Bolsheviks had no reliable armed force of their own after seizing power in 1917, so the Council of People's Commissars decreed the creation of the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army on 28 January 1918. Leon Trotsky, appointed Commissar for War that March, built it from volunteer Red Guards, mutinied soldiers and, controversially among old Bolsheviks, thousands of former Tsarist officers whose expertise he judged worth the political risk.

Trotsky introduced conscription and strict discipline, including the reintroduction of the death penalty for desertion, despite objections from other Bolsheviks. The force he assembled grew to roughly five million men by 1920 and won the civil war against White forces and other opponents. It remained the Soviet Union's army, under later names, until the state dissolved in 1991.

Fire gutted the German parliament building in Berlin on the night of 27 February 1933, less than a month after Adolf Hitler became chancellor. Police found a young Dutch bricklayer and former communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, inside and arrested him at the scene; he confessed to acting alone, though the Nazi leadership immediately blamed a wider communist conspiracy.

Within a day President Hindenburg signed a decree suspending most civil liberties, and thousands of communists and other opponents were arrested. The Reichstag, meeting elsewhere weeks later, passed the Enabling Act that let Hitler's cabinet legislate without parliament. Whether the fire was a lone act or a Nazi provocation remains disputed among historians.

The Convention formalised the Terror in September 1793 by passing the Law of Suspects, which allowed the arrest of anyone whose conduct, associations or even silence suggested disloyalty to the Republic. The Revolutionary Tribunal, already sitting since the spring, expanded its caseload sharply, and the guillotine became a near daily fixture in Paris and in provincial cities put down after federalist revolts.

Estimates of those killed during the roughly ten months of the Terror run to around 16,000 by tribunal sentence, with thousands more dying in prison or in summary killings outside any trial, notably at Lyon and Nantes. Robespierre, who had justified the killings as revolutionary virtue enforced by terror, was himself arrested and guillotined in July 1794, ending the period that bears the name.

Robert Kennedy had just finished a victory speech to supporters at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles after winning California's Democratic primary when he was led through a kitchen passageway shortly after midnight on 5 June 1968. Sirhan Sirhan, a Palestinian immigrant angered by Kennedy's support for Israel, fired a revolver into the crowd there, hitting him three times.

Kennedy died the following day, 6 June, at the age of 42, less than five years after his brother John's assassination. Sirhan was convicted and remains in prison. Kennedy's death, coming two months after Martin Luther King's, ended the campaign of a candidate many Democrats had seen as their strongest chance of retaking the White House that year.

In 43 CE Emperor Claudius sent four legions, some 40,000 men under Aulus Plautius, across the Channel to make good on Julius Caesar's failed expeditions a century earlier. Claudius himself crossed later, reportedly bringing elephants to overawe the Britons, and joined the final push to capture the Catuvellauni stronghold at Camulodunum, modern Colchester.

Resistance did not end there: the Silures, Ordovices and later Boudica's revolt in 60 or 61 CE kept parts of the island fighting Roman rule for decades, and the far north was never fully held. Even so, the province of Britannia, organised with roads, garrisons and towns on the Roman model, lasted until the legions withdrew in the early 5th century.

Romulus Augustulus was a teenager placed on the western throne by his father in 475, and he never held real power. In September 476 the Germanic general Odoacer, commanding troops who had gone unpaid, deposed him and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople rather than naming a new emperor of his own.

Odoacer ruled Italy afterward as a king, not a Caesar, and contemporaries barely marked the change. Later historians fixed on 476 as the end of the western empire mainly because no successor followed Romulus Augustulus, but the eastern half continued from Constantinople for nearly another thousand years, and much of Roman administration in Italy carried on under Odoacer largely unaltered.

Before dawn on 24 February 2022, Russian forces crossed into Ukraine from the north, east and south, and missiles struck cities including Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa. Vladimir Putin announced what he called a special military operation, meant, he claimed, to demilitarise and denazify a country whose president is Jewish.

Russian columns aiming to take Kyiv within days were stopped and pushed back within weeks, and the war settled into grinding fighting along a front in the east and south. It became the largest land war in Europe since 1945, displacing millions of Ukrainians and drawing sweeping sanctions and arms shipments from Western governments.

Organised White resistance had already collapsed by late 1920, when General Pyotr Wrangel's forces evacuated Crimea, but pockets of fighting against Bolshevik rule dragged on in Central Asia and the Far East for two more years. The last significant White stronghold, Vladivostok, fell to the Red Army in October 1922, and the Far Eastern Republic that had briefly buffered the region was absorbed into Soviet Russia in November.

The war had killed an estimated seven to twelve million people, most from famine and disease rather than combat, and left the economy in ruins. Its end cleared the way for the formal creation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics that December, uniting the Bolshevik controlled territories under a single state for the first time.

Yermak Timofeyevich led a Cossack band, hired and armed by the merchant Stroganov family, across the Ural Mountains in 1582 with several hundred men and firearms the Siberian Khanate's forces largely lacked. He took the khanate's capital near modern Tobolsk the following year and sent word to Tsar Ivan IV that a new territory lay open.

Yermak drowned in the Irtysh River in 1585 after a Siberian counterattack, and Moscow's hold nearly collapsed before fresh troops secured it. Within decades Russian traders and soldiers had pushed forts all the way to the Pacific, drawn on by the fur trade the conquest had opened.

Japan opened the war in February 1904 with a surprise torpedo attack on the Russian fleet at Port Arthur, a Chinese port Russia had leased on the Manchurian coast that Japan regarded as its own sphere of interest. Neither side had declared war before the shooting started.

Japanese armies then besieged Port Arthur and won the grinding land battle of Mukden, while its navy annihilated Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima in May 1905. Theodore Roosevelt mediated the peace at Portsmouth that September, and Japan's win over a major European power reshaped how the rest of the world assessed it, feeding ambitions that led to further expansion in Korea and Manchuria.

Russia went to war with Sweden in 1590 hoping to reverse losses from an earlier Baltic conflict fought under Ivan the Terrible. Fighting spread along the Gulf of Finland and into Karelia, with garrison towns changing hands more than once before either side could hold what it took.

The Treaty of Tyavzino in 1595 ended this round on terms mostly favourable to Russia, restoring towns lost decades earlier, but Sweden kept the deeper foothold in Ingria it had already built. The border it drew held only until the next war a generation later, when Sweden reversed nearly every gain.

The killing began on 7 April 1994, the day after President Habyarimana's plane was shot down over Kigali, and it was not spontaneous: militia lists of Tutsi names had been compiled in advance. Roadblocks went up across the country within hours, and ordinary Hutu civilians were pressed alongside soldiers and militia into killing their neighbours.

The United Nations estimated that roughly 800,000 people were killed in about a hundred days, most by machete rather than gun. A small UN peacekeeping force under General Romeo Dallaire was barred from intervening under its mandate, and the killing ended only when Paul Kagame's Rwandan Patriotic Front took Kigali that July.

Between 16 and 18 September 1982, Lebanese Christian militiamen entered the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps in Beirut and killed Palestinian and Lebanese Shia residents, moving house to house over roughly 36 hours. Israeli forces, which had occupied west Beirut days earlier after the assassination of president elect Bashir Gemayel, controlled the checkpoints around the camps and did not intervene.

Estimates of the dead range from around 800, the figure reached by the Kahan Commission, Israel's own inquiry, to several thousand recorded by Palestinian researchers; the true number is unresolved because many bodies were buried in unmarked graves or removed before investigators arrived. The Kahan Commission also found Defence Minister Ariel Sharon indirectly responsible and recommended his removal from that post.

The Vandal king Geiseric sailed from North Africa and entered Rome in June 455, invited in some accounts by the widow of the murdered emperor Valentinian III seeking help against his usurper successor. Pope Leo I met Geiseric and negotiated a pledge against murder and burning, though it did not stop two weeks of systematic looting.

Vandal soldiers stripped the city of what earlier sacks had left, including gilded roof tiles from the Temple of Jupiter, and shipped much of it back to Carthage. The episode gave later writers, particularly in the eighteenth century, the word vandalism for wanton destruction, though Geiseric's own restraint on killing was closer to calculated plunder than blind wreckage.

Alaric's Visigoths entered Rome on 24 August 410 through the Salarian Gate, reportedly opened from within, after two earlier sieges had already forced the city to pay ransom and negotiate. His army looted for three days, stripping gold and silver but largely sparing the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, which he had declared off limits.

Rome had not fallen to a foreign army since Gauls under Brennus took it around 390 BCE, so the shock reached far beyond Italy. Jerome, then living in Bethlehem, wrote that the city which had conquered the world was itself now captive. Alaric died within months, before he could use the sack to force a lasting settlement with the western empire.

American soldiers of the 4th Infantry Division found Saddam Hussein on 13 December 2003 near his hometown of Tikrit, hiding alone in a narrow dug-out pit beneath a mud hut on a farm outside the village of Ad-Dawr. He had a pistol within reach but did not resist, and photographs of a bearded, dishevelled Saddam were released within hours.

He had been in hiding for eight months since the fall of Baghdad, moving between a small number of trusted safe houses. Tried by an Iraqi tribunal for crimes committed against the town of Dujail in 1982, he was convicted and hanged in December 2006, a swift end that left much of his broader record unexamined in court.

At Chaldiran in 1514 an Ottoman army under Selim I met Shah Ismail's Safavid forces on a plain in what is now northwestern Iran. Ottoman cannon and janissary musket fire cut into cavalry charges that had served Ismail well against less well armed enemies, and the Safavids broke, though estimates of the casualties on each side vary widely between chroniclers.

Selim occupied the Safavid capital, Tabriz, briefly before withdrawing, unable to hold territory so far from Ottoman supply lines. The frontier that hardened afterward, roughly along the modern Turkish-Iranian border, separated a Sunni Ottoman state from a Shia Safavid one for the next two centuries of intermittent war.

With the Crusader field army destroyed at Hattin two months earlier, Jerusalem had little left to defend it beyond its walls and a hastily armed civilian population organised by Balian of Ibelin. Saladin's siege began in September 1187 and the city surrendered on 2 October, on terms allowing most inhabitants to buy safe passage out rather than face the massacre of 1099.

Saladin let many residents leave for a fee and reportedly freed others who could not pay, a restraint contemporaries on both sides noted against the memory of the earlier crusader conquest. News of the loss reached Europe within months and helped push Richard the Lionheart, Philip II and Frederick Barbarossa into launching the Third Crusade the following year.

The main source for Samudragupta's wars is a 33-line Sanskrit inscription he had carved onto an Ashokan pillar at Allahabad, praising him as a poet, musician and conqueror in the same breath. It names roughly a dozen rulers he fought in the south, from Kosala down toward the Krishna river.

Rather than annexing the Deccan kingdoms outright, Samudragupta's practice, as the inscription records it, was to defeat a king, capture him, then release him on payment of tribute and submission. That policy let the Gupta empire claim influence over a much larger area than it directly administered, stretching Gupta prestige far beyond its garrisoned territory in the north.

On 2 December 2015, Syed Rizwan Farook walked out of a training event and Christmas party for San Bernardino County health workers, then returned with his wife Tashfeen Malik carrying rifles and pipe bombs. They shot into the room for roughly four minutes, killing fourteen coworkers and guests, before fleeing in an SUV. The bombs they had planted failed to detonate.

Police tracked the couple's vehicle and killed both in a shootout after a chase through nearby streets. Investigators later said Malik had pledged allegiance to Islamic State on Facebook around the time of the attack. The case became a national fight over encryption after the FBI asked a court to force Apple to unlock Farook's iPhone, a request Apple resisted before the FBI found another way in.

At dawn on 29 November 1864, Colonel John Chivington led roughly 675 Colorado volunteer troops against a Cheyenne and Arapaho camp on Sand Creek whose leader, Black Kettle, had already agreed to peace terms and was flying a US flag and a white flag over his lodge as instructed.

The soldiers killed an estimated 150 to 230 people, most of them women, children and the elderly, and mutilated many of the bodies afterward as trophies. A subsequent US Army and congressional inquiry condemned the attack as a deliberate massacre rather than a battle, though Chivington, by then out of the military, was never punished for it.

Sargon began as a cupbearer to the king of Kish, according to the later Sumerian King List, before he seized power and built a capital at Akkad, a city whose exact location has never been found. From there he conquered the Sumerian city states one by one, folding Ur, Uruk and Lagash into a single realm ruled from one centre rather than a patchwork of rival kings.

His empire stretched from the Persian Gulf toward the Mediterranean, held together by governors he appointed and a standing army rather than by conquest alone. Later Mesopotamian scribes remembered him for centuries, copying tales of his birth and rise long after Akkad itself had crumbled and its ruins vanished under the sand.

Bulgaria had taken the heaviest losses fighting the Ottomans in 1912 but felt cheated of Macedonian territory in the peace that followed, and in June 1913 it attacked its former allies Serbia and Greece to seize a larger share by force. Romania and the Ottoman Empire, seeing an opportunity, joined against Bulgaria within weeks.

Fighting on four fronts at once, Bulgarian forces collapsed quickly, and the war lasted barely a month. The Treaty of Bucharest in August 1913 stripped Bulgaria of most of the gains it had made the previous year and handed southern Dobruja to Romania. The bitterness Bulgaria carried from this defeat shaped its decision to side with the Central Powers when the wider European war began the following year.

On the evening of 22 April 1915, German troops released roughly 168 tonnes of chlorine gas from thousands of cylinders dug into the front line near Langemarck, Belgium. French colonial and territorial troops broke and fled as the yellow-green cloud drifted across their trenches, opening a gap in the Allied line four miles wide.

German commanders had not planned for the scale of the breakthrough and failed to exploit it before Canadian and British units plugged the gap, some soldiers improvising by urinating on cloths to neutralise the gas over their faces. Both sides adopted gas warfare afterward, and by the war's end it had caused an estimated one million casualties.

News that Edessa had fallen to Nur ad-Din's forces in 1144 reached Europe as the first crusader state lost since the conquests of the 1090s, and Pope Eugene III called for a new expedition to recover it. King Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany led separate armies east by different routes in 1147, both suffering heavy losses to ambush and hunger before either reached Antioch.

Rather than march on Edessa, the surviving crusaders were persuaded to attack Damascus instead, a city with no bearing on the original goal, and the siege there collapsed within days in 1148. The failure discouraged further large royal expeditions for decades and left Edessa in Muslim hands, a loss the crusader states never reversed.

Ariel Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount compound in Jerusalem on 28 September 2000, days after the Camp David summit had failed to reach a final peace deal, was followed by clashes that spread into a much wider uprising. Palestinian stone throwing and Israeli live fire in the first days quickly escalated on both sides.

Suicide bombings inside Israeli cities and Israeli military incursions into West Bank towns became routine over the following years, a marked shift from the largely unarmed protest of the first intifada a decade earlier. The violence eased gradually after 2004 and 2005, having killed roughly three thousand Palestinians and around a thousand Israelis by most tallies of the period.

The spark was a rumour about rifle cartridge grease, said to be made from beef and pork fat and therefore religiously unclean for both Hindu and Muslim soldiers who had to bite it open. Sepoys at Meerut refused the cartridges in May 1857, were court-martialled, and their comrades then broke open the jail, killed several British officers and marched on Delhi.

The revolt spread across northern and central India for over a year, with sieges at Lucknow and Cawnpore marked by massacres on both sides. Britain's response was similarly brutal, including mass executions after the fall of Delhi. Parliament dissolved the East India Company in 1858 and transferred its territories to the Crown, ending Company rule outright.

Nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers took control of four commercial airliners on the morning of 11 September 2001. Two struck the World Trade Center's twin towers in New York, one struck the Pentagon outside Washington, and the fourth crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought to retake the cockpit.

Both towers collapsed within two hours of impact, and the attacks killed nearly 3,000 people. Osama bin Laden was identified within days as the operation's architect, and the United States invoked NATO's mutual defence clause for the first time in the alliance's history before launching the war in Afghanistan that October.

In May 1756, Britain declared war on France, formalising a conflict that had already begun the previous year in the forests of North America. Austria and Prussia soon reversed their old alliances in what diplomats called the Diplomatic Revolution, with Austria, France and Russia now ranged against Frederick the Great's Prussia and its British ally.

The fighting spanned Europe, India, West Africa, the Caribbean and North America, drawing in enough combatants that some historians have called it a world war before that term existed. Britain's gains in Canada and India reshaped its empire, while Prussia's survival against three larger powers, chiefly through Frederick's generalship, kept it a major European state through to the war's end in 1763.

Louis IX landed in Egypt in 1249 and took Damietta almost without a fight, the Egyptian garrison having withdrawn before he arrived. He then repeated the Fifth Crusade's route south toward Cairo, a decision that had already failed once a generation earlier for the same reason: the Nile flood.

Trapped by rising water and harassed by Egyptian forces at Fariskur in 1250, Louis's army was destroyed and the king himself was taken prisoner, ill with dysentery. He bought his release with a huge ransom and the return of Damietta, then spent four more years in the Levant before sailing home to France in 1254.

Shaka became chief of the small Zulu clan in 1816 after the death of his father, Senzangakhona, with backing from the neighbouring Mthethwa chief who had sheltered him during an earlier exile. He reorganised his fighters around the short stabbing spear, or iklwa, and close formation tactics that abandoned the long-range thrown spear favoured elsewhere in the region.

Through conquest and absorption of defeated clans, Shaka built the Zulu from a minor lineage of perhaps a few thousand people into a kingdom of several hundred thousand within roughly a decade. His campaigns and the wars they triggered among displaced neighbouring peoples, sometimes called the Mfecane, reshaped the political map of southern Africa well beyond Zulu borders.

On 21 March 1960, thousands gathered outside a police station in Sharpeville, south of Johannesburg, to hand in the passbooks Black South Africans were required to carry under apartheid laws. Officers opened fire on the unarmed crowd without warning. Most of the dead were shot in the back as they fled, and many of the wounded were shot while running away.

The Pan Africanist Congress had organised the protest as a deliberate act of mass defiance, expecting arrests rather than gunfire. South Africa banned both the PAC and the African National Congress within weeks, pushing both underground and toward armed struggle. The United Nations Security Council condemned the killings, and 21 March later became South Africa's Human Rights Day.

Muhammad Shaybani Khan led Uzbek forces south out of the steppe and took Bukhara, then Samarkand, from the descendants of Timur who had ruled Central Asia for generations. Among those he pushed out was a young prince named Babur, who would spend years trying and failing to retake his family's old capital.

Babur eventually gave up on Central Asia and turned south instead, conquering Kabul and later Delhi to found the Mughal Empire. Shaybani's own dynasty held Bukhara for roughly a century, making the city the centre of a settled Uzbek state rather than a nomadic confederation passing through it.

Massachusetts farmers, many of them Revolutionary War veterans paid in nearly worthless certificates, faced court seizures of their land and livestock over debts and state taxes in the mid 1780s. In 1786, groups led by Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain, began forcing courts to close by blocking their doors, stopping the foreclosure hearings that were sending debtors to jail.

The rebellion's largest act, an attack on the federal arsenal at Springfield in January 1787, was repelled by a state militia force paid for by Boston merchants, since Congress had no funds and no army of its own to send. The episode convinced many, including George Washington, that the weak Articles of Confederation could not keep order, adding urgency to the convention that drafted the Constitution later that year.

William Sherman abandoned his own supply lines when he left Atlanta on 15 November 1864, choosing instead to feed his roughly 60,000 men off the Georgia countryside as they marched toward Savannah. Soldiers were ordered to destroy railroads, mills and warehouses, and foragers, nicknamed bummers, stripped farms of food and livestock along a corridor tens of miles wide.

Sherman reached Savannah on 21 December and telegraphed Lincoln offering the city as a Christmas present. Confederate resistance along the route was thin, and the campaign's deliberate destruction of the region's capacity to feed Confederate armies, rather than any single battle, was what Sherman meant by making Georgia howl.
