Peasants and dispossessed samurai on the Shimabara peninsula rose against crushing taxes and the persecution of Christian converts in December 1637, rallying around a teenage figurehead, Amakusa Shiro. They fortified the ruined castle at Hara and held it through the winter against a shogunate army that eventually numbered well over 100,000.

The siege ended in April 1638 with the defenders killed almost to the last person, by most estimates tens of thousands. The shogunate read the revolt as proof that Christianity and foreign contact bred rebellion, and within years it expelled the Portuguese and sealed Japan's ports, a policy that held for two centuries.

The Onin War broke out in 1467 over a dispute about who would succeed as shogun and head the Hosokawa and Yamana warrior clans, and it dragged the imperial capital Kyoto into a decade of street fighting that left much of the city burned. The Ashikaga shogunate survived on paper but never regained real authority over the regional lords who had done the actual fighting.

Those lords, the daimyo, kept their private armies mobilised long after 1467 and began fighting each other directly for territory rather than for any claim on the shogunate. The resulting century of shifting alliances and open warfare across Japan became known as the Sengoku, or Warring States, period.

German and Finnish forces closed the ring around Leningrad on 8 September 1941, cutting the city off from overland supply and beginning a siege that would last 872 days. Civilians ground wallpaper paste and sawdust into food once flour ran out, and the winter of 1941 to 1942 brought temperatures that froze the city's water pipes along with its dead, who could not be buried fast enough.

A narrow supply line across frozen Lake Ladoga, known as the Road of Life, kept a trickle of food and evacuees moving in the worst months. Estimates of civilian deaths from starvation, disease and shelling range widely, with Soviet postwar figures citing roughly 632,000 dead in the city, though later historians have argued the true toll was considerably higher.

Soviet forces broke the German blockade of Leningrad on 27 January 1944 after nearly two and a half years, driving encircling forces back from the city's approaches in an offensive that finally reopened land routes for supply. The date is still marked in the city, now Saint Petersburg, with fireworks over the Neva.

By the siege's end, hundreds of thousands of residents had died of starvation and cold, most of them during the first, worst winter when rations fell to a few hundred grams of bread a day cut with sawdust filler. Leningrad was awarded the Soviet title Hero City after the war, one of a handful of cities recognised for what its population had endured under occupation and bombardment.

Roman forces under Lucius Flavius Silva reached the fortress of Masada in 73 and, unable to storm its cliffs, built a massive earthen ramp up its western side over several months, remains of which still stand. Several hundred Jewish rebels, the Sicarii, had held the site since early in the revolt.

Once the ramp let Roman siege engines breach the wall, the historian Josephus writes that the defenders chose death over capture, drawing lots so that a small number killed the rest before taking their own lives. He puts the number at 960, with two women and five children found alive in hiding. His account is the only detailed narrative, and its precision has been questioned by later historians.

Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik brought roughly 80,000 troops and a fleet said to number in the hundreds of ships to the walls of Constantinople in August 717, hoping to finish what an earlier Arab army had failed to do a generation before. Emperor Leo III had only just seized the throne, but the city's triple land walls held, and its harbour could be sealed by chain.

Greek fire, sprayed from siphons mounted on Byzantine ships, burned much of the Arab fleet in the Bosphorus, and a brutal winter starved the besiegers camped outside the walls. Bulgar forces harried the Arabs from the rear, and by August 718, after roughly a year, the survivors withdrew. The failure ended Umayyad hopes of taking Byzantium's capital by force.

Khalid ibn al-Walid's army surrounded Damascus in August 634, and the siege dragged on for weeks against a city still garrisoned by Byzantine troops. It ended in a curious split: Khalid stormed the eastern gate by night after a bishop showed his men a weak point in the wall, while at almost the same hour his own deputy, Abu Ubayda, was negotiating a peaceful surrender at another gate.

The two Arab columns met inside the city having taken it by force and by treaty simultaneously, and the terms of Abu Ubayda's surrender, guaranteeing residents their property and churches, were honoured over Khalid's claim of conquest. Damascus became the springboard for further campaigns into Syria and, within a century, a Umayyad capital ruling from Spain to Central Asia.

Jacobite forces loyal to the deposed James II arrived outside Derry in April 1689, after the city's Protestant apprentices had already shut its gates against an incoming garrison they distrusted. Inside, food ran short as the siege dragged on through the summer, and accounts describe residents eating dogs, rats and tallow candles as supplies collapsed.

Ships sent to relieve the city were blocked by a boom the Jacobites had built across the River Foyle, until the merchant vessel Mountjoy broke through it on 28 July 1689, ending the siege after 105 days. The defence became a founding story for Ulster Protestant identity, still marked in Londonderry each year, and it deprived James's cause of a base in the north of Ireland.

The Byzantine patriarch Sophronius refused to hand Jerusalem to anyone but the Caliph himself, so Umar ibn al-Khattab travelled from Medina to accept the surrender in person. He arrived, by most tellings, in patched clothes on a plain mount rather than as a conqueror, and issued a covenant promising the city's Christians their churches, property and freedom of worship.

Umar was reportedly invited to pray inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and declined, wary of setting a precedent that Muslims might later claim the building. He prayed instead nearby, on a site later marked by the small Mosque of Umar. The terms he granted shaped how Jerusalem's communities coexisted under Muslim rule for centuries afterward.

Titus, son of the newly proclaimed emperor Vespasian, brought four legions against Jerusalem in the spring of 70 CE, four years into a Jewish revolt against Rome. The city's defenders were divided among themselves, and factional fighting inside the walls destroyed food stores that might have let the siege drag on longer. Roman troops broke through the outer walls in stages over several months.

The Jewish historian Josephus, who had fought against Rome before switching sides, watched the fall of the Temple from the Roman camp and wrote that soldiers set it alight against Titus's orders. The building burned on the ninth of the Hebrew month of Av, a date still marked as a fast, and its destruction ended the priestly sacrifices that had defined Jewish worship there for centuries.

A royal and church army besieged the Cathar fortress of Montsegur, in the Pyrenean foothills of southern France, from May 1243 until its surrender in March 1244. The defenders held out on their mountain for close to ten months before the besiegers finally hauled siege engines onto a spur overlooking the walls and made the position untenable.

Around 210 Cathars who refused to renounce their faith, most of them ordained perfecti, were burned together in a single fire below the mountain on 16 March 1244. The siege effectively ended organised Cathar resistance in the region, and Montsegur's ruins became, centuries later, a focus of later myth making about hidden treasure and secret survivors that has little basis in the surviving record.

Bosnian Serb forces began encircling Sarajevo on 5 April 1992, days after Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence from Yugoslavia, positioning artillery and snipers in the hills overlooking the city. Residents crossing open intersections came to know one stretch as Sniper Alley, where gunmen in surrounding buildings fired on civilians crossing in the open, including children.

The siege lasted almost four years, ending in February 1996, and became the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare, outlasting the siege of Leningrad. A United Nations tribunal later put the civilian and military dead in Sarajevo at over eleven thousand, and residents survived largely on aid flown in through an airlift and supplies carried through a tunnel dug under the airport runway.

Rome besieged Syracuse from 213 to 212 BCE during the Second Punic War, and the city held out partly because of devices credited to Archimedes: grappling cranes that Plutarch says lifted Roman ships out of the water, and catapults ranged to hit approaching vessels at fixed distances. How much of this is engineering fact and how much later embellishment is disputed.

The city fell in 212 BCE after a Roman soldier found a poorly guarded section of wall during a festival. Archimedes was killed in the sack despite orders to spare him, reportedly while working on a mathematical problem in the sand and telling the soldier not to disturb it.

Suleiman the Magnificent brought an Ottoman army to Vienna in September 1529, at the end of a campaign season that had already cost him time and men on the long march up from Constantinople. The city's Habsburg garrison, far smaller than the besieging force, had strengthened its walls and dug in behind earthworks that blunted repeated Ottoman assaults through October.

Early winter weather, exhausted supply lines and heavy losses among his siege troops forced Suleiman to withdraw before the city fell, retreating in poor conditions that cost him further casualties on the way home. The failure marked the practical limit of Ottoman expansion into central Europe by that route, though Vienna would face another Ottoman siege a century and a half later.

Guru Gobind Singh gathered followers at Anandpur on Baisakhi day in 1699 and, according to Sikh tradition, called for five volunteers willing to give their heads for their faith. He initiated them with sweetened water stirred by a sword, gave them the shared surname Singh, and set out the five articles of dress members of the Khalsa still keep.

The Khalsa replaced a looser community of disciples with an organised body bound by discipline and open to any caste, reshaping how Sikhs would defend themselves against Mughal persecution in the decades that followed. Gobind Singh himself led Khalsa forces in battle against Mughal and hill state armies for the rest of his life.

Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, spent the years around 1704 and 1705 fighting Mughal and hill-state forces after his fortress at Anandpur was besieged and his family scattered at Chamkaur and Sirhind. Two of his young sons were executed by the Mughal governor of Sirhind, hardening Sikh resistance in Punjab.

The fighting drew on grievances stretching back three decades, to the 1675 execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur, Gobind Singh's father, for refusing forced conversion. After Gobind Singh's death in 1708, his follower Banda Singh Bahadur carried the campaign forward, briefly seizing Sirhind and issuing coins in the name of the Sikh faith before his capture and death in 1716.

Sima Yan had already deposed the last Wei emperor in 266 and declared himself the first ruler of the Jin dynasty. Wu, the southern kingdom that had outlasted both its rivals from the Three Kingdoms era, was the last piece left to take, defended by the Yangtze and a navy built over decades.

In 279 Jin forces advanced along the river on several fronts at once, and by 280 the Wu emperor Sun Hao surrendered at his capital, Jianye. It closed nearly a century of division that had run from the fall of the Han through the Three Kingdoms period, though the unity Sima Yan achieved did not outlast his own dynasty by much.

Fighting broke out at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing on 7 July 1937, after a Japanese unit conducting night exercises clashed with Chinese troops nearby. Japan used the incident to launch a full invasion rather than a limited punitive strike, sending forces that captured Shanghai, Nanjing and much of eastern China within the following year.

Nationalist and Communist Chinese forces, nominally allied under a strained united front, retreated inland and fought a war of attrition that lasted eight years and merged into the wider Pacific War after 1941. Estimates of Chinese deaths, military and civilian combined, range from roughly 10 to 20 million, a toll that made this the deadliest single theatre of the Second World War in Asia.

Israel opened the war on 5 June 1967 with a pre-emptive strike that destroyed most of Egypt's air force on the ground within hours, after weeks of Egyptian troop movements into Sinai and the closure of the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. Jordan and Syria entered the fighting soon after, and Israeli forces struck all three fronts before any of them could organise a coordinated defence.

By the ceasefire on 10 June, Israel held the Sinai Peninsula and Gaza Strip from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria, more than tripling the territory it controlled in under a week. The war displaced several hundred thousand Palestinians and Syrians, and the occupied territories it created remain at the centre of the region's unresolved disputes.

Emperor Frederick II, already excommunicated by the Pope for delaying his crusade, negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa with the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil in February 1229 without fighting a single major battle. The agreement handed Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth and a corridor connecting them to the coast back to Christian control for a fixed ten year term, while leaving the city's Islamic holy sites under Muslim administration.

Frederick crowned himself king of Jerusalem in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre days later, an act so irregular that no bishop would perform the coronation and it was met with jeers rather than celebration from parts of the local clergy. The truce held for most of its term, but Jerusalem's Christian hold proved temporary: it fell again within fifteen years.

Skandagupta inherited an empire already strained by his father Kumaragupta's wars and by a disputed succession, and almost immediately faced Hephthalite Hun raiders pushing into northern India from Central Asia. An inscription on the Bhitari pillar credits him with restoring the fortunes of his family after this near collapse.

He beat back the Hun incursions in the 450s, buying the Gupta empire another generation, but the cost showed in the coinage: gold content dropped and mints grew less consistent under his rule. After his death around 467 the empire fragmented into competing regional rulers, and the Huns he had held off returned within decades.

Askia Muhammad seized the Songhai throne in 1493 after deposing Sunni Baru, and he justified much of his subsequent campaigning as bringing Islamic rule to peoples he judged insufficiently observant, including his 1498 conquest of the Mossi kingdom to the south. He also absorbed large stretches of the former Mali empire's western territory piece by piece over the following decade.

Under his administration Songhai grew into the largest state West Africa had yet seen, with Gao as its capital and Timbuktu flourishing as a centre of Islamic scholarship and manuscript production. He was eventually deposed and blinded by his own son in 1528, ending a thirty five year reign that had reshaped the region's borders.

Firearms reached the Sahel not through a single conquest but through the caravan routes that had already carried salt, gold and slaves across the desert for centuries. Songhai traders and rulers obtained muskets from North African middlemen, adding them to an army that still relied mainly on cavalry, spearmen and river-based infantry along the Niger.

The weapons never fully displaced older arms, and the empire's real military strength stayed in its mounted nobility and provincial levies. Within a century Moroccan forces armed more thoroughly with firearms, including arquebusiers, would defeat Songhai outright, a reminder that owning some guns and fielding a gun army were not the same thing.

Askia Muhammad came to power after overthrowing the son of Sunni Ali, and one of his most durable changes was administrative rather than territorial. He divided the Songhai military into provincial commands, each under an officer answerable to the crown, replacing looser arrangements built around personal loyalty to individual warlords.

Professional garrisons were stationed in key towns along the Niger, giving the empire a standing force it could call on without waiting for levies to assemble. The system helped Songhai control trade routes and river traffic across a huge stretch of West Africa, though it depended heavily on the ruler holding the provincial officers' loyalty in turn.

Moshoeshoe led a small band of followers onto Thaba Bosiu, a flat topped sandstone mountain with only a few narrow approaches, in the early months of 1824, during the upheavals of the Mfecane. The site's cliffs and single defensible paths let a small force hold off much larger attackers.

Moshoeshoe drew in refugees from the fighting spreading across the region, absorbing them into a growing Basotho identity rather than simply conquering them, and used marriage alliances and negotiated tribute to bind neighbouring chiefs to him. Thaba Bosiu was besieged repeatedly by rival African armies and later by Boer and British forces, but it was never taken by force.

By late 1963, Ngo Dinh Diem's crackdown on Buddhist protesters had cost him support in Washington and among his own generals. On 1 November, army officers surrounded the presidential palace in Saigon; Diem and his brother Ngo Dinh Nhu fled to a church in the Cholon district and surrendered the next morning. Both were killed in an armoured personnel carrier on the way to military headquarters.

Washington had been told of the coup plan in advance through cables between the Saigon embassy and the State Department, and did nothing to stop it, though the killings themselves went beyond what US officials expected. The junta that replaced Diem proved unstable, and South Vietnam went through a series of further coups over the next two years while the war against the Viet Cong continued.

Soviet troops airlifted into Kabul on 24 December 1979, and within three days special forces stormed the presidential palace and killed President Hafizullah Amin, whose own communist party the Soviets no longer trusted to hold the country. A rival faction leader, Babrak Karmal, was installed in his place.

The occupation drew Afghan mujahideen fighters into a guerrilla war that the Soviet army never subdued, despite committing over 100,000 troops at its peak. The United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia funnelled weapons and money to the insurgents, and Soviet forces withdrew in February 1989 after nearly a decade of fighting that killed roughly a million Afghans.

Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on 25 December 1991, the day after signing over control of the nuclear arsenal, and the Soviet flag over the Kremlin was lowered for the last time that evening. The dissolution followed a failed coup against him that August, after which republic after republic declared independence rather than remain under Moscow's authority.

Russia, Ukraine and Belarus had already agreed in early December to form a Commonwealth of Independent States, and most of the remaining republics joined within weeks, leaving fifteen separate countries where one union had stood. The change ended a state that had existed since 1922 and reshaped the map of Europe and Central Asia almost overnight.

On 16 June 1976, thousands of students in Soweto marched toward Orlando Stadium to protest a rule requiring some subjects to be taught in Afrikaans. Police blocked the route and released tear gas, then opened fire on the crowd. Hector Pieterson, 12, was among the first killed, and a photograph of his body being carried by another student became one of the defining images of the apartheid era.

The unrest spread from Soweto to townships across South Africa in the following months as students kept marching and police kept shooting. The government's own count put the dead at 176, but the Truth and Reconciliation Commission later found the true figure was substantially higher and could not be fixed with certainty. Afrikaans instruction was withdrawn within weeks, but protests continued nationwide.

The battleship USS Maine exploded in Havana harbour in February 1898, killing 266 sailors, and American newspapers blamed Spain before any inquiry could establish a cause. Congress declared war that April, and the fighting that followed lasted barely four months, ending with Spain's colonial navy destroyed at Manila Bay and Santiago.

The peace treaty signed in Paris that December transferred Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to American control and ended Spanish rule over Cuba, which it had held since Columbus. The United States paid Spain twenty million dollars for the Philippines, and Filipino revolutionaries who had fought alongside the Americans found themselves fighting a new occupying power within months.

Philip II sent roughly 130 ships north in 1588 to escort an invasion army across the Channel from the Spanish Netherlands and depose Elizabeth I. English fireships scattered the Armada's tight formation off Calais on the night of 28 July, and a following battle off Gravelines the next day forced the Spanish fleet away from its intended rendezvous and out into the North Sea.

With no safe harbour open to it, the Armada was driven north around Scotland and down past Ireland's west coast, where storms wrecked dozens of ships on the rocks. Fewer than a third of the fleet's roughly 130 ships made it back to Spain intact, and disease killed far more of the roughly fifteen thousand Spanish dead than English guns did.

Spain sent further fleets against England in 1596 and 1597, both scattered by Atlantic storms before they could land troops. The 1588 Armada had already lost more ships to weather and disease on the retreat around Scotland and Ireland than to English gunfire, and the pattern repeated: Spanish crews were skilled, but the ocean beat them as often as any enemy.

None of this bankrupted Spain outright. Silver fleets from the Americas kept arriving through the 1590s, and Spanish infantry still dominated land campaigns in the Netherlands. What eroded was the navy's ability to force a landing on English soil, which never happened again after 1588.

Army garrisons across Spain and its Moroccan protectorate rose against the elected Republican government on 17 and 18 July 1936, a coup intended to be swift that instead split the country and its military roughly in half. General Francisco Franco, who flew from the Canary Islands to take command of troops in Morocco, soon emerged as the rebel Nationalists' leader.

Germany and Italy sent troops, aircraft and materiel to Franco, while the Soviet Union backed the Republic and volunteers from dozens of countries joined the International Brigades. The war became a rehearsal ground for tactics used in the larger conflict that followed, including the bombing of civilian towns such as Guernica in 1937. It killed an estimated 500,000 people and ended with Franco's victory in April 1939.

Pizarro's men marched to Cusco after Atahualpa's death and installed a puppet ruler, Manco Inca, whose cooperation lasted only a few years before he rebelled and besieged the Spanish garrison in the old capital. The Inca state that had governed a huge stretch of the Andes fractured into resistance movements rather than surrendering outright.

Manco Inca eventually retreated to Vilcabamba, a remote mountain refuge where a rump Inca state survived for nearly forty more years. Spain treated Cusco's fall as the conquest's decisive moment, but organised Inca resistance in fact continued long after the empire's formal centre had been dismantled.

Charles V's ordinance of 1534 grouped Spanish infantry into tercios, units of roughly three thousand men mixing pikemen, sword and buckler troops and a growing proportion of arquebusiers. The pikemen protected the gunners from cavalry while they reloaded, solving the main weakness of early firearms on an open battlefield.

The formation proved itself across Italy, the Netherlands and Germany, and rival powers spent the rest of the century copying and adapting it. Spanish infantry built this way stayed feared well into the 1600s, even as gradual increases in the ratio of muskets to pikes slowly changed how the tercio itself was built.

Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator training at a school in Capua when he and around seventy others broke out in 73 BCE using kitchen knives and whatever weapons they could seize. The escaped group armed itself properly from a wagon of gladiatorial weapons and grew quickly as enslaved people across southern Italy joined them.

At its height the rebel force is thought to have numbered in the tens of thousands, and it beat several Roman armies sent against it before Crassus finally cornered and defeated it in 71 BCE. Spartacus died in the final battle. Roman accounts say six thousand captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way as a warning.

Riots in Palermo in January 1848 were followed within weeks by uprisings in Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Budapest and dozens of smaller cities, as urban workers, liberal professionals and nationalist movements pressed governments that had barely changed since 1815. Louis Philippe abdicated the French throne in February, and Metternich, the architect of that older order, fled Vienna in March.

Almost none of it held. Conservative armies retook Vienna and Berlin by the end of the year, Hungary's republic was crushed with Russian help in 1849, and France elected a president, Louis Napoleon, who made himself emperor within four years. The uprisings still forced monarchies across the continent to grant constitutions, even where they later clawed the powers back.

Bosnian Serb forces under General Ratko Mladic overran the UN-declared safe area of Srebrenica on 11 July 1995. Dutch peacekeepers, lightly armed and denied air support, could not stop them. Men and boys were separated from women in the following days and taken to fields, warehouses and school gymnasiums to be shot.

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia found that Bosnian Serb forces killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys, a toll established largely through mass grave exhumations and DNA matching that continued for decades afterward. The tribunal ruled the killings genocide, and both Mladic and the Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadzic were later convicted.

The killing began before dawn on 24 August 1572, when royal guards and armed Catholic mobs in Paris murdered Huguenot leaders gathered for the wedding of Henry of Navarre. The Protestant admiral Gaspard de Coligny was stabbed in his bed and his body thrown from a window. Church bells signalled the start, and the killing spread street by street through the city for several days.

News of the Paris killings triggered further massacres in Rouen, Lyon, Orleans and other provincial towns over the following weeks. Modern historians' estimates for the total dead across France range widely, from around five thousand to considerably higher, since bodies were often thrown into the Seine rather than counted. The massacre deepened the French Wars of Religion for another generation.

Fighting inside Stalingrad had ground down to house by house and floor by floor combat through the autumn of 1942 before a Soviet counteroffensive, Operation Uranus, encircled the German Sixth Army that November. Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus asked Hitler for permission to break out; Hitler refused and ordered him to hold, promising supply by air that never arrived in sufficient quantity.

Paulus surrendered on 2 February 1943 with roughly 91,000 starving survivors of an army that had numbered close to 300,000, in defiance of Hitler's earlier order that no German field marshal had ever been taken prisoner. Fewer than 6,000 of those captured are thought to have survived Soviet camps to return home after the war.

Spartan boys entered a state education system called the agoge around age seven, living apart from their families in barracks-like groups and training continuously in combat, endurance and obedience until adulthood. No other Greek city put its male citizens through anything comparable, and the system was funded by a helot underclass who worked the land the citizen-soldiers no longer had time to farm.

The result was a citizen body that trained as its full-time occupation rather than assembling only for campaigns, unusual enough that other Greeks treated a Spartan hoplite line as fearsome even before it moved. The system also kept Sparta's population of full citizens small and its politics rigid, and by the fourth century BCE it could no longer field the numbers its reputation implied.

Stilicho's father was a Vandal cavalry officer in Roman service, and Stilicho rose through the same army to become Theodosius I's magister militum. When Theodosius died in 395 he left the empire split between two young sons, and Stilicho became guardian and effective ruler of the western half under the boy emperor Honorius.

He spent the next decade fighting off the Visigoths under Alaric and other groups pressing into Italy and Gaul, winning at Pollentia in 402 and stripping troops from Britain and the Rhine frontier to do it. That gamble left those borders thin. In 408 Honorius's court, suspicious of his power and his barbarian blood, had Stilicho arrested and executed at Ravenna.

Stirrups developed in Asia centuries earlier than their spread into Europe, reaching Frankish territory gradually through contact with Avar and Byzantine horsemen rather than in a single dated introduction. By around 700 they were becoming common enough among Frankish cavalry to change how riders fought rather than merely how they mounted.

A rider braced in stirrups could deliver a lance thrust or a sword blow without being knocked from the saddle, which made a mounted charge a far more decisive weapon than earlier cavalry tactics allowed. Maintaining armoured horsemen was expensive, and the historian Lynn White argued the cost helped push Frankish society toward granting land in exchange for military service, an argument later historians have both built on and disputed.

On 10 August 1792, National Guard units and armed sections of Paris marched on the Tuileries Palace, where Louis XVI and his family had lived since being forced from Versailles. The king abandoned the palace for the nearby Legislative Assembly before the fighting started, leaving his Swiss Guard to defend an empty building.

The Swiss Guard resisted until a written order from Louis himself told them to stand down, but by then the crowd had already broken in, and several hundred guards were killed in the fighting and its aftermath. The Assembly suspended the king that same day. Six weeks later the monarchy was formally abolished, and Louis stood trial as a private citizen rather than a sovereign.

Fighting broke out in Khartoum on 15 April 2023 between the national army and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary built from the Janjaweed militias behind the Darfur killings two decades earlier. The two forces had jointly overthrown a civilian transitional government in 2021 but fell out over a plan to merge the RSF into the army; the immediate trigger was RSF troop movements the army treated as a threat.

Within days artillery and airstrikes had reduced parts of Khartoum to rubble, and the RSF seized Darfur, where United Nations investigators reported ethnically targeted killings echoing 2003. Millions fled into Chad, Egypt and South Sudan in what aid agencies called the world's largest displacement crisis, while army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo stayed in the field.

Egypt's President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956, after Britain and the United States withdrew funding for the Aswan Dam. Britain, France and Israel responded with a secret plan: Israel would invade Sinai, giving Britain and France a pretext to send troops in as peacekeepers and retake the canal by force. The invasion began that October and quickly succeeded militarily.

It collapsed diplomatically within days. President Eisenhower, angry at not being consulted, threatened to sell off British bonds, and the Soviet Union threatened intervention of its own. Britain and France withdrew under that pressure, and Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned in January 1957 with his health and his government's standing both broken.

Suharto's rise followed an attempted coup in October 1965 that killed six army generals, which he blamed on the Communist Party and used as justification for a campaign of mass killing that took an estimated 500,000 lives over the following months. He took over executive authority from Sukarno in March 1966 and was formally named president in March 1967, ending Sukarno's presidency without a vote.

He called his government the New Order, in deliberate contrast to Sukarno's rule, and built it on close ties with the military, foreign investment and strict limits on political dissent. It brought Indonesia three decades of rapid economic growth alongside heavy corruption and repression, and it lasted until mass protests during the 1997 Asian financial crisis forced his resignation in 1998.

The pledge was read out on 28 October 1928 at the close of the Second Indonesian Youth Congress in Batavia, a gathering of young delegates from organisations built along ethnic and island lines, Javanese, Sumatran, Ambonese and others, who had spent two days arguing over how a future Indonesia should hold together. The song Indonesia Raya was played publicly for the first time at the same congress.

The three lines bound the delegates to a single homeland, a single nation and a single tongue, deliberately choosing Malay, the trading language already spoken across the archipelago, over Javanese, the language of the largest ethnic group. That choice did more than any other clause to shape independence around a shared Indonesian identity rather than a Javanese one.

Gustavus Adolphus landed a Swedish army on the Baltic coast of Germany in 1630 to back the Protestant side in the Thirty Years' War, and by 1632 he had pushed deep into Catholic Bavaria. His infantry fought in thinner, more mobile lines than the deep blocks other armies used, and his artillery was light enough to move and reload faster than anyone else's on the field.

He was killed at the Battle of Lutzen in November 1632, reportedly shot from his horse while separated from his own men in fog and smoke. Sweden kept fighting for another sixteen years under other commanders, but never again had a monarch leading troops directly on a German battlefield.

Protests against Bashar al-Assad's government began in the southern city of Deraa in March 2011 after teenagers were arrested and tortured for painting anti-government graffiti. Security forces opened fire on demonstrators there and in other cities, and the crackdown pushed the opposition toward armed resistance within months.

The conflict drew in Hezbollah and Iranian forces backing Assad, a range of rebel and jihadist factions including the Islamic State, Kurdish militias, and eventually direct Russian and American military intervention. It displaced more than half of Syria's pre-war population before Assad's government finally fell to rebel forces in December 2024.

Hong Xiuquan, a failed civil service candidate who came to believe he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, launched an uprising against the Qing dynasty from Guangxi province in January 1851. His Taiping movement banned opium, foot binding and private land ownership, and by 1853 had captured Nanjing and made it their capital.

The war lasted fourteen years across central and southern China, fought with sieges, famine and reprisal killings on both sides. Conservative estimates put the dead at twenty to thirty million from combat, starvation and disease, with some historians arguing the true figure is far higher; either way it remains among the deadliest conflicts ever recorded. Qing forces, aided by foreign-officered units, retook Nanjing in 1864.

Three brothers from the village of Tay Son, Nguyen Nhac, Nguyen Lu and Nguyen Hue, rose against heavy taxation in 1771 and quickly gathered a peasant army in Vietnam's southern highlands. Within a decade their forces had toppled both the Nguyen lords ruling the south and the Trinh lords ruling the north.

Nguyen Hue, the most capable of the three, crowned himself Emperor Quang Trung and in 1789 routed an invading Qing army at Ngoc Hoi and Dong Da near Hanoi in a rapid winter campaign. The brothers' rule fractured after his early death in 1792, and by 1802 a surviving Nguyen prince, Nguyen Anh, had reunified Vietnam under a restored Nguyen dynasty.

Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin held their first meeting together in Tehran between 28 November and 1 December 1943, the only wartime summit all three attended. Stalin, wary of assassination, insisted on staying inside the grounds of the Soviet embassy, and Roosevelt accepted his invitation to lodge there rather than risk the drive across the city.

The three leaders committed to opening a second front in France the following year, the invasion that became D-Day, in exchange for Stalin's promise to launch a coordinated Soviet offensive in the east. They also began sketching Poland's postwar borders and discussed Stalin's pledge to enter the war against Japan once Germany was defeated.

North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launched coordinated attacks on more than 100 South Vietnamese cities and towns on 30 January 1968, timed to the Tet lunar new year holiday when many South Vietnamese soldiers were on leave. Fighters even breached the grounds of the American embassy in Saigon before being killed or repelled within hours.

American and South Vietnamese forces recaptured nearly every position within weeks, at a cost to attackers historians estimate in the tens of thousands killed. The offensive was a military defeat for Hanoi but a political shock in the United States, where officials had recently promised the war was nearly won, and the gap between that promise and the footage on American television eroded public support for the war.

Mexican forces under Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna besieged the Alamo mission in San Antonio for thirteen days before storming it before dawn on 6 March 1836. The roughly 200 defenders inside, including William Travis and Jim Bowie, were killed in the assault or shortly after; accounts of a handful of survivors and executions vary between Mexican and Texan sources.

Santa Anna's own report put his losses near 600, a figure later Mexican officers disputed as too high. Six weeks later Sam Houston's army surprised and defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto, reportedly shouting Remember the Alamo, and secured Texan independence within eighteen minutes of fighting.

Amanullah Khan, newly enthroned as Afghan emir after his father's assassination, ordered his forces across the border into British India in May 1919, calculating that Britain, exhausted by the First World War and facing unrest in Punjab, could not mount a serious response. Fighting was brief and inconclusive around the Khyber Pass and Waziristan through May and June.

The British used aircraft to bomb Kabul and Jalalabad, a shock that pushed Amanullah toward a truce that summer. The resulting 1919 Treaty of Rawalpindi ended British subsidies to Afghanistan but also dropped Britain's earlier control over Afghan foreign policy, letting Amanullah declare full independence and open direct relations with other states, including the new Soviet Union.

News that Saladin had retaken Jerusalem in 1187 drew three European monarchs into a new crusade launched in 1189: Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II of France and Richard I of England. Barbarossa drowned crossing a river in Anatolia before reaching the Holy Land, leaving Richard and Philip to lead the campaign that followed.

Richard and Saladin never met in person despite their reputations as rivals, negotiating instead through envoys and occasional truces. Richard's forces retook the coastal city of Acre and won a battle at Arsuf, but failed to retake Jerusalem itself. The two sides settled on a truce in 1192 letting Christian pilgrims visit the city while it stayed under Saladin's rule.

Carthage had rebuilt itself as a trading city with no real army by the time Rome picked a final quarrel in 149 BCE, demanding concessions steep enough that the Carthaginians chose to fight rather than accept them. The siege of the city itself lasted into 146 BCE, with house to house fighting recorded street by street in the final days.

Roman forces under Scipio Aemilianus burned what was left and, according to later writers, sold the surviving population into slavery. The claim that Rome salted the earth so nothing would grow there again comes from modern historians, not ancient sources, and is now generally treated as a myth rather than fact.

In May 1618, Protestant nobles in Prague threw two of the Habsburg emperor's councillors from a castle window into a moat, an act of defiance now called the Defenestration of Prague. It followed a dispute over the emperor's efforts to limit Protestant worship in Bohemia, and it turned a regional quarrel over religious rights into an open revolt against Habsburg rule.

The revolt drew in Spain, Denmark, Sweden and France in turn, each entering for its own mix of religious and territorial reasons, until fighting had spread across most of the Holy Roman Empire. Armies living off the land through repeated campaigning seasons brought famine and plague to large stretches of Germany, and estimates of the population lost by 1648 run into the millions.

Troops and tanks moved into central Beijing on the night of 3 to 4 June 1989 to clear student led protests that had occupied Tiananmen Square for seven weeks, and soldiers opened fire on unarmed civilians along the approach routes as well as in the square itself. China's government declared martial law and treated the crackdown as necessary to end what it called counter revolutionary turmoil.

China's official figure put the dead near 300, but a British diplomatic cable declassified decades later cited an internal Chinese estimate of at least 10,000, and independent researchers have suggested tolls in the low thousands. No full account has ever been published, discussion of the crackdown remains censored in China, and no government body has been held accountable for the killings.

The People's Liberation Army crossed into eastern Tibet in October 1950 with around 40,000 troops against a Tibetan force of a few thousand poorly equipped soldiers concentrated at Chamdo. The garrison fell within days, and its governor was captured after the town's radio operator sent a final message asking Lhasa for orders that never arrived in time.

With no realistic military option left, Tibetan representatives signed the Seventeen Point Agreement in Beijing in May 1951, which recognised Chinese sovereignty while nominally preserving Tibetan autonomy and the status of the Dalai Lama. Resistance continued in pockets for years, culminating in the 1959 uprising that sent the fourteenth Dalai Lama into exile in India.

Tikal had spent over a century under Calakmul's shadow, its own historical inscriptions falling silent for more than a hundred years after an earlier defeat. King Jasaw Chan Kʼawiil I, who took the throne in 682, rebuilt the city's strength and on 5 August 695 met Calakmul's ruler, Yikʼin Chan Kʼawiil's rival Yuknoom Yich'aak K'ahk', in open battle.

Tikal's warriors captured the enemy king's palanquin and its patron deity effigy, a defeat recorded in stone on Tikal's Temple I. Calakmul never fully recovered the regional dominance it had held for generations, and Tikal used the victory to rebuild its ceremonial core, including the pyramid where the triumph itself is commemorated.

Timur was born near Samarkand around 1336 and rose through Central Asian warlord politics rather than royal descent, marrying into the Mongol Chagatai line to claim legitimacy he did not have by blood. He never took the title of khan himself, ruling instead as an amir who governed through puppet rulers of Genghisid descent.

From the 1370s his armies moved through Persia, Mesopotamia and the Caucasus, and in 1398 sacked Delhi, reportedly leaving pyramids of skulls behind at captured cities as a deliberate warning to the next town on his route. He died in 1405 marching toward China, and the empire he built fragmented among his descendants within decades.

On the evening of 2 October 1968, thousands of students gathered in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas in Mexico City to protest government repression. Army units and a plainclothes unit called the Olympia Battalion surrounded the square and opened fire from the buildings around it. The government reported four dead; later investigations put the toll far higher, though an exact count was never fixed because bodies were removed overnight.

The killings came ten days before Mexico City hosted the 1968 Olympics, and the government suppressed reporting on them so the games could proceed on schedule. Documents declassified decades later showed the shooting had been planned rather than a response to student gunfire, contradicting the official account that stood for years.

The Tu'i Tonga dynasty ran a maritime network from Tongatapu that reached Samoa, Fiji, and Niue using double-hulled canoes capable of ocean voyages of several hundred kilometres. Tribute in mats, canoes, and food moved back toward the centre, and Tongan chiefs married into Fijian and Samoan lines to bind the outer islands in.

Oral genealogies name roughly two dozen Tu'i Tonga rulers across the period, though the dates before European contact rest on those genealogies rather than written record. By the fifteenth century the system had grown too large to govern from one office, and a second, more political title was created alongside the sacred Tu'i Tonga to run day to day affairs.

Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and treaties signed under pressure, the United States forced Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole nations from their homelands in the southeast to territory west of the Mississippi. The Cherokee removal of 1838 and 1839, carried out largely in winter under army escort after most refused to leave voluntarily, is the removal most often called the Trail of Tears.

Estimates of Cherokee deaths from the journey vary by source, from around 2,000 to as many as 8,000 of the roughly 16,000 people removed, killed by exposure, starvation and disease in camps and along the route. The land the nations left behind was opened to white settlement, much of it soon put to cotton grown with enslaved labour.

Delegates signed the treaty on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, the same room where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871. Germany was not permitted to negotiate the terms and was presented with the finished document to sign. It lost around thirteen percent of its territory, had its army capped at 100,000 men, and was assigned sole responsibility for the war under Article 231.

That article underpinned a reparations bill that was still being finalised into 1921 and eventually totalled 132 billion gold marks. Many Germans across the political spectrum viewed the treaty as a national humiliation, a grievance that Adolf Hitler exploited repeatedly over the following decade. The United States Senate never ratified it, and America made a separate peace with Germany in 1921.

Fighting broke out in 1627 between two families who both claimed loyalty to the same figurehead Le dynasty emperor while ruling their own halves of Vietnam. The Trinh held the Red River delta and Hanoi in the north; the Nguyen governed from Hue southward, and each hired European gunners, Dutch for the Trinh and Portuguese for the Nguyen, to cast cannon along a fortified border wall near modern Dong Hoi.

Neither side broke through in more than a century of intermittent war, and both used the peace to expand elsewhere: the Nguyen pushed south into former Champa and Khmer territory, giving Vietnam roughly the shape it has now. The division only ended in the 1770s, when a peasant rebellion toppled both ruling houses.

Leon Trotsky had survived one attack on his fortified villa in Coyoacan, Mexico, months earlier, machine gunned by a raiding party that missed him entirely. Ramon Mercader, a Spanish communist posing as a sympathiser under a false identity, had spent months courting Trotsky's staff and secretary to gain access to the house before he struck.

On 20 August 1940 Mercader entered Trotsky's study, pulled an ice axe from under his coat and struck him in the skull. Trotsky fought back and lived long enough to identify his attacker before dying the next day. Mercader served twenty years in a Mexican prison and was later awarded the Order of Lenin after moving to the Soviet Union.

The 1920 Treaty of Sevres had partitioned Ottoman Anatolia among Greece, Italy, France and Armenia, leaving the sultan's government in Constantinople to accept terms that many Turkish officers refused to recognise. Mustafa Kemal, a general who had defended Gallipoli in 1915, left for Anatolia in May 1919 and built a rival nationalist assembly and army at Ankara.

Greek forces advanced deep into Anatolia before Turkish troops halted and then broke them at the Battle of Dumlupinar in August 1922, driving the Greek army back to Smyrna within weeks. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne replaced Sevres and recognised the new borders. Mustafa Kemal abolished the sultanate that same year and took the name Ataturk in 1934.

Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Ulysses Grant at Wilmer McLean's house in Appomattox Court House, Virginia on 9 April 1865, after his exhausted force was surrounded with no route left to escape. Grant let Confederate soldiers keep their horses and sidearms and sent them home with rations rather than to prison camps.

Other Confederate armies held out for weeks after Appomattox, and the last significant force did not surrender until late May, so the war's actual end is a matter of which surrender is counted. Lincoln did not live to see any of it settled; he was shot five days after Lee's surrender and died the next morning.

On 7 August 1998, truck bombs exploded within minutes of each other outside the American embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam. The Nairobi blast collapsed a neighbouring building, and most of the dead were Kenyan bystanders and office workers rather than embassy staff. Osama bin Laden had declared a fatwa against American forces two years earlier; the attacks were al-Qaeda's first strike on two targets at once.

The FBI opened its first major overseas terrorism investigation, and the case put bin Laden on the agency's most wanted list before the September 2001 attacks. Four men were later convicted in a New York federal court and given life sentences. President Clinton ordered cruise missile strikes against a Sudanese factory and Afghan training camps within weeks, achieving little.

Woodrow Wilson had won re-election in 1916 partly on the slogan he kept us out of war. Germany's resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare in early 1917 sank American merchant ships, and British intelligence intercepted a telegram from foreign secretary Arthur Zimmermann proposing that Mexico recover Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined Germany against the United States.

Congress voted for war on 6 April 1917, with six senators and fifty representatives opposed. The regular US Army numbered barely 130,000 men at the time, and it took over a year to raise, train and ship a force large enough to matter on the Western Front, where the first sizeable American divisions did not fight until spring 1918.

The USS Pueblo, a lightly armed Navy intelligence-gathering ship, was surrounded by North Korean patrol boats off Wonsan on 23 January 1968. American accounts placed the ship in international waters; North Korea claimed otherwise. When the Pueblo tried to withdraw, the patrol boats opened fire, killing one sailor, and the crew scrambled to destroy classified equipment before the ship's commander, Lloyd Bucher, surrendered.

North Korea held the remaining 82 crewmen for eleven months, extracting a confession of spying under threat of torture while the men signalled their defiance by raising middle fingers in propaganda photographs, which their captors did not recognise. The United States issued a formal apology it later disavowed, and the crew walked across the Bridge of No Return into South Korea on 23 December 1968.

Washington's Continental Army withdrew to Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, in December 1777 after losing Philadelphia to the British. Roughly 12,000 troops built log huts on the frozen ground while supply failures left many without proper shoes, blankets or regular rations through the worst of the winter.

Disease and exposure killed an estimated 2,000 soldiers over the encampment, more than had died in that year's battles. A Prussian volunteer, Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben, arrived in February 1778 and drilled the survivors in European-style tactics and sanitation, and the army that marched out that June fought with a discipline it had lacked going in.

The Vandals, pushed out of Spain by rival Gothic forces, crossed the Strait of Gibraltar into Roman North Africa in 429 under their king Geiseric, reportedly at the invitation of a disgruntled Roman governor named Boniface. Roman Africa had few troops of its own to resist them, since its garrisons had long relied on the rest of the empire for reinforcement in a crisis.

Geiseric's army moved east along the coast, besieging cities as it went, and within a decade it had taken the region's richest province outright. Roman Africa's grain shipments had fed the city of Rome itself for centuries, so a Vandal kingdom sitting astride that supply line left the western empire's food security in the hands of a power it no longer controlled.

Geiseric took Carthage in 439 without a formal siege, entering the city during a public festival when much of its garrison and population were occupied elsewhere. It had been Rome's principal African city since Augustus refounded it on the ruins of Punic Carthage, and its harbour gave the Vandals a base for a fleet rather than just a foothold on land.

With Carthage in hand, Geiseric built ships and turned to raiding the Mediterranean's coasts and shipping lanes, a threat Rome's western government could no longer match at sea. That fleet later carried his forces to Rome itself in 455, and its reach forced the eastern empire into a costly, unsuccessful naval expedition against him in 468 before a peace was finally struck.

Vercingetorix was chief of the Arverni, one Gallic tribe among many that had fought each other as often as they fought Rome, and his achievement in 52 BC was persuading most of them to unite behind a single command. He avoided open battle where he could, burning Gallic farms and towns to starve Caesar's legions rather than risk his own army in the field, a strategy that nearly forced Caesar to withdraw from Gaul.

Vercingetorix gathered his forces inside the hilltop fortress of Alesia, where Caesar's engineers built a double ring of fortifications around the town, facing the defenders on one side and a huge Gallic relief army on the other. Both assaults on the Roman lines failed. Vercingetorix surrendered in person and was kept prisoner for six years before Caesar had him executed in Rome.

North Vietnamese tanks reached the gates of the presidential palace in Saigon on 30 April 1975, and South Vietnam's government surrendered hours later. The final American evacuation had run through the night before, with helicopters lifting staff and refugees off the embassy roof as the last US personnel left Vietnam.

Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City the following year, once the country was formally reunified under communist rule from Hanoi. The images of the embassy evacuation, thousands of Vietnamese trying to reach the last helicopters, became the lasting picture of a twenty year American commitment ending in withdrawal rather than victory.

American Marines waded ashore at Da Nang on 8 March 1965, the first US ground combat troops sent to South Vietnam rather than the advisers who had been there for years already. President Johnson authorised the landing after a Viet Cong attack on the American base at Pleiku that February, and after the Gulf of Tonkin resolution had given him broad authority the previous August.

The deployment grew fast: fewer than 25,000 American troops were in Vietnam at the start of 1965, and more than 180,000 were there by the year's end. Johnson had campaigned in 1964 promising not to send American boys to fight an Asian war, which made the scale of the escalation, once it began, difficult for his administration to explain to the public.

Norse raiders had been striking Irish monasteries for decades before 841, when they built a longphort, a fortified ship base, on the River Liffey where the Poddle stream joins it in a dark tidal pool the Irish called Dubh Linn. The site let ships be hauled ashore for repair and gave raiding parties a secure base for winter rather than a return voyage home.

What began as a seasonal camp grew into a permanent town with its own kings, minting coins by the late tenth century and trading slaves, silver and hides across a network reaching Iceland and the Volga. Dublin changed hands between Norse and Irish rulers repeatedly over the following centuries but never stopped being a port, and its street layout still traces the ninth century waterfront.

On 8 June 793, raiders arrived by longship at the monastery on Lindisfarne, an island off the Northumbrian coast reachable on foot only at low tide. They killed some monks, drove others out to drown, and made off with the monastery's treasures, leaving the buildings ransacked.

The scholar Alcuin, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote home in horror that nothing like it had been seen in Britain before and called it a judgement on the kingdom's sins. Lindisfarne was not the first Viking raid on record, a smaller strike on Portland had happened a few years earlier, but its wealth and its shock among literate churchmen made it the raid that later writers took as the start of the Viking Age.

A small fleet of Norse ships beached at Lindisfarne, off the Northumbrian coast, on 8 June 793, and its crews killed monks, took captives and looted the priory's silver. The monk Alcuin, then living at Charlemagne's court, wrote to the Northumbrian king that he had never before seen such an attack made from the sea, nor imagined a place so holy could be violated.

Lindisfarne held relics of Saint Cuthbert and was among the wealthiest and least defended religious sites in Britain, which made it an obvious first target rather than a random one. Raids on Iona and other coastal monasteries followed within a few years, opening roughly two and a half centuries during which Norse fleets raided, traded and eventually settled across much of Britain, Ireland and beyond.

Fifteen Nazi officials met at a lakeside villa in Berlin's Wannsee district on 20 January 1942, convened by Reinhard Heydrich of the Reich Security Main Office. Adolf Eichmann, who organised the deportation of Jews across occupied Europe, was among those present. The meeting did not decide whether mass murder would happen; that decision had already been made higher up.

Its purpose was logistics: coordinating the ministries, railways and occupation administrations needed to deport Jews from across Europe to killing centres in the east. The single surviving copy of the minutes, discovered after the war, describes this in bureaucratic euphemism, final solution and evacuation to the east, rather than naming murder outright.

France's Legislative Assembly voted to declare war on Austria on 20 April 1792, egged on by Girondin politicians who believed a foreign war would expose royalist traitors and rally the nation behind the revolution. Austria's emperor was the brother of Queen Marie Antoinette, giving the declaration a personal edge at court.

The war went badly at first, with poorly organised French armies retreating before Austrian and, soon, Prussian forces advancing on Paris. Volunteers rallied at Valmy that September to stop the invasion, and the conflict that began with this single declaration widened over the next twenty three years into a near continuous set of European wars.

For years the Royal Navy stopped American ships at sea and forced sailors it claimed were British deserters into service, a grievance Congress cited alongside British support for Native resistance in the northwest when it voted for war on 18 June 1812, the closest war vote in American history. Britain had already agreed to suspend those restrictions, but news had not yet crossed the Atlantic.

British troops burned Washington, including the President's House, in August 1814 in retaliation for earlier American raids in Canada. Weeks later, Francis Scott Key watched an all night British bombardment of Fort McHenry in Baltimore harbour and wrote the verses that became The Star Spangled Banner after seeing the American flag still flying at dawn. The war ended in a treaty that changed no borders.

Charles VI of Austria had spent years securing other rulers' agreement that his daughter Maria Theresa could inherit the Habsburg lands intact, only for Frederick II of Prussia to invade the rich province of Silesia within weeks of Charles's death in October 1740. Bavaria and France then backed rival claims to the throne, treating the agreement as worthless the moment it was tested.

Maria Theresa, twenty three and newly in charge of an empire under attack on several fronts, rallied support from Hungary and eventually Britain, which feared French gains on the continent. The war spread to colonies in North America and India and lasted eight years, ending in 1748 with her succession confirmed but Silesia lost to Prussia for good.

Robert Jenkins, master of the brig Rebecca, said Spanish coastguards boarded his ship off Cuba in 1731 and cut off his ear while accusing him of smuggling. The story resurfaced in 1738 when Jenkins was said to have shown Parliament a pickled ear as proof of Spanish abuses against British shipping in the Caribbean, though there is no solid record he actually appeared before the Commons to display it.

Opposition politicians seized on the tale to push a reluctant government toward war, and Britain declared it on Spain on 19 October 1739. The fighting produced little beyond a failed British assault on Cartagena and a costly siege of Havana, and by 1742 it had merged into the wider War of the Austrian Succession, its original grievance long since forgotten.

Charles II of Spain, the last Habsburg king there, died in November 1700 leaving no children and a will naming Louis XIV's grandson Philip of Anjou as his heir. Accepting the will meant a Bourbon on the Spanish throne alongside the one already in France, and within months England, the Dutch Republic and the Holy Roman Emperor formed an alliance to stop the two crowns from ever uniting.

War followed across Europe and its colonies, fought by commanders including the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy, and it lasted until 1714. The peace at Utrecht let Philip keep Spain on condition he renounce any claim to the French throne, while Britain gained Gibraltar and Minorca, marking its arrival as a leading power in continental affairs.

A Chilean mining company's dispute over an export tax on nitrate deposits in Bolivia's Atacama coast escalated into war in 1879, drawing in Peru under a defence pact it had signed with Bolivia years earlier. Chile's navy, built up in the previous decade, gave it control of the sea lanes early and let it land troops wherever it chose along the coast.

Chilean forces took Antofagasta, then pushed north through Tacna, Arica and eventually occupied Lima itself before peace treaties in 1883 and 1884 confirmed Chile's gains. Bolivia lost its entire Pacific coastline and has been landlocked ever since, while Peru ceded the nitrate-rich Tarapaca province and, for a time, Tacna and Arica.

Fighting between French Catholics and Protestant Huguenots broke out in 1562 and returned in waves for the next thirty six years, punctuated by short-lived peace edicts that neither side observed for long. Massacres such as the killing of thousands of Huguenots in Paris and other cities in 1572 sat alongside pitched battles and long sieges.

Historians' estimates of the total dead, including those lost to famine and disease the fighting caused, range into the low millions out of a population of some sixteen to eighteen million, though the higher figures are difficult to verify. The wars ended only when Henry IV, a former Huguenot turned Catholic, issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, granting Protestants limited toleration.

Fighting broke out in 1455 at St Albans between supporters of the House of Lancaster, holding the crown under the ineffective Henry VI, and the House of York under Richard, Duke of York, who claimed a better right to the throne through an older line of descent from Edward III. The name came later, from the white rose associated with York and the red rose later attached to Lancaster.

Over the next three decades the crown changed hands repeatedly among rival cousins, with major battles at Towton, Barnet and Tewkesbury killing thousands of the nobility who led the opposing retinues. The conflict only settled when Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth in 1485 and married a Yorkist heir, folding both rival lines into the new Tudor dynasty.

When German forces entered the Warsaw ghetto on 19 April 1943 to resume deportations to Treblinka, fighters of the Jewish Combat Organisation and the Jewish Military Union met them with smuggled pistols, grenades and petrol bombs. It was the largest single act of Jewish armed resistance during the Holocaust, and the fighters knew from the start that they could not win.

SS General Jurgen Stroop's troops burned the ghetto block by block to force people out of hiding, and organised resistance collapsed by mid May after roughly a month of fighting. Most of the surviving fighters and remaining inhabitants were killed or deported to camps; a small number escaped through the sewers to join partisans outside the city.

When the Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in June 1775, fighting had already broken out at Lexington and Concord and militia were besieging British troops in Boston. Congress needed a single commander to unify the colonial forces and, on 15 June, chose George Washington, a Virginia planter with militia experience from the French and Indian War.

Washington accepted no salary for the post, asking only for his expenses. He rode north to take command of the assembled militia outside Boston, where he found a force short of gunpowder, discipline and any shared chain of command, and spent his first months simply organising it into something resembling an army.

Nixon resigned on 8 August 1974, the only US president to leave office before his term ended. The scandal began two years earlier with a break in at the Democratic National Committee's offices in the Watergate complex, but it was the White House tapes, and Nixon's own recorded efforts to obstruct the investigation, that destroyed his support in Congress.

The House Judiciary Committee had already voted to recommend impeachment on obstruction of justice and abuse of power when Republican senators told Nixon his conviction in the Senate was certain. He announced his resignation on television the evening before it took effect, and Gerald Ford, who had never run on a national ticket, was sworn in the next morning.

On 29 December 1890, the US 7th Cavalry moved to disarm a band of Lakota Sioux camped at Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota, many of them followers of the Ghost Dance movement that promised the return of the buffalo and the dead. A struggle over a deaf man's rifle during the disarming set off gunfire at close range, and troops then opened fire with Hotchkiss guns on the camp.

Roughly 250 to 300 Lakota were killed, including many women and children shot as they fled, against 25 army dead, some from their own crossfire. Survivors were left in the winter cold for days before burial in a mass grave. The killing at Wounded Knee is generally treated as the last major armed clash of the Indian Wars on the northern plains.

German officials met Allied representatives in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiegne, France, and signed an armistice at 5am on 11 November 1918. The fighting stopped six hours later, at eleven o'clock, a timing chosen for its symmetry rather than any military need. Germany's army was retreating but had not been invaded, a fact that fed later claims the country had been betrayed rather than beaten.

The armistice was a ceasefire, not a peace: the legal end of the war came only with the Treaty of Versailles the following June. Roughly nine million soldiers and a comparable number of civilians had died since 1914. Marshal Ferdinand Foch, who signed for the Allies, is said to have remarked that the settlement was not peace but a twenty year truce, a prediction that came close to the mark.

A Bosnian Serb nationalist, Gavrilo Princip, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, on a day when the couple's car had already survived one bomb attack and then took a wrong turn back into Princip's path. Austria-Hungary used the assassination as grounds to issue Serbia a deliberately harsh ultimatum.

A chain of alliances turned a Balkan dispute into a continental war within five weeks: Russia mobilised to back Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and German troops crossed into Belgium, which brought Britain in on 4 August. Few of the governments involved expected the war to last past Christmas.

Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender in a radio broadcast on 15 August 1945, telling a population that had never before heard his voice that the war situation had developed not necessarily to Japan's advantage, a deliberate understatement covering two atomic bombings and a Soviet invasion of Manchuria launched days earlier. The formal instrument of surrender was signed aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September.

General Douglas MacArthur accepted the surrender on behalf of the Allies and went on to oversee Japan's postwar occupation. The ceremony closed a war that, across all theatres and by widely varying estimates, killed between 60 and 80 million people, more than any conflict in recorded history.

German representatives signed an unconditional surrender at Reims on 7 May 1945, and a further ceremony took place in Berlin the following day at Soviet insistence, which is why Western Europe marks Victory in Europe Day on 8 May while Russia marks it on 9 May. Hitler had killed himself in his Berlin bunker a week earlier, on 30 April, as Soviet troops fought through the city above him.

Crowds filled the streets of London, Paris, Moscow and New York, though the war itself was not over: fighting continued against Japan in the Pacific for another three months. Churchill broadcast to Britain that afternoon, and King George VI appeared with his family on the Buckingham Palace balcony to acknowledge crowds still gathering below.

German forces crossed into Poland before dawn on 1 September 1939, following a staged border incident that gave Hitler a pretext already prepared regardless of what happened. Poland's air force and much of its army were destroyed within days by an assault combining fast moving armour with air support, a method soon labelled blitzkrieg by foreign journalists rather than by the Germans themselves.

Britain and France had guaranteed Polish independence and declared war on Germany on 3 September, though neither launched an attack that could have relieved Poland in time. The Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September under the terms of its secret pact with Germany, and Poland was partitioned between the two within the month. The war that followed killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people worldwide.

When the Han dynasty was founded around 200 BC, its first emperor, Liu Bang, marched north against Xiongnu raids and was trapped by their cavalry at Baideng for several days before escaping through negotiation. Rather than fight a steppe power the young dynasty could not match, Han rulers adopted a policy called heqin, sending grain, silk and imperial princesses to Xiongnu leaders in exchange for peace.

That arrangement held, unevenly, for decades while Han armies rebuilt their cavalry and finances. It broke down under Emperor Wu, who from the 130s BC abandoned tribute for open war, sending expeditions deep into Xiongnu territory. The fighting that followed lasted generations and pushed Han authority as far as the Tarim Basin, reshaping routes that carried goods toward the Silk Road.

Commodus's murder in 192 left the throne open, and the Praetorian Guard sold it outright to Didius Julianus, who outbid a rival senator at an auction inside the camp itself. Roman legions on the frontiers, unwilling to accept a throne bought rather than earned, put forward their own candidates: Pescennius Niger in Syria, Clodius Albinus in Britain, and Septimius Severus, commanding the Danube legions.

Severus moved fastest, marched on Rome, had the Guard disbanded and Julianus executed within weeks, then spent the following years defeating Niger and finally Albinus in Gaul. His victory installed a new dynasty and made plain what the Year of the Four Emperors had already suggested a century earlier, that whichever army reached Rome first, rather than the Senate, now decided who wore the purple.

Galba, the first man proclaimed emperor after Nero's death in 68, lasted barely seven months before his own guard murdered him in the Forum and handed power to Otho. Otho held it for three months before losing a battle to the legions of Vitellius, a general acclaimed by the armies stationed along the Rhine.

Vitellius himself was overthrown within the year by forces loyal to Vespasian, a commander fighting the Jewish revolt in Judea, whose troops in Egypt and the eastern provinces declared him emperor instead. Vespasian's arrival in Rome in 69 ended the cycle and founded the Flavian dynasty, but the year had shown that armies far from the capital could now make and break emperors on their own authority.

Famine, flooding of the Yellow River and years of official corruption had left much of eastern China's peasantry destitute by 184, when a Daoist sect led by three brothers named Zhang rose up wearing yellow cloth wrapped around their heads. Their leader Zhang Jue preached healing and an approaching age of peace, and hundreds of thousands reportedly joined him within months across several provinces.

The Han court crushed the main rebel armies within a year, but only by handing military authority to regional generals and warlords who never fully gave it back afterward. Those men, including Yuan Shao, Cao Cao and Sun Jian's family, became the rival power bases that carved China into competing states once the dynasty they had nominally served finally gave out.

On 6 October 1973, Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal and Syrian tanks pushed into the Golan Heights while much of Israel's reserve army was at home for Yom Kippur. The timing gave Egypt's crossing early success, and Israeli lines on the Golan nearly broke before reserves mobilised.

Israel reversed both fronts within three weeks, crossing the canal into Egypt and driving Syrian forces back before a ceasefire took hold on 22 October. The war's aftermath mattered more than its battles: Egypt's initial crossing gave Anwar Sadat the political standing to negotiate directly with Israel, leading to the Camp David talks and a peace treaty by 1979.

Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, and within days the Yugoslav People's Army moved to stop them. The fighting in Slovenia lasted barely ten days, but Croatia's war ran for years and drew in Serb militias defending communities that did not want to leave a Serb-led Yugoslavia.

The breakup exposed how mixed the federation's borders had never matched its peoples. Bosnia and Herzegovina, the most ethnically intermixed republic, would be pulled into the same logic within a year, and the fighting that began outside Ljubljana and Zagreb in 1991 set the pattern for the far longer war that followed there.

Field Marshal John Okello led a few hundred armed followers against the Sultan's police armoury on the night of 11 to 12 January 1964, seizing weapons and broadcasting the revolution's declaration from the radio station before dawn. The Sultan, Jamshid bin Abdullah, fled by yacht within hours, ending an Arab dynasty that had ruled Zanzibar since the 1800s.

The days that followed saw organised killing of Zanzibar's Arab minority, whom the revolutionaries associated with the old order; estimates of the dead range from a few hundred to figures in the thousands, and the true toll has never been settled. Abeid Karume became president of the new republic, which merged with mainland Tanganyika later that year to form Tanzania.

Shaka, who took the Zulu throne around 1816, insisted his warriors train with a shortened stabbing spear called the iklwa, named for the sound it made being pulled from a wound, rather than the traditional long throwing spear that left a fighter unarmed after one cast. He did not invent the weapon, but he made its use compulsory.

Shaka reorganised his fighters into amabutho, age-based regiments housed in dedicated barracks and marked by distinct shields and dress, which let him mobilise and command far larger forces than neighbouring chiefdoms. Warriors were also drilled to fight barefoot at speed, using encircling tactics that let smaller Zulu forces overwhelm rivals still fighting in loose bands.

British forces invaded Zululand in January 1879 after issuing King Cetshwayo an ultimatum to dismantle his kingdom's military system, which he had no intention of meeting. At Isandlwana on 22 January a Zulu army of more than 20,000 overran a British camp of under 2,000, one of the worst defeats the British army suffered against a non-industrial force in the whole colonial era.

That same afternoon a smaller Zulu column attacked the supply post at Rorke's Drift, defended by fewer than 150 men under warning from Isandlwana's survivors. The garrison held through the night, and eleven Victoria Crosses were later awarded there, a contrast Britain publicised heavily to soften the humiliation of Isandlwana before the war ended in Zulu defeat that July.
